sens: theft with violence or fraud
stolen or pillaged goods
unjust act of exploitation
H1500.detail:
1. Plunder is theft accompanied by force or cunning: taking what belongs to someone by stripping them of it. In Ezekiel 18:7, the righteous man "does not commit plunder," meaning he does not steal from others, even if he has the power or opportunity to do so.
2. The word also refers to the goods themselves that have been stolen or pillaged, the spoils. Isaiah 3:14 states that "the spoils of the poor are in [the] houses" of the leaders who have stolen them unjustly.
3. More broadly, it encompasses any act of exploitation or oppression, any unjust appropriation of another's property. One who "commits plunder" (Ezekiel 18:12) acts against justice, abusing his strength or authority to enrich himself at the expense of the weak.
H1500.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to tear away" or "to remove." It describes the action of taking by force, hence the idea of spoils or violent theft. In Hebrew, the same lexical field includes verbs and nouns related to the idea of taking away or stealing.
H1500.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the writings of the prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel. In Leviticus 5:23, it refers to restoring what has been stolen or withheld by fraud. In Ezekiel (18:7, 18:12, 18:16, 33:15), the word appears in lists of just or unjust acts: one who does not "commit" plunder is righteous, while one who does is guilty. Isaiah uses it to denounce the systematic theft of the poor by the powerful. The meaning remains constant: the unjust appropriation of another's property.
H1500.portee: God firmly condemns plunder. The Bible does not tolerate stealing or exploiting the weak, even legally or under the guise of authority. For the Christian, this word serves as a reminder that justice begins with respect for the property of others and honesty: it is a fundamental moral requirement at the heart of the fear of God.

sens: type of devastating grasshopper or cricket
insect that ravages crops and vegetation
symbol of divine judgment and punishment
H1501.detail:
1. The locust is a variety of grasshopper or cricket, an insect that devours vegetation. In Joel 1:4, it is listed among other types of locusts (jélek, hasil) that succeed one another to consume the harvests: "What the locust has left, the grasshopper has eaten."

2. This insect represents a formidable agricultural calamity that destroys crops and fruit trees. Amos 4:9 describes how gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees "have been devoured by locusts" (including the locust), showing the extent of the devastation.

3. In the biblical prophetic vision, the locust and other types of locusts symbolize God's judgment sent against His unfaithful people. In Joel 2:25, the Lord speaks of "My great army that I sent against you," identifying these insects as a divine army of punishment.
H1501.origine: The Hebrew word locust comes from a root that evokes the idea of cutting or slicing, as these insects gnaw and shred the plants in their path. It belongs to a family of words designating various types of locusts and grasshoppers in Hebrew (arbé, jélek, hasil), each possibly at a different stage of development or a slightly different species.
H1501.emploi: The locust appears three times in the Old Testament, all in the minor prophets (Joel and Amos) in the 8th-9th century BC. In Joel 1:4 and 2:25, it is included in a list of four types of locusts that devastate the land, symbolizing a progressive and total punishment. In Amos 4:9, it is part of a series of plagues (rust, mildew, locusts) that God sends to call the people to repentance, but they refuse to return to God.
H1501.portee: The locust reminds the Christian that God can use the forces of nature to correct His people and call them to conversion. The text also shows that a series of judgments, even terrible ones, is not always sufficient: what matters is the reaction of the heart. For the modern reader, this insect illustrates the fragility of harvests and the importance of depending on divine providence rather than solely on one's riches.

sens: Head of a family of temple servants returning from exile
H1502.detail: Gazzam is the name of a man who lived during the time of the exile and the return from Babylon. He is mentioned as the head of a family of temple servants (the "sons of Gazzam") who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, the governor appointed by the Persians to rebuild Jerusalem and its temple. These temple servants formed a distinct group: neither priests nor Levites, but auxiliaries attached to the service of the sanctuary. This family is listed twice in the records of the exiles who returned (Ezra 2:48 and Nehemiah 7:51), demonstrating its importance and stability among the families rebuilding the Jewish community.
H1502.origine: The name Gazzam literally means "the devourer" or "consuming," coming from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of consuming or engulfing. This type of name was common in ancient Israel: it reflected a characteristic, an action, or a parental aspiration. Here, the exact meaning given to the child eludes us—perhaps a quality noticed in the newborn, or a family wish.
H1502.emploi: Gazzam appears only in the lists of families returned from Babylonian captivity during the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra. He is cited in the register of Ezra 2 and in the parallel of Nehemiah 7, both enumerating the families of Israel that returned to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and the city. This presence in two independent sources confirms his historical role as an officially recognized family head at the time of the return.

sens: main part of a tree, between the roots and the branches
what remains of a cut down or dead tree
lineage, descent of a family
H1503.detail:
1. The stump is the solid and central part of a tree, the one that supports the branches and rests on the roots. It is the living heart of the tree, its woody skeleton. In Job 14:8, a stump is described that ages in the ground and dies in the dust: the image shows the tree degrading over time.
2. The stump also refers to what remains when the tree is cut down or dried up. In Isaiah 40:24, idols and kings of the world are like plants whose stump does not even have roots: an image of radical fragility, as if the base is missing.
3. Figuratively, the stump becomes an image of lineage or descent: it is what future generations come from, like the branches of the stump. In Isaiah 11:1, a shoot will come forth from the stump of Jesse, meaning a descendant will be born from this family. The Messiah will emerge from the lineage of Jesse, whose reign seems to be over.
H1503.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of cutting or slicing, related to what is cut or separated from the rest. The stump is literally what remains when the rest (branches, leaves) disappears or is removed. The same root appears in other words designating distinct portions or parts.
H1503.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in poetic or prophetic texts. In Job 14:8, it describes the progressive death of a tree, an image of human fragility in the face of time. In Isaiah 40:24, it illustrates the impotence of earthly idols. In Isaiah 11:1, the richest passage, it becomes a messianic image: from the stump of Jesse, supposedly politically dead after the fall of the kingdom of Judah, the Messiah will emerge. This indicates that hope does not die, even when everything seems lost.
H1503.portee: This word reminds the believer that God works through generations, even when the future seems blocked or the present disastrous. The stump in Isaiah 11:1 speaks to those going through trials: new life can spring from ruins, fresh hope can emerge from dead wood. It is a promise that God never gives up on His descendants and His plans.

sens: To divide or separate into two or more parts
To fell, remove by cutting
To cut off, eliminate, completely destroy
To put an end to, interrupt
To decree, decide in a definitive manner
H1504.detail:
1. To divide or separate into two or more parts: this is the most concrete and direct meaning of the verb. King Solomon says, "Cut the living child in two" (1 Kings 3:25) to test which of the two women is the true mother.

2. To fell, remove by cutting: one "cuts" wood at the Jordan (2 Kings 6:4), meaning trees are felled. This meaning remains very physical.

3. To cut off, eliminate, completely destroy: when the psalmist says, "I am lost" (Lamentations 3:54), he describes his state as if the waters that overwhelmed him had cut him off from life. It is a destruction, a definitive separation from the world of the living.

4. To put an end to, interrupt: the psalm mentions those "separated from your hand" (Psalms 88:6), meaning cut off from the relationship with God. The link is severed.

5. To decree, decide in a definitive manner: "the decision that had been made regarding her" about Queen Vashti (Esther 2:1): this is no longer a physical action, but a word that cuts and irrevocably establishes the king's will.
H1504.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a primitive root expressing the act of cutting. Its basic image is that of the gesture that divides: one separates, one detaches. In biblical Hebrew, the word can also mean "to decree" because a royal decision, once pronounced, "cuts" the situation in the same way a blade cuts: it is definitive, irrevocable. The family of the word includes nouns designating the "cut" or the "portion" obtained after division.
H1504.emploi: The verb gazar appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in historical narratives and psalms. Its uses show a gradual transition from the physical and concrete meaning to the figurative and decisional meaning. Literally, one cuts wood (2 Kings 6:4) or a child (1 Kings 3:25). Figuratively, one is "cut off" from God or from life (Psalms 88:6, Lamentations 3:54), "separated" by illness (2 Chronicles 26:21). And in the fully abstract sense, one "decides" or "decrees" (Esther 2:1, Job 22:28). The context determines which of these meanings prevails: material or spiritual, visible or invisible.
H1504.portee: This word enriches our understanding of God's word as sharp and definitive: it decides, it separates, it does not return. It also reminds us that God can "cut us off" if we turn away from Him, but also that His will is irrevocable and fixes our destiny. For the believer, it is an invitation to take God's decisions seriously and not treat them as provisional.

sens: One who claims to know the future or hidden secrets
One who interprets dreams and signs
One who is separated or set apart for this function
H1505.detail: 1. A diviner is a person who claims to have the power to discover what is hidden or to know what is to come: in Daniel 2:27, Daniel tells the king that the diviners cannot uncover the secret the king is asking for. 2. The term particularly designates one who interprets dreams and mysterious visions: in Daniel 4:7, King Nebuchadnezzar calls the diviners to explain his dream, as he does in Daniel 5:7. 3. The word also evokes the idea of someone who is separated or cut out from the ordinary mass for this specialized practice, like a detached stone (same root): it is a man set apart for this function, at the king's court.
H1505.origine: The word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to cut" or "to sever" (hence "detached" in Daniel 2:34 for the stone that is cut out from the mountain). A diviner is thus originally one who "cuts" or "separates" secrets, one who isolates the hidden meaning of things. This image of separation or distinction is at the heart of the meaning: the diviner is one who separates the true meaning from the apparent meaning, the future from present ignorance.
H1505.emploi: The word appears six times in the book of Daniel, always in the plural in a Babylonian context. Each time, it designates a category of scholars at the royal court, classified alongside magicians, astrologers, and Chaldeans. In Daniel 2:27 and 4:7, the diviners fail to provide the requested explanation: they are unable to uncover divine secrets. In Daniel 5:7 and 5:11, they are listed among the wise men of the kingdom, but without success. Daniel himself, although established as chief of these diviners (Daniel 5:11), receives his wisdom from God alone, highlighting the contrast between false human wisdom and true divine knowledge.
H1505.portee: This word shows that human claims to discover the future or secrets without God are vain. The Babylonian diviners, with all their reputation and rank, remain powerless before what God alone can reveal. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that true wisdom and true knowledge of what is to come come from God alone, not from human practices or supposed occult sciences.

sens: Part of an animal separated from the others during a sacrifice or partition
Division of a reality into two distinct elements
H1506.detail:
1. In the account of the covenant in Genesis 15, God asks Abraham to bring animals and cut them in pieces: the word designates each part of the animal cut in two. This is a ritual practice where the pieces of sacrificed animals solemnly marked a commitment. Abraham then sees the divine flames passing between these pieces, confirming the covenant (Genesis 15:17).
2. By extension of the meaning of "division," the word can also refer to a separation, a clear cut in two. In Psalm 136:13, when celebrating the one who "cut the Red Sea in two," the word evokes this spectacular partition of the waters, which God parts to let His people pass.
H1506.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to cut" or "to divide." It expresses the action of slicing, separating into fragments. Words of the same family all speak of cutting and division: it is the fundamental image of sharing into distinct pieces.
H1506.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Genesis 15:17, it designates the pieces of animals shared during the covenant ceremony between God and Abraham—a ritual where the separation of the beasts into two parts symbolizes solemn commitment. In Psalm 136:13, it evokes the division of the waters of the Red Sea, a spectacular image of the miracle of the Exodus. In both cases, the word carries the idea of a clear and significant separation.
H1506.portee: This word reminds us that biblical covenants were based on visible and concrete gestures: for Abraham, seeing the separated pieces and the divine fire passing between them made the divine commitment tangible and unforgettable. Likewise, the Red Sea "cut in two" shows how God acts radically, creating divisions that are impossible naturally to save His people. It is an invitation to recognize the powerful and concrete acts of God in history.

sens: Fortified city in the land of Canaan, located at the border of Ephraim
Levitical city assigned to the priests descended from Aaron
Military and political stake in the hands of successive kings
H1507.detail: Gezer is an important city of ancient Canaan, situated on the edge of the territory of Ephraim, between the coastal region and the inland. It is among the cities conquered by Joshua during the entry into Canaan (Joshua 10:33). Later, it is assigned to the Levites, priests and servants of the temple, as indicated in Joshua 21:21 and 1 Chronicles 6:67 — a city of refuge where unintentional murderers found protection. Gezer also holds great strategic importance: David recaptures it from the Philistines (2 Samuel 5:25), and Solomon fortifies it as one of his major strongholds (1 Kings 9:15-17). The Pharaoh of Egypt had taken possession of it, burned it, and massacred its inhabitants before giving it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife (1 Kings 9:16).
H1507.origine: The name Gezer comes from the Hebrew gezer, which literally means "portion" or "part." This term evokes the idea of land that is cut, divided, or allocated. The underlying root suggests a delineated city, marking a boundary or a well-defined portion of territory in the landscape of Canaan.
H1507.emploi: Gezer appears 14 times in the historical books of the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Joshua, Kings, and Chronicles. It is first a fortified Canaanite city that Joshua must conquer (Joshua 10:33 and 12:12). It then becomes a Levitical city, part of the system of allocating cities to the priests (Joshua 21:21, 1 Chronicles 6:67). In the time of the kings, it acquires major strategic status: David recaptures it from the Philistines, and Solomon makes it a key fortified center of his kingdom (1 Kings 9:15-17). The context changes according to the periods — conquest, religious administration, then royal military defense — but the city remains consistently a territorial and political stronghold.
H1507.portee: Gezer embodies the vicissitudes of God's people in the promised land: from the initial conquest to the religious organization of communal life, then to the consolidation of royal power. Its history reminds us that faith is not limited to the spiritual realm, but is expressed in the concrete management of territory, justice (through cities of refuge), and political strength. It also shows how God directs military and political events for the benefit of His people.

sens: space that separates, free space
distinct part of an architectural ensemble
H1508.detail:
1. The word designates a space that separates two things or that is clear, free. It conveys the idea of something cut off, separated from other parts. In Lamentations 4:7, the word translated as "figure" (the visible aspect of a person) refers to what distinguishes it, what "separates" it in some way from others.
2. In Ezekiel's visions of the temple, this word designates a courtyard or an empty space, a distinct area enclosed by walls and separating the different buildings of the sanctuary. It is a well-defined place, measured by the prophet: it is one hundred cubits long and is surrounded by galleries and chambers (Ezekiel 41:12-15).
H1508.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to cut, to slice." It designates what is cut, separated, distinct. The same Hebrew root appears in other words of the family that express the idea of cutting or separation. The basic image is that of a clear separation, like what is obtained by slicing.
H1508.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Bible, concentrated in two very different contexts. Once in Lamentations (4:7) where it designates the figure, the appearance of a person. But the majority of the uses are found in Ezekiel 41-42, where the prophet receives a detailed vision of the future temple: the word there always designates a courtyard or an empty space, an architecturally important area, measured and delineated. It is a technical term in the description of the sacred building, which recurs several times to locate the different parts of the sanctuary.
H1508.portee: This word reminds us that in the house of God, every space has its place and function. The empty spaces and separations of the temple are not voids: they are measured, organized, significant in the divine plan. For the reader, this invites us to see that order and distinction are marks of God's sanctuary.

sens: A separated, isolated, desert place
A place emptied of all human life
A place of abandonment and desolation
H1509.detail:
1. This word designates a place removed and separated from the inhabited world, a secluded spot where no one can be found — it is an abandoned land, far from any human presence. In the ritual of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:22), the goat bearing the sins of Israel is sent into this "desolate land," a place of isolation that symbolizes the removal of evil from the reconciled people.
2. This word also describes the state of the land itself: a desert, a region where solitude and absence of life reign. It is an emptied space, separated, a no man's land where no communion exists among the inhabitants.
3. Finally, the word evokes spiritual desolation and punishment: the desolate land is where one is banished, where one is rejected, far from the sanctuary and the people of God. It embodies the distance from salvation and the rupture with the community.
H1509.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to cut," "to separate," "to divide." The noun gezerah thus designates first what is separated, hence the idea of a region cut off from the rest, isolated, uninhabitable. The notion of separation naturally produces that of desolation and abandonment.
H1509.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 16:22, in the context of the atonement ritual of the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur). The "scapegoat" or sin offering was symbolically charged with all the sins of the children of Israel and was then led into a desolate land — the desert — so that the evil would be taken far from the community. This isolated place thus embodies the total rejection of sin and its radical removal from the people and the sanctuary.
H1509.portee: This word reminds us that sin cannot remain within the people of God: it must be entirely separated, rejected, sent far into a spiritual desert. For the Christian, this foreshadows the cross of Christ, who bore our sins and took them far away, thus making us pure and reconciled. Understanding this radical separation from evil helps us grasp the depth of forgiveness and the holiness required to approach God.

sens: An official and solemn decision, stated with authority
A command that imposes itself and necessarily comes to pass
H1510.detail: 1. A decree is a decision promulgated by someone in authority — a king, celestial powers — to determine what must be done. In Daniel 4:17, it is a "sentence" that the celestial beings "who watch" pronounce concerning the affairs of the human kingdom: this term evokes a judgment that is weighed, considered, and irrevocable. 2. However, the word also carries the idea of a word that comes to pass, that creates a reality. When speaking of the "decree of the Most High" (Daniel 4:24), it is not a mere suggestion: it is a will that will necessarily be fulfilled, like a word from God that does not return void.
H1510.origine: The Aramaic word גְּזֵרָה comes from the root גזר (gazar), which means "to cut" or "to decide." This image of cutting expresses the idea of a decisive decision, which cuts short any hesitation: one cuts, one decides, and it is final. The root is common to both Hebrew and Aramaic, and the word decree naturally comes from this idea of a cut that separates doubt from certainty.
H1510.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the same chapter of the book of Daniel (4:17 and 4:24), during the interpretation of King Nebuchadnezzar's dream. In the context of the prophetic dream, the word first designates a "sentence" pronounced by celestial beings concerning the king's destiny — not a mere prediction, but a cosmic decision that must be fulfilled. Then, Daniel applies this same term to the judgment of the Most High Himself, emphasizing that the divine decree is never a vague threat, but a word that will infallibly be executed.
H1510.portee: For the believing reader, this word teaches that God never speaks lightly: His words are decrees, judgments that come to pass. This instills awe and reverence for the word of God — it is not consultative, it is executive. When God says something, even through the prophets, it takes effect like a royal decree that cannot be revoked.

sens: people or tribe of antiquity living in the southern Canaan, near the land of Egypt
H1511.detail: 1. The Gurzians are a people or tribe mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 27:8. They lived in the southern region of Canaan, between the territory of Shur and Egypt, in lands that did not belong to Israel. The text cites them alongside the Geshurites and the Amalekites as established nations in this border region.
H1511.origine: The name "Gurzians" likely comes from a Hebrew word meaning "portions" or "fragments," perhaps related to the idea of divided or separated lands. It is possible that this is the name of a minor Canaanite tribe of which we know almost nothing outside of this biblical mention. The absence of any other usage makes it difficult to specify the etymology with certainty.
H1511.emploi: The Gurzians appear only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 27:8. David, while he was a refugee with King Achish of Gath, was raiding (making incursions) against several peoples in the southern border regions: the Gurzians, the Geshurites, and the Amalekites. This passage shows that the Gurzians formed an established community, living in the desert or semi-arid lands to the south and east of Judea, a region little controlled at that time.

sens: The lower part of an animal's body, particularly that by which reptiles move
The abdominal region of a creature that crawls or slithers on the ground
H1512.detail: 1. The belly refers to the part of the body located beneath the thorax, that by which reptiles crawl. In Genesis 3:14, after his rebellion, the serpent is condemned to crawl on his belly: this is the punishment that transforms his creature, forcing him to move by dragging the lower part of his body on the ground rather than standing. 2. The word also characterizes all creatures that crawl or slither on their bellies. In Leviticus 11:42, among the unclean creatures forbidden for consumption, all reptiles "that crawl on their bellies" are listed — these are the animals whose bellies continuously touch the ground as they move. The word thus emphasizes the humiliating and degrading mode of locomotion of reptiles.
H1512.origine: The Hebrew word גָּחוֹן (gachon) literally designates the belly, particularly in the context of crawling animals. It comes from a root expressing the idea of crawling or slithering, making it a very concrete and vivid term, attached to movement and posture. The word belongs to a semantic field related to crawling and bodily humiliation.
H1512.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in relation to reptiles. In Genesis 3:14, it expresses the curse of the serpent, which will be reduced to crawling on its belly — a punishment that denotes both humiliation and suffering. In Leviticus 11:42, it enters into the technical list of unclean creatures, serving to designate one of the categories of animals whose consumption is forbidden to the Israelites: those that crawl on their bellies. In both cases, the word carries a negative connotation, related to the curse, impurity, or humiliation.
H1512.portee: This word reminds us of the divine judgment on sin: the serpent, instrument of temptation, is humiliated and reduced to the lowest state, constantly bringing to mind the consequence of rebellion. For the believer, it illustrates how sin degrades and distances from the dignity that God grants to His creatures. It also underscores the order established by God among creatures and the holiness He requires of those who follow Him.

sens: Piece of wood or material that is burning, incandescent and radiating heat
Incandescent ember used for incense or worship
Divine symbol of destructive power, judgment, or anger
Image of a dispute or quarrel that ignites
Figure of purification or transformation by fire
H1513.detail:
1. The burning coal is primarily a piece of material in combustion — wood, coal, residue from fire — that burns intensely and radiates heat. This is seen in Ezekiel's visions, where the sacred creatures have "the appearance of burning coals of fire" (Ezekiel 1:13), bright and luminous like torches.
2. The Bible uses burning coal in worship: the priest takes a censer full of "burning coals taken from the altar" to carry the incense beyond the veil of the sanctuary (Leviticus 16:12), for it is the sacred fire that must consume the offering.
3. The coal becomes a symbol of divine power: it is requested that "burning coals" be thrown upon enemies (Psalms 140:11), an image of God's judgment that consumes the wicked by His wrath.
4. In daily life, a "quarrelsome man stirs up strife" like coal produces a blaze (Proverbs 26:21) — the quarrel grows and ignites like embers that are rekindled.
5. The coal also carries a purifying significance: fire consumes and transforms, a biblical image of sanctification and God's purifying judgment.
H1513.origine: The Hebrew word gachelet comes from a root meaning "to burn" or "to blaze." It designates coal in its most active phase, when it radiates heat and light, as opposed to ordinary wood. The term evokes the intensity and fervor of the sacred fire, the one that consumes and illuminates. Several related words in the Old Testament express different forms of fire: this word specifically emphasizes incandescent coal.
H1513.emploi: The term "burning coal" (gachelet) appears 18 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms, Proverbs, and among the prophets. It first refers to the concrete material of worship: the embers from the altar used for incense (Leviticus 16:12). But very often, it takes on a theological charge: the coals become an image of divine judgment or God's anger that bursts forth from heaven (Psalms 18:13, 2 Samuel 22:13). In Proverbs, coal symbolizes human conflicts that ignite (Proverbs 26:21). In Ezekiel, the celestial creatures have the appearance of burning coals (Ezekiel 1:13), expressing the fervor and purity of the divine realm. The context varies, but the coal always retains its charge: intensity, power, transformation by fire.
H1513.portee: Understanding that God is a fire that consumes and transforms, not just an abstract distant force. The burning coal also reminds us that small conflicts, like a spark, can ignite relationships and disputes — a practical lesson for community life. And finally, fire purifies: the biblical image of coal invites the believer to accept God's purifying work in their life, even when it is challenging.

sens: son of Nahor and Reumah
nephew of Abraham
H1514.detail: Gaham is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:24. He is the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his concubine Reumah. He has three brothers from the same mother: Tebah, Tahash, and Maacah. Through his father Nahor, he is Abraham's nephew and the half-brother of several other children that Nahor had with his wife Milcah.
H1514.origine: The name Gaham literally means "burning" or "fervor" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of heat and fire. This name, like many names from this patriarchal period, carries a semantic weight that may reflect the circumstances or feelings surrounding the birth.
H1514.emploi: Gaham appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:24, where he is listed among the sons of Nahor after Abraham received divine promises. This genealogical enumeration establishes the familial link between Abraham and his distant relatives, showing how Abraham's family branched out. The context shows that Nahor, although he remained in Mesopotamia, had significant descendants.

sens: Chief of a family of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H1515.detail: Gachar is the name of a man who lived during the time of exile and the return to the Promised Land. He is mentioned as the chief of a family of temple servants (the "sons of Gachar") who left the captivity of Babylon to return to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, the governor, shortly after 538 B.C. These genealogical lists (Ezra 2:47 and Nehemiah 7:49) enumerate the families of temple servants who participated in this restoration, and Gachar appears among them as a founding ancestor of lineage.
H1515.origine: The name Gachar literally means "hidden place" or "refuge." This meaning evokes protection, a shelter — which is fitting for a man of the temple community, a place of spiritual refuge for Israel. The name belongs to the period of the return from exile, when the people of Israel, scattered and weakened, sought to re-establish themselves in Jerusalem.
H1515.emploi: Gachar appears only twice in the Bible, always in parallel genealogical lists: in Ezra 2:47 and Nehemiah 7:49. These two passages, nearly identical, provide the enumeration of the families of temple servants who returned from captivity under the leadership of Zerubbabel. Gachar is listed between "the sons of Giddel" and "the sons of Reaiah," with no further details about his personal life. His name simply marks that a family bearing this name participated in this major restoration of the Jewish people.
H1515.portee: Gachar reminds us that upon returning from exile, the scattered people rebuilt not through warrior leaders, but in part through the humble commitment of families of temple servants. Each name on this list represents a lineage that chose to return and participate in the restored worship. It is a lesson in humility and faithfulness: the "small" ones of the people played an essential role in the spiritual rebirth of Israel.

sens: Elongated depression of the terrain, between heights
Narrow and steep ravine
Fertile or habitable region in the hollow of the mountains
Valley of Hinnom, a place associated with divine judgment
H1516G.detail:
1. A valley is a depression in the terrain that extends between slopes or mountains: it is a hollow in the ground, more or less wide and deep. In Joshua 18:16, we see Jerusalem bordered by natural valleys, notably the Hinnom Valley which forms a clear geographical boundary.
2. The word sometimes emphasizes the steepness and narrowness of the ravine: it is a confined and steep passage rather than a simple gentle depression. These enclosed valleys marked the boundaries between the territories of the tribes.
3. A valley can also be a habitable, fertile, and protected territory where cities are established. In Nehemiah 11:30, the Hinnom Valley serves as a geographical reference for locating the cities of southern Judah in their territorial context.
4. The Hinnom Valley (Gehenna) becomes in the Bible a symbol of divine judgment and destruction, both for its historical use (profane sacrifices) and for its spiritual significance.
H1516G.origine: The Hebrew word gaï comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to divide," as a valley is essentially a divided land, separated by slopes. It is a concrete geographical reality that every inhabitant of the Levant recognized at the sight of the mountainous and rugged landscapes. The word belongs to the simple and ancient vocabulary of terrain description.
H1516G.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible with the meaning of "valley" as a geographical marker. In both cases, it designates the Hinnom Valley (Gehenna in Greek), which borders Jerusalem. In Joshua 18:16, it marks the southern boundary of the territory assigned to Benjamin. In Nehemiah 11:30, it serves as a landmark for locating the colonies of Judah south of Jerusalem. This valley is also mentioned elsewhere under different names ("valley of the son of Hinnom"), but always as a major geographical place and an important spiritual symbol in the topography of Jerusalem.
H1516G.portee: The Hinnom Valley, described here by a simple and concrete word, becomes in the subsequent Scripture a symbol of judgment: it reminds believers that there are visible places and realities that speak of judgment and separation from evil. For the Christian, this geographical place anchors in physical reality a spiritual truth: God delineates, separates, and will ultimately judge. The sacred geography of Jerusalem thus becomes a silent catechesis of the plan of salvation.

sens: depression of the terrain between two heights
narrow rocky gorge
H1516H.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the terrain, a hollow that extends between hills or mountains. It is a low passage through which water often flows. The valley of Jiphthach-El, mentioned at the borders of the territory of Zebulun (Joshua 19:14, 19:27), served as a geographical marker to delineate the lands given to this tribe.
2. The word can also refer to a narrow and steep gorge, a ravine with steep walls. This meaning emphasizes the confined and enclosed nature of the place, rather than a simple wide depression.
H1516H.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root evoking the idea of digging or splitting. It naturally designates the hollows of the terrain that have formed through the action of water or time. It is a fundamental word in biblical geography, as valleys play a major role in the topography of the Levant.
H1516H.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Joshua, chapter 19, where the borders of the territories assigned to the tribes of Israel are enumerated. These two occurrences describe exactly the same place: the valley of Jiphthach-El (whose name means "God opens"), which formed a northern boundary of the territory of Zebulun. These passages show that valleys served as natural and precise markers for establishing boundaries between tribal lands.
H1516H.portee: For the biblical reader, valleys remind us that God knows and delineates every place in the promised land. They also symbolize humility and dependence: one who dwells in the valley must lift their eyes to the heights. Finally, they illustrate how God guides His people by giving them a well-defined territory, with clear and visible boundaries.

sens: depression of the terrain between two heights
narrow and enclosed passage between slopes
H1516I.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the terrain, a low area that extends between two ranges of hills or mountains. In 1 Samuel 13:18, it refers to the valley of Tseboïm, a land passage that marks the border of the country and runs alongside the desert — a path that the Philistines could take to invade the territory of Israel.
2. The word can designate a particularly narrow and steep passage, almost a ravine, that creates a natural bottleneck. This type of relief was important in the geography of Israel, both for movement and for defending the territory.
H1516I.origine: The Hebrew word gay comes from a root expressing the idea of hollow or void. The term literally describes a form of the terrain: a depression, a lowered area. It is a simple and concrete word that applies to the real geography of the land.
H1516I.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, to designate the valley of Tseboïm in 1 Samuel 13:18. It is mentioned in the military context of Philistine incursions during the time of Saul. This passage shows that this valley was a strategic and well-known access route.
H1516I.portee: The valleys of the promised land remind us that God has shaped the territory given to Israel in its geographical details. They served both as natural resources and strategic routes. For the reader, this word invites us to see that divine Providence also operates in concrete geography.

sens: Depression of the terrain between two heights
Low and elongated terrain, often crossed by a watercourse
Narrow and enclosed space between cliffs or mountains
H1516J.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the terrain, a hollow that sinks between two hills or two mountains. It is the opposite of a mountain: instead of rising, the ground descends, creating a low and often elongated space. In the Bible, this word designates both a wide fertile valley and a narrow steep gorge.

2. Often, a valley is traversed by a watercourse that flows naturally through it, as water flows to lower points. In Israel, valleys provide important passages between mountainous regions and are strategic locations for movement and battles.

3. The word can also refer to a narrow and enclosed pass, a deep gorge. It is in such a place, the valley of Salt, that David and his generals won several decisive victories against the Edomites (2 Samuel 8:13; 2 Kings 14:7).
H1516J.origine: The Hebrew word gay comes from a root that evokes the idea of something that sinks or hollows out. It is very common in the Old Testament to designate all types of low and enclosed spaces. The valley of Salt, mentioned repeatedly in the usages, is a historically well-known region near the Dead Sea, used repeatedly as a battlefield.
H1516J.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Segond, always in the expression "valley of salt" (in Hebrew: gay hammelah). All usages are accounts of battles: David (2 Samuel 8:13; 1 Chronicles 18:12), Amaziah (2 Kings 14:7; 2 Chronicles 25:11), and the title of Psalm 60:2. This valley was an important border place between Israel and Idumea (the land of Edom), strategically significant. Each mention accompanies the description of a great victory, highlighting the importance of the place.
H1516J.portee: The valley of Salt is the site of victories that strengthen the reign of the kings of Israel and remind us of the power that God gives to His people. These accounts show that God places His kings above their enemies and establishes them over border territories. For the believer, the valley also invites us to remember that God acts in geographically concrete and historically real places, and that no land escapes His lordship.

sens: elongated depression of the terrain between two heights
narrow gorge carved by water
enclosed space conducive to work or community life
H1516K.detail: 1. A valley is a depression in the terrain, a hollow that extends between two mountains or two hills. It is the opposite of a mountain or a ridge; it naturally forms a passage or a low place. In 1 Chronicles 4:14, Joab is called "father of the valley of workers," suggesting that a well-known valley hosted a group of workers, likely attracted by the water and shelter it provided. 2. The word can more specifically refer to a narrow and steep gorge carved by a watercourse over time, where the rock walls rise abruptly. This type of formation offers natural refuge and resources (water, shelter). 3. Beyond simple geographical relief, a valley becomes a inhabited and productive space, a home or seat of activity: this is why Joab can name the "valley of workers," a recognized place of collective activity.
H1516K.origine: The Hebrew word גַּיְא (gai or gayé) literally means "hollow" or "depression." It is related to Semitic roots expressing the idea of "to dig" or "to sink." The word describes less a simple elevation of the terrain than a naturally carved formation, often by the water flowing through it. In biblical Hebrew, this term applies to these folds of terrain characteristic of the Levantine geography, where valleys are axes of circulation, life, and work.
H1516K.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:14. It refers to the "valley of workers," a place identified with Joab, ancestor or founder of a community of workers (likely artisans or builders). The genealogical context suggests that a specific valley was famous for hosting an active and organized population. Although hapax (a word that appears only once), this term fits into the rich Hebrew terminology of terrain reliefs, where each geographical formation carries a social and economic meaning.

sens: Depression of the terrain between two heights
Narrow and steep gorge
Place of gathering or battle
H1516L.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the terrain, a low area between two hills or two mountains. It is the inverse relief of a mountain: while the mountain rises, the valley sinks. In 2 Chronicles 14:9, King Asa and his army position themselves for battle in the valley of Zephathah, a terrain that offered a passage or strategic position between the heights.

2. The word can also refer to a narrow and steep gorge, a ravine with steep walls, more dramatic than a simple depression. These tight passages in mountainous terrain are naturally important places for movement and confrontations.

3. Figuratively, a valley becomes a place of gathering or confrontation: it is where peoples meet, armies deploy, and destinies intertwine. The valley of Zephathah is the stage where God intervenes to grant victory to Asa.
H1516L.origine: The Hebrew word gai comes from a root that evokes the idea of depth and hollow. It literally designates a depression in the terrain, this natural hollow that water and erosion carve into the earth. The word belongs to a set of simple but essential geographical terms to describe the land of Israel, whose topography is marked by the Jordan valleys and the mountains of Judea.
H1516L.emploi: The word gai appears only once in the provided biblical usage: in 2 Chronicles 14:9, during the battle in the valley of Zephathah. It is a real valley, a specific geographical site where King Asa of Judah encounters and defeats Zerah the Ethiopian. The context is that of a battle, a decisive military confrontation where God acts on behalf of His people. The valley is the stage where divine providence unfolds: it is here, in this particular place, that the outcome of the battle is sealed by the intervention of the Lord.
H1516L.portee: The valley of Zephathah reminds the reader that concrete geographical places are the scenes where God acts in history. It is not by chance that the battle takes place in a valley: it is a place where forces meet, where human fragility is tested, and where the Lord manifests His power. For the believer, this invites recognition that God intervenes in the concrete and geographical realities of our lives, not just in the abstract.

sens: A depression in the terrain between two heights, often narrow and steep
A gate of Jerusalem providing access to a valley
H1516M.detail:
1. A valley is a low area of terrain enclosed between hills or mountains, often marked by steep slopes. It is a natural passage in the relief, sometimes traversed by a watercourse. The Hebrew word particularly evokes narrow and steep gorges rather than simple gentle depressions.
2. In Jerusalem, the "valley gate" is one of the gates of the city wall, named because it opens onto a valley — likely the Kidron Valley or the Tyropoeon Valley that bordered Jerusalem. Nehemiah mentions it while inspecting the ruined walls (Nehemiah 2:13), and it was restored during the reconstruction (Nehemiah 3:13).
H1516M.origine: The Hebrew word gai comes from a root that expresses the idea of hollow or depth. It specifically designates steep and narrow valleys, gorges, and ravines, rather than simple wide valleys. This term is common in biblical Hebrew to describe the terrain features around Jerusalem and in Judea.
H1516M.emploi: The word "valley" (gai) appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in the books of Chronicles and Nehemiah, and always with the complement "valley gate." It is a well-known gate of Jerusalem during the time of the kings and the post-exilic reconstruction. Uzziah built a tower there to fortify the city (2 Chronicles 26:9). When Nehemiah arrives to rebuild the walls, he goes out through this gate at night to assess the state of the fortifications (Nehemiah 2:13-15), and then it is repaired as part of the restoration project (Nehemiah 3:13). The use of the term is very contextualized and topographical.
H1516M.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible describes concrete places and real reconstruction projects. The repeated mention of the "valley gate" shows how Nehemiah meticulously proceeds to restore Jerusalem, gate by gate, section by section. It is a detail that underscores the importance of perseverance and attention to detail in God's work.

sens: depression of the ground between two heights, low and narrow space
figuratively, burial place, place of death and desolation
H1516N.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the ground, a low area enclosed between heights. It is a terrain that dips down, forming a hollow path or narrow passage in the geography. In Ezekiel 39:11, the "valley of travelers" refers to a natural passageway, a lowland that people regularly crossed.

2. By extension, the valley becomes the place where the dead rest, where corpses accumulate: an image of desolation and end. Ezekiel speaks of the "valley of the multitude of Gog" (39:11 and 39:15) as the grave where Gog and his armies will be buried, transforming this geographical relief into a symbol of divine judgment and the death of Israel's enemy.
H1516N.origine: The Hebrew word גַּיְא comes from a root that denotes a hollow, a depression in the ground. It paints the initial image of low terrain, enclosed between slopes. The word is simple and concrete: any depression between two mountains or hills is a valley. It is a word from the common geography of Israel, a mountainous region where valleys structure the landscape.
H1516N.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament Hebrew (here in Ezekiel), and always in the prophet Ezekiel to designate the valley of the multitude of Gog. In the prophetic context of chapter 39, God announces that Gog's armies will be destroyed and buried in Israel; Ezekiel first mentions this valley as a place of passage (39:11), then as the cemetery where the grave diggers will bury all the corpses (39:15). The meaning remains geographical and concrete, but laden with eschatological significance: it is the place where God executes His judgment on the enemy.
H1516N.portee: This valley, in Ezekiel's vision, reminds believers that God controls the course of history and defends His people. The transformation of a simple depression in the ground into a grave for enemies affirms divine victory and the certainty that no one can triumph over Israel when God protects it.

sens: Depression of the ground between two heights
Place of passage and burial
Image of the human condition
H1516O.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the ground, enclosed between heights or mountain ranges. It is a hollow, often a narrow gorge that travelers must cross. In Ezekiel 39:11, God promises Gog a grave in "the valley of travelers" to the east of the sea, a place of passage where all will see this judgment.
2. The valley becomes a place of funeral destination: it is where the dead are buried, and in this specific case, the entire multitude of Gog. It closes the passage, becoming a monument of divine judgment. Scripture calls it "the valley of the multitude of Gog," a name that perpetuates the memory of the punishment.
3. In the broader biblical imagery, the valley often symbolizes lowliness, humiliation, or trial — a difficult passage that man must traverse — opposed to the heights of divine glory.
H1516O.origine: The Hebrew word גַּיְא (gay) literally denotes a valley or a depression in the ground. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of hollow, of void. It is a simple and descriptive word, very concrete, that paints the mountainous landscape of Canaan where valleys and ravines are numerous and often formidable. It regularly appears in the geographical descriptions of the Bible.
H1516O.emploi: The word appears only once in the known biblical usages here: in Ezekiel 39:11, in the prophecy against Gog. There, God designates a real valley (probably the Jordan Valley or a recognizable place in Israel) as the place where this defeated tyrant will rest. The use of the word emphasizes humiliation: instead of an honorable burial on high, Gog will be thrown into a depression, a hollow of earth. The proper name "valley of the multitude of Gog" perpetuates this judgment in the memory of the people.
H1516O.portee: This prophecy teaches that God's judgment is real and visible, inscribed in the very geography of the promised land. The valley becomes a permanent testimony: all who pass through it will see this place and remember the power of the Lord who crushes His enemies. For the believer, it is an assurance that God's enemies do not go unpunished, and that the Eternal controls history.

sens: depression of the ground between two heights
narrow passage between two rock walls
H1516P.detail:
1. A valley is a low area of land, carved between hills or mountains. It is a natural passage space in a rugged landscape. In 1 Samuel 17:52, the Israelites pursue the fleeing Philistines "even into the valley," meaning they catch up with them in these depressed areas of land near Gath and Ekron.
2. The word can also refer to a narrow gorge or a tight passage between two rock walls, a winding path carved by water or the passage of caravans. Such an enclosed valley facilitated movement and offered refuge or an ambush point.
H1516P.origine: The Hebrew word gai (גַּיְא) comes from a root that denotes lowering, a hollow. It is related to gat (גַּת, "Gath"), the name of the Philistine city, which shares the same image: a place that is hollow, sunken. The word belongs to the simple vocabulary of topography: it describes the relief without artifice.
H1516P.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 17:52, in the account of David's battle against Goliath. After the giant's death, the Israelites put the Philistine army to flight and pursue them "even into the valley," meaning to the lowlands bordering the Philistine cities. The context shows that the valley is a passage and pursuit area, an intermediate terrain between the battlefield and the fortified cities.
H1516P.portee: This word reminds us that geography shapes historical and military events. Valleys are necessary passages: they testify to the concrete reality of the world where the battles of the Bible take place, far from the abstract. For the reader, it is an invitation to see God's hand guiding Israel not only in heaven but also on earth, in its landscapes and paths.

sens: Depression of the land between two heights, narrow passage between mountains
Geographical location used to delineate territories and borders
The valley of Hinnom, site of idolatrous worship and child sacrifices
H1516Q.detail:
1. A valley is a low area of land framed by mountains or hills, often narrow and steep. It is a natural passage in the terrain that can serve for movement or to delineate regions. In Joshua 15:8 and 18:16, the valley of Ben-Hinnom marks the borders between the territories of the tribes of Israel.
2. Valleys served as precise geographical landmarks to describe the extent of the lands assigned to each tribe. They marked natural boundaries that could be easily recognized on the ground, such as the valley of the Rephaim mentioned in Joshua 15:8.
3. The valley of Hinnom, also called Topheth, became infamous as a site of abominable religious practices. Kings of Judah like Ahaz and Manasseh made their children pass through the fire to honor the god Molech, a practice strictly forbidden by the Law of Moses (2 Kings 23:10; 2 Chronicles 28:3). This valley symbolizes the place of divine judgment and perdition.
H1516Q.origine: The Hebrew word גַּיְא (gaï) literally denotes a depression or hollow in the land. It is an ancient and common word in Hebrew to describe the geography of the land of Canaan. In the Greek Old Testament, the valley of Hinnom is also called "Gehenna," a term that will become in the New Testament the name of the place of eternal punishment.
H1516Q.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of territorial boundaries (Joshua) and in the accounts of the Judean monarchy (2 Kings and 2 Chronicles). In Joshua 15:8 and 18:16, it is a simple topographical description used to trace the borders. But starting from 2 Kings 23:10 and parallel passages in 2 Chronicles, the valley of Hinnom becomes tragically famous: it is there that the idolatrous kings of Israel sacrificed their children to foreign gods, committing an abomination that even Jeremiah denounces (Jeremiah 7:31-32).
H1516Q.portee: The valley of Hinnom reminds the reader that geographical locations can be marked by sin and become symbols of God's judgment. It shows how much God hates idolatry and crimes against innocence, particularly the sacrifice of children. What the kings did in secret in a remote valley was visible in the eyes of the Lord, and this sin cries out for vengeance. This valley teaches that even the holiest lands can be defiled by evil and idolatry.

sens: depression of the land between two heights
narrow and steep gorge
low and fertile region
refuge or place of danger
H1516R.detail:
1. A valley is primarily a natural depression of the soil, a hollow between mountains or hills: it is the land that lowers between two elevations (Numbers 21:20: "the valley that is in the territory of Moab").
2. The word can refer to a narrow and steep gorge, sometimes daunting, where one walks between high and rocky walls: this is the image of Psalm 23:4 ("the valley of the shadow of death") and Jeremiah 19:2 ("the valley of Ben-Hinnom").
3. In productive regions, a valley can be fertile and green: Isaiah 28:1 speaks of "the fertile valley" where the drunkards of Ephraim live.
4. Finally, a valley can represent a refuge where one flees or hides in times of danger: Ezekiel 7:16 describes the fugitives who escape "on the mountains" and "in the valleys" to find safety.
H1516R.origine: The Hebrew word גַּיְא (gay) comes from a root that evokes the idea of something that lowers or hollows out. It is linked to the image of the land sinking, hence its primary meaning of depression, hollow. The word appears 29 times in the Old Testament, mainly in geographical and prophetic accounts, always to denote a natural formation of the landscape. Its usage reflects the daily experience of the inhabitants of the Levant, where valleys are major geographical features.
H1516R.emploi: The word valley (גַּיְא) is very common in biblical Hebrew, used 29 times to describe specific places or geographical situations. In historical accounts (Joshua 8:11, 1 Samuel 17:3), it situates events concretely: Joshua camps near Ai "separated by the valley." In prophecies (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), the word takes on a broader significance: Jeremiah announces judgment in "the valley of Ben-Hinnom," while Ezekiel sees the valleys of Israel restored. In the Psalms, "the valley of the shadow of death" (23:4) symbolizes the believer's trials. The word can thus be purely geographical or carry a spiritual and metaphorical weight.
H1516R.portee: The valley in the Bible is the place where the believer experiences both vulnerability and God's protection. By reading "the valley of the shadow of death," we learn that even in the dark and difficult passages of life, the Lord accompanies us. Valleys are also places of transformation and promise: they will be lifted up when God restores His people. This word reminds us that God acts in concrete and geographical history, and that lands that seem low or abandoned are never truly so in His eyes.

sens: depression of the land between heights
narrow and steep gorge
the valley of Ben-Hinnom, place of divine judgment
H1516S.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression of the land, a hollow between heights or mountains. In the Promised Land, valleys are important features of the terrain.
2. The word can specifically refer to a narrow and deep gorge with steep walls, such as those carved by erosion in the mountains of Judea.
3. In particular, this word designates the valley of Ben-Hinnom, located near Jerusalem, where child sacrifices took place and where the Lord announces a terrible judgment: the corpses of the rebels will be piled up without a proper burial, and it will be called "valley of slaughter" (Jeremiah 7:32). This valley becomes a symbol of divine punishment.
H1516S.origine: The Hebrew word gay (or gai) is common in the Old Testament to designate the valleys of the Palestinian relief. It comes from a root likely evoking something hollow or sunken. The word appears in many biblical geographical names. The valley of Ben-Hinnom (literally "son of Hinnom") has become in Jewish tradition a symbolic name for hell, which is reflected in the Greek gehenna and our French term.
H1516S.emploi: This word is attested only once in the Segond, in Jeremiah 7:32, where it designates the valley of Ben-Hinnom, a site of idolatrous worship near Jerusalem. The Lord denounces these abominable practices and prophesies that this valley will change its name: instead of being called Topheth or valley of Ben-Hinnom, it will be called "valley of slaughter" because the corpses of the judged will be accumulated there. This passage concentrates on this word all the weight of divine judgment against idolatry and impiety.
H1516S.portee: This valley, now a symbol of eternal punishment, reminds the reader that God takes seriously the worship of idols and actions contrary to His law. The image of judgment denounced in Jeremiah 7:32 has profoundly influenced later biblical thought on the place of final condemnation. It invites one to turn away from what displeases God.

sens: Tendon or ligament that connects muscles to bones
Tissue that provides strength and cohesion to the body
Physical strength, vigor
Rigidity, moral hardness
H1517.detail:
1. The nerve is primarily the tendon or ligament, this white cord that connects muscle to bone: in Genesis 32:32, after wrestling with the angel, Jacob is struck in the nerve of his hip, this specific tendon that allows leg movement.
2. More broadly, the nerve refers to all the ligaments and tendons that hold the body together: in Ezekiel 37:6-8, during the vision of the dry bones coming to life, God "gives nerves" to the skeleton, these essential tissues that bind the bones and enable the body to exist and function.
3. The nerve represents the strength and vigor of the body: in Job 40:12, the "nerves of the thighs" of the Behemoth are mentioned, referring to the concentrated muscular power in this enormous beast.
4. Figuratively, the nerve becomes moral rigidity and stubbornness: in Isaiah 48:4, God says of Israel that "your neck is an iron bar," an image of the hard and unyielding nerve, refusing to bend to divine will.
H1517.origine: The Hebrew word gîd comes from a root that evokes what binds and holds together. In ancient Hebrew, the nerve is what ensures the cohesion of the body: bones without nerves are dead, with no possible movement. This image of the nerve as a unifying force is found in biblical thought: the nerve unites, the nerve holds firm, the nerve resists. Figuratively, this shifts from "what physically binds" to "what is hard and inflexible."
H1517.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom and prophetic vision books. In the account of Genesis 32:32, it designates the specific tendon of the hip, an anatomical detail that forever marks Israel with a dietary prohibition. In Job (10:11 and 40:12), the nerve is the connective tissue that weaves the human or animal body, a symbol of construction and strength. In Ezekiel 37:6-8, during the resurrection of the bones, the nerves appear as the crucial step between the bare skeleton and the living body: without nerves, there is no connection, no life. In Isaiah 48:4, the nerve becomes an image of moral rigidity, of hardening of the heart. Thus, the same word shifts from concrete anatomical to psychological figurative.
H1517.portee: The nerve reminds the reader that the human body is not a mere accumulation of parts, but a coherent creation where each element is connected to the other. This solidarity of the body invites respect for the body as a gift from God. The prohibition of the nerve in Genesis 32:32 marks Israel with a permanent scar, a living reminder of the encounter with God. Finally, the image of the "iron nerve" speaks to each one: am I stiff and inflexible before God, or supple, yielding to His will?

sens: To leap or spring forth with impetuosity, like a troop charging into attack
To burst forth, to emerge suddenly
To leap or rush forward
To manifest forcefully, speaking of an emotion or a lament
H1518.detail:
1. The primary sense is physical: to leap or spring forth quickly and with force. It is the image of a troop that surges from the place where it was hidden to attack (Judges 20:33: Israel's ambush surges from Maaré-Gibeah). It is also water that surges with impetuosity, like the sea that leaps from the maternal womb (Job 38:8).
2. The word can describe a sudden and forceful irruption into a space: the Jordan rushing into the crocodile's jaws (Job 40:18), or Pharaoh surging into his rivers, disturbing the waters (Ezekiel 32:2).
3. By extension, the verb can express the emergence of an emotion or a lament: to groan is also to bring forth a cry, a lamentation (Micah 4:10: the daughter of Zion groans like a woman in labor).
H1518.origine: The Hebrew root GYCh evokes the idea of surging, leaping, or bursting forth. The word is related to the Aramaic term meaning "to strive" or "to apply oneself." The basic image is one of a force that is released and suddenly surges forth, whether physically (water, a troop) or emotionally (a cry, a lament).
H1518.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in contexts of rapid movement and irruption. In Judges 20:33, it describes the attack of an ambush. In Job, it characterizes impressive natural phenomena: the sea surging at its origin, the river rushing. In Ezekiel 32:2, it depicts the impetuosity of Pharaoh surging into the waters. In Micah 4:10, it takes on an emotional hue: groaning expresses the lament of one who suffers. The context varies, but the word always suggests a force that surges or escapes with impetuosity.
H1518.portee: This verb invites the reader to recognize in rapid and impetuous movements — whether military, natural, or emotional — the action of a power that is released. For Israel in ambush, it is the force of God propelling them to attack. For the crocodile or the river, it is the vigor of creation. For the daughter of Zion who groans, it is the suffering of the people that escapes. The word reminds us that nothing is inert: everything that lives can surge, leap, cry out.

sens: action of surging, manifesting suddenly with force
speaking of a force, an event that emerges unexpectedly and irresistibly
H1519.detail:
1. The irruption is a sudden and violent surge. In Daniel 7:2, the four winds of heaven surge upon the sea: they burst forth, unleash themselves, dominating the landscape with a power that cannot be stopped. It is the image of something that breaks the silence or tranquility and imposes its presence.

2. More broadly, an irruption marks the unexpected appearance of a force or event. It is not a gradual arrival: it is a manifestation that imposes itself, taking control, often in an impressive or unsettling manner. In Daniel's vision, these winds act upon the great sea like a power that surges from nothingness and produces chaos.
H1519.origine: The Aramaic word גִּיחַ (giach) comes from the same root as the Hebrew גִּיחַ (H1518), which literally means "to leap, burst forth, to come out with force." The starting image is that of a spring that surges, a door that is broken down, a flood that overflows. The form used in Daniel is the Aphel, a form that reinforces the idea of causality and intensity: it emphasizes that what makes an irruption does so truly, with all its power.
H1519.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in Daniel 7:2. It designates here the four winds of heaven that unleash upon the great sea in Daniel's prophetic vision. This apocalyptic context underscores its dramatic and irresistible nature: the irruption is not controlled, it is imposed by a force that surpasses earthly powers. It is a key element in the vision concerning future kingdoms.
H1519.portee: The irruption of the winds upon the sea reminds the reader that God can intervene with sudden and irresistible powers in history. By rereading this verse, the Christian understands that major events — judgment, salvation, divine intervention — do not always follow a predictable course: they can surge forth with a force that disrupts the established order. It is an invitation not to be passive in the face of God's manifestations.

sens: Place near Gibeon in Benjamin
H1520.detail: Giah is a location situated near Gibeon, in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. The name appears only once in the Bible, in the account of the pursuit of Abner by Joab and Abishai after a battle between the men of David and those of Ish-Baal (2 Samuel 2:24). The text locates it precisely on the road of the desert of Gibeon, opposite the hill of Amma, which allows it to be situated in the region of the heights that overlook Gibeon.
H1520.origine: The name Giah literally means "to surge" or "to pierce" in Hebrew, possibly evoking a water source or a place where water springs from the ground — a natural geographical feature that may have marked this place and justified its name.
H1520.emploi: Giah appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 2:24. It is mentioned in the context of the first battle between the armies of David and the house of Saul, when Joab and his brother Abishai pursue General Abner after the defeat of Ish-Baal's troops. The mention of this specific geographical location helps the reader to situate the unfolding of the battles in the region of Gibeon in Benjamin.

sens: one of the four rivers of the Garden of Eden
a water spring in Jerusalem
H1521.detail:
1. Gihon is one of the four rivers that watered the Garden of Eden, according to the Creation account. Its name means "the one that bursts forth" or "the one that rises," evoking water that flows powerfully from a spring. The Bible describes it as the river that "surrounds the whole land of Cush" (Genesis 2:13), meaning it flows around an important region of ancient Africa.
2. In Jerusalem, Gihon is a major water spring near the City of David, sharing the same name as a paradisiacal river. It is where kings were anointed: Solomon was anointed there by the priest Zadok and the prophet Nathan to be king, "celebrating with joy" and "the city was stirred" (1 Kings 1:45). King Hezekiah channeled its waters, directing them westward to strengthen Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:30).
H1521.origine: The Hebrew name Gihon comes from a root meaning "to burst forth" or "to rise," painting the image of water that flows powerfully from an underground source. It is a theologically rich name: by applying it to a spring in Jerusalem, the Bible connects this city to the rivers of the lost paradise, suggesting that Jerusalem is a place of divine grace. The word reflects the vital importance of water in the lands of the Middle East.
H1521.emploi: Gihon appears six times in the Bible. Twice in Genesis: a description of the rivers of the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:13). Four times in the books of Kings and Chronicles: it is the site of Solomon's anointing (1 Kings 1:33, 38, 45), a crucial moment when a king is anointed to reign, and it is modified by King Hezekiah to strengthen the defenses of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:30; 33:14). Gihon is a place of political and spiritual power, associated with royal anointing and the survival of the holy city.
H1521.portee: Gihon invites the reader to see Jerusalem not only as a human city but as linked to the divine order of the world. That the anointing of a king takes place near a spring named after a river of paradise suggests that God blesses His kings through this water, a symbol of life and renewal. The story of Hezekiah channeling Gihon also shows how human wisdom collaborates with divine provision to protect God's people.

sens: the servant and assistant of the prophet Elisha
H1522.detail: Gehazi is the personal servant of the prophet Elisha. He assists him in his actions, carries out his orders, and witnesses his miracles. For example, Elisha commands him to take his staff and lay it on the face of the resurrected child (2 Kings 4:29). Later, he loses his integrity by fraudulently enriching himself and lying to the prophet, which results in him receiving an incurable leprosy (2 Kings 5:20-27).
H1522.origine: The Hebrew name גֵּיחֲזִי literally means "valley of vision." It is composed of ge (valley) and hazzi (vision). This name evokes the idea of a place or condition privileged for seeing and receiving divine revelations, although the character himself fails to take advantage of it.
H1522.emploi: Gehazi appears in twelve verses of the second book of Kings, primarily in chapters 4 and 5. He is first presented as the faithful servant of the prophet Elisha, tasked with carrying out his orders (2 Kings 4:12 and 4:29). Witnessing the miracles of the resurrection of the Shunammite child and the healing of Naaman the Syrian, he represents a disciple who lives alongside a man of God. However, his story takes a turn when he secretly pursues Naaman to extort a gift through deceit (2 Kings 5:21-25), which leads to his condemnation to leprosy. The king later questions him about Elisha's miracles (2 Kings 8:4), showing that he remains a memorable figure of that time.
H1522.portee: The story of Gehazi teaches the reader the danger of greed and dishonesty, even in one who has had the privilege of being close to a prophet and witnessing divine works. His sin shows that proximity to the power of God does not save one from temptation, and that disobeying God's servant to satisfy the love of money brings divine judgment. It serves as a warning against spiritual pride and moral corruption.

sens: to experience lively joy, gladness, exultation
to be in gladness, to take pleasure in something
to vibrate, to tremble with joy
to exult in the face of a happy event or victory
H1523.detail:
1. Rejoice expresses a deep and overflowing joy that fills the whole being. It is to feel gladness, an inner jubilation that leads to exultation. In Psalms 21:2, the king rejoices in divine protection with a gladness that fills his whole heart.
2. The word also denotes being in gladness, finding pleasure and satisfaction in something. It is to take joy in an event or reality: Proverbs 23:24 shows the father who is glad to have a righteous son.
3. To rejoice can mean to vibrate or tremble with joy — a reaction of the whole body, physical and emotional. Isaiah 35:1 describes the desert rejoicing and blooming with joy.
4. The word also carries the idea of exulting, that is, to manifest one's joy with strength, particularly in the face of a victory or judgment of God: Psalms 2:11 calls to rejoice with trembling before His power.
H1523.origine: The Hebrew root גִּיל denotes the joy that moves the heart, the lively and joyful emotion. It is linked to the idea of vibrating, of trembling. The word belongs to the family of verbs expressing the movements of the heart and soul under the impact of strong emotion. It is an energetic joy, not tranquil or passive, but active and communicative.
H1523.emploi: This verb appears 44 times in the Old Testament, very often in the Psalms and in the prophets Isaiah and Joel. It expresses the reaction of the believer or of all creation in response to God's acts: His judgments, His justice, His protection, His kingship. The heavens rejoice (1 Chronicles 16:31), the earth exults, the desert blooms and rejoices (Isaiah 35:1-2). The word is also used for the personal joy of the believer who glorifies in God (Psalms 89:17) or of the father happy to have a righteous son (Proverbs 23:24). It is a joy that is never isolated, but always linked to God or His salvation.
H1523.portee: This word reminds the reader that Christian joy is a concrete, visceral reality: it fills the heart, it overflows, it transforms the entire believer. It is not a mere passing emotion, but an exultation born of trust in God and the experience of His protection. For the Christian, to rejoice is an act of worship, a rightful reaction before the power and goodness of God.

sens: intense and manifested joy
exultation, transports of joy
state of collective rejoicing during festivals or celebrations
atmosphere of cheerfulness and enthusiasm
H1524A.detail: 1. Joy is primarily a vivid and overflowing happiness, one that seizes someone deeply. In Job 3:22, the poet asks: who would be "transported with joy and seized with gladness" upon finding the grave? — showing that it is a strong, physical joy that cannot be contained. 2. It is the joy of worship and communion with God. The psalmist says: "I will go to the altar of God, to God, my joy and gladness" (Psalms 43:4) — joy springs forth in the presence of God; it is celebration and thanksgiving. 3. It also characterizes the feasts and rejoicings of the people: "They are brought in with gladness and joy" (Psalms 45:16); it permeates solemn moments of collective joy. 4. It can finally color everything that lives — nature itself can be "girded" with it (Psalms 65:13) — an overflow of life and vitality. Conversely, its absence marks desolation: in Isaiah 16:10 and Jeremiah 48:33, "joy and gladness have disappeared" when judgment comes.
H1524A.origine: The Hebrew word גִּיל (gil) is rooted in the idea of turning, dancing, rejoicing while spinning. It evokes movement, effusion, a joy that is not contained but expressed through the body and action. Cognate to the root "gîl" which carries the idea of joyful agitation, the word passes into Greek as ἀγαλλίασις (agalliasis) when expressing this same overflowing joy.
H1524A.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the Psalms and the prophets. It always denotes authentic and intense joy, never superficial joy. The psalmists associate it with the presence of God and worship (Psalms 43:4). The prophets use it to evoke moments of celebration for the people — harvests, feasts — or its absence to signify mourning and judgment (Isaiah 16:10; Jeremiah 48:33; Joel 1:16). It is also shared with creation when it enjoys blessing (Psalms 65:13). It is a full joy, linked to abundance and life in communion with God.
H1524A.portee: For the believer, joy speaks of joy beyond mere feeling: it is the celebration of life with God, exultation in His presence. It invites not to dissociate joy from sincere worship and communion. And the silence of joy, in passages of judgment, reminds us that it is never guaranteed — it is a gift, dependent on faithfulness and blessing.

sens: Period of life, particularly youth
Group of people of the same age, generation
H1524B.detail:
1. The word designates a stage of human life, especially youth. In Daniel 1:10, the chief of the eunuchs speaks of the "young men of your age" — he refers to adolescents or young men who belong to the same period of life as Daniel and his companions.
2. By extension, it can mean a group or generation of people born at the same time, those who share the same age. It is the idea of an age group, a segment of society that has lived through the same years.
H1524B.origine: The Hebrew word gîl comes from a root that first evokes the idea of a circle or rotation — the image of a cycle that returns, hence the passage of time. From this concrete sense, it transitions to that of period, stage, or generation. The term belongs to the simple vocabulary of daily life.
H1524B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 1:10. Daniel and his three friends are young men taken captive to Babylon. The chief of the eunuchs fears that their different diet will make them visibly weaker than the other adolescents of the same age — which would endanger his own life before the king. The usage emphasizes a comparison between individuals belonging to the same generation or age group.
H1524B.portee: This word reminds us that youth is a stage of life that deserves attention and kindness. The story of Daniel shows that even in captivity, in a hostile environment, God can protect the young who remain faithful to Him. This encourages the reader to see their young years not as a weakness, but as a season where faith and obedience bear fruit.

sens: Great shining and shared joy
Explosion of joy joyfully manifested
Public festive jubilation
