H1525.detail: 1. Joy is a deep and visible happiness that expresses itself freely: it is not a tranquil satisfaction, but an overflowing exultation. In Isaiah 35:2, the earth is covered with flowers and "rejoices with songs of joy and shouts of triumph" — it is a joy that sings, that cries out, that puts itself on display. 2. It is a joy of a collective, communal nature. In Isaiah 65:18, God calls to rejoice "always in joy" — He creates Jerusalem and its people for this shared joy. Joy implies gatherings, celebrations, the communion of hearts in a shared happiness. 3. Joy is tonal and sonorous: it is accompanied by music, joyful shouts, exuberant manifestations. It carries within it a victory or a blessing, something that surpasses mere personal satisfaction.
H1525.origine: The Hebrew word גִּילָה (gilah) comes from the root גִּיל (gil), which expresses the quivering, the trembling, the oscillation of joy — a joy that shakes the whole body. It is an image of vibration, movement, effervescence. The word thus designates less the silent joy than the overflowing joy that manifests itself, that cannot remain contained. This root is found in other words of the joy family in biblical Hebrew.
H1525.emploi: The word joy (gilah) appears only twice in the Old Testament, in the two cited passages. In both cases, it is in a context of joyful eschatology — God's messianic or final promises. In Isaiah 35, it is the glorious restoration of the desert: the earth is adorned with flowers and cries out with joy at the manifestation of God. In Isaiah 65, it is the new creation: Jerusalem and its people will be created for eternal joy, to dwell in perpetual happiness. These two contexts show that biblical joy is linked to the revelation of God's glory and goodness.
H1525.portee: For the Christian, joy reminds us that authentic joy is not a private and selfish emotion, but a response of the whole being — body and soul — to the magnificence of God. It invites us to step out of restraint or guilt in the face of joy: celebrating God's glory and His promises is not a luxury, it is a command. It also opens a hope: the messianic promises will transform the world into a place of eternal joy, and the Christian can begin to taste its first fruits even now.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Giloh
H1526.detail: 1. Gilonite designates an inhabitant or native of the city of Giloh, a locality in the mountainous region of Judah. The term is a gentilice, meaning a name that indicates a person's geographical origin. Ahithophel, David's advisor who revolts with Absalom, is referred to as "the Gilonite" in 2 Samuel 15:12, marking his belonging to this city.
H1526.origine: The word Gilonite derives from Giloh (גִּלֹה), a city in Judah. In Hebrew, gentilices are formed by adding a suffix to the name of the place of origin. It is a simple geographical derivative: it has no other meaning than to indicate where a person came from.
H1526.emploi: The term appears twice in the text of Samuel. In 2 Samuel 15:12, Ahithophel is called "the Gilonite" when he joins Absalom's revolt against David: this detail emphasizes his identity and origin. In 2 Samuel 23:34, Eliam, son of Ahithophel, is also said to be "of Giloh," confirming that Ahithophel's family came from this city. The term is purely identificatory.

sens: father of Tibni, a figure from the time of the divided kings in Israel
H1527.detail: Guinath is a man whose name appears briefly in the history of Israel during the political division of the kingdom. He is the father of Tibni, a man around whom a rival faction crystallized.
H1527.origine: The name Guinath means "protection" in Hebrew, evoking a quality of guarding or defense. It is a personal name borne by this minor figure in Israel's monarchical history.
H1527.emploi: Guinath appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Kings 16, during a succession crisis for the throne of Israel. After the death of Ahab and Joram, the people divide: one part supports Tibni, son of Guinath, while the other supports Omri. This schism reflects the internal tensions of the Northern kingdom. Tibni ultimately succumbs, and Omri establishes himself as king.

sens: White powdery substance obtained by heating limestone, used for whitening or coating walls
Limestone coating that covers a surface
Figuratively: that which is visible and exposed to all eyes
H1528.detail:
1. Lime is a white powder obtained by heating chalk or limestone. It is mixed with water and sand to make mortar or plaster used to coat and whiten walls. It is precisely on this white lime coating that mysterious fingers trace the frightening inscription: "Daniel 5:5" describes fingers writing on "the lime of the wall of the royal palace."
2. By extension, the word refers to the coating itself, this white layer that covered the walls of ancient palaces and was easy to see and notice.
3. The image of lime also evokes what is white and visible, a surface that hides nothing — which makes the invisible hand writing on it all the more striking, exposing a terrible message to the light of day.
H1528.origine: The Aramaic word גִּיר (gir) literally means "chalk" or "limestone." It is related to the Hebrew גִּר (gir, H1615), which has the same meaning. These terms simply evoke the raw white powdery material extracted from the earth.
H1528.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 5:5. It is used in the context of the great feast of King Belshazzar of Babylon. At the precise moment when the proud monarch takes the cups from the temple of Jerusalem, a mysterious hand appears and writes words on the whitewashed wall. This detail — writing on the lime — emphasizes the supernatural aspect and clarity of the message: it is a visible act, impossible to hide or ignore.
H1528.portee: This mention of lime reminds us that God marks the history of men in a visible and indelible way. Just as the inscription on the wall of Babylon was a public sign of divine judgment, the word of God is written in our lives in a way that cannot be evaded. Nothing can erase what God wants to manifest.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy
Son of Jahdai and grandson of Caleb
H1529.detail: 1. Guéschan is a man who belongs to the lineage of Judah, living during the period of the Divided Monarchy (approximately 10th-6th centuries BC). His name appears only once in the entire Bible, in the genealogy of Caleb. 2. He is the son of Jahdai, who is himself counted among the descendants of Caleb. His name appears alongside his brothers: Reguem, Jotham, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph, all listed in the genealogical record preserved in the heart of the Chronicles.
H1529.origine: The Hebrew name Guéschan (גֵּישָׁן) literally means "piece" or "mass." It belongs to a family of Levantine genealogy and reflects the concrete and descriptive names common among the Hebrews. This name appears in the context of the genealogies of Judah, an important part of the genealogical work of the compiler of the Chronicles who aimed to preserve the memory of the families and tribes of Israel.
H1529.emploi: Guéschan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47, in the long genealogy of Caleb son of Jephunneh. This passage lists the children of Jahdai, including Guéschan. This unique usage shows that Guéschan was a minor figure in the history of Israel, important enough to be included in the official genealogical records, but with no particular role reported in Scripture. His mention in the Chronicles highlights the importance attached by the post-exilic community to the traceability of tribal and family lineages.

sens: Heap or accumulation of stones
Mass of ruins
Entanglement, intertwining
Waves (figuratively to denote God's punishments)
H1530G.detail:
1. A heap of piled stones: this is the most concrete and frequent meaning. Jacob and Laban raise a heap of stones as a testimony of covenant between them (Genesis 31:46), and Joshua has one erected over the body of Achan to remind of his punishment (Joshua 7:26). It is a public, memorial act: the heap of stones speaks to future generations.
2. A mass of ruins resulting from the destruction of a city or fortification. Isaiah announces that God will reduce Jerusalem to a heap of stones if it persists in evil (Isaiah 25:2). It is the image of complete destitution, a city reduced to nothing: where walls and palaces once stood, only shapeless debris remains.
3. The entanglement or intertwining: Job 8:17 speaks of the roots of a tree intertwining among the stones. The word here describes a dense network, a knot of threads or roots interwoven with one another.
4. Figuratively, the waves or floods of divine punishment. Although less attested, this meaning reminds us that the word gal can also evoke movement and wave, used metaphorically for the misfortunes that fall like a deluge upon the wicked.
H1530G.origine: The word gal fundamentally means "to roll" or "to tumble." A heap of stones is an accumulation that rolls together naturally, piling up. The verb galal (to roll) shares the same root, as does the noun gal in the sense of "wave" or "flow" that rolls on the sea. This image of rolling and accumulation permeates the word: whether it is stones piling up or water accumulating and rolling, it is always an idea of collective movement and mass.
H1530G.emploi: The word appears about 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly to designate heaps of stones that men raise as testimony or to seal a place. In Genesis (31:46-52), the heap marks a covenant between Jacob and Laban: it is a cairn, a landmark. In Joshua and Samuel, the heap of stones covers the body of a man executed or slain, marking the place of ignominy or divine judgment. In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah), the word is used to describe the complete ruin of a city: "You have reduced it to a heap" (Isaiah 25:2). An occurrence in Job 8:17 gives the word the sense of intertwining. It is a concrete and memorial term: the heap speaks, testifies, marks the territory and history of the people.
H1530G.portee: The heap of stones reveals how God orders history and how a people remembers. Each heap in Scripture is a monument: it consecrates a covenant, a judgment, a victory. For the believer, it is a lesson: the silent stones become witnesses, the ruins tell of God's faithfulness or anger. The word invites us to recognize in the visible events of this world the marks of the Lord's judgment and grace.

sens: Wave, undulating movement of the sea
Set of waves, agitation of the water's surface
Jet or spring of water (source)
Image of the force that invades and submerges
Divine punishment coming in successive waves
H1530H.detail:
1. The wave is primarily a moving swell: a rising of the sea water. God commands the waves of the sea not to exceed certain limits: "You shall not pass beyond" (Job 38:11), as if to say that each wave has its boundaries.
2. The word also refers to the entirety of these waves that roar and rise. Psalms 65:8 speaks of the "roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves," suggesting a continuous noise of raging waves.
3. The wave can also be a spring of gushing water: in Song of Solomon 4:12, the beloved is compared to "a sealed fountain," water that gushes but remains contained.
4. Figuratively, the wave becomes what advances, invades, submerges like an irresistible wave: Jeremiah 51:42 states that Babylon will be "covered by the waves of the sea."
5. The waves also represent the Lord's punishment that comes in repeated waves: Psalms 42:8 says, "All your waves and your billows have gone over me," an image of misfortune that submerges the heart.
H1530H.origine: The Hebrew word גַּל (gal) comes from a root that evokes the movement of rolling and wave. Its basic image is that of something rolling, rising, and falling — like a wave on the sea. This same root can also evoke the idea of gushing, hence the meaning of source or jet of water. In the vocabulary of the sea, it is the key word for talking about moving waves.
H1530H.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, among the prophets (Jeremiah, Isaiah, Ezekiel), and in a few wisdom books. In marine contexts, it designates the waves that God governs: He raises the sea, calms the waves, and sets their limits (Jeremiah 5:22 and 31:35). Figuratively, the waves become an image of disaster or suffering: when God punishes, His chastisements come "like waves" (Jonah 2:4). The word is also used for gushing water, the spring (Song of Solomon 4:12).
H1530H.portee: Understanding the word wave helps the reader grasp how the Bible speaks of God's power over nature: the fiercest waves obey the Lord, who marks their limits and calms them. It is a comfort for those going through trials: their misfortunes, however terrible, do not overflow the boundaries that God has set. The word also reminds us that our lives, like water, can be either turbulent or calm depending on the intervention of the sovereign God.

sens: One who shaves the beard and hair with a razor
H1532.detail: 1. The barber is a craftsman who uses a razor to shave or cut the beard and hair. In Ezekiel's vision (5:1), the Lord commands the prophet to take a barber's razor to completely shave his head and beard, a symbolic act that announces the destruction of Jerusalem: the shaved hair represents the judgment that falls upon the city and its inhabitants.
H1532.origine: The Hebrew word gallāb comes from a root that expresses the idea of "shaving" or "removing by shaving." This occupational name designates one who practices this art. The word evokes a profession known in the ancient Near East, where shaving was a common practice for hygiene and appearance.
H1532.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 5:1. It is situated in a dramatic passage where the prophet must perform a symbolic act: completely shaving with a barber's razor. This act serves as a sign of the divine judgment threatening besieged Jerusalem. The unique use of the term anchors the prophetic vision in the concrete reality of daily life: it is a true razor, such as a barber would use, that is the instrument of the divine message.
H1532.portee: This word reminds us how God uses ordinary objects of life to convey His prophetic message. The barber's razor becomes, in Ezekiel's hands, an instrument of proclamation of judgment and warning. It also shows that no profession, no everyday object escapes divine intention in the Scriptures.

sens: Mountain range east of the Jezreel Valley
Site of the death of Saul and Jonathan against the Philistines
H1533G.detail:
1. Gilboa is a mountain range that rises at the southeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley in Israel. In 1 Samuel 28:4, the Philistines and Saul set up their camps there before the decisive battle.
2. Gilboa is primarily the mountain where Saul and his son Jonathan meet their death in battle against the Philistines (2 Samuel 21:12). It is a place of tragic defeat for Israel: David curses the mountain in 2 Samuel 1:21, wishing that it receive neither dew nor rain, for the heroes and the king were defeated there.
H1533G.origine: The name Gilboa literally means "swollen heap" or "bulging mound," an image describing the shape of this mountain. Its spelling in the Segond is Gilboa. It is located in Upper Galilee, at the boundary between the fertile plain and the mountainous territories.
H1533G.emploi: Gilboa appears three times in the Bible, all in the books of Samuel. It is the site of the battle where Saul loses his life against the Philistines (2 Samuel 21:12), a foundational event marking the transition of kingship to David. In 2 Samuel 1:21, David pronounces a poetic curse on this mountain as a sign of mourning and anger over this defeat. These three uses forge the image of Gilboa as the place where Saul's former kingdom collapses.
H1533G.portee: Gilboa reminds us that faithfulness to God is more important than military strength or prestige: Saul, a king from whom God had turned away, loses everything there. For the believer, this mountain symbolizes the stakes of following or rejecting divine will.

sens: mountain at the southeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley
H1533H.detail: Gilboa is a mountain range that overlooks the great fertile plain of Jezreel to the southeast. It is the site of a decisive battle between the Israelites and the Philistines: Saul, the first king of Israel, and his son Jonathan met their deaths there (1 Samuel 31:1). The day after the battle, the Philistines discovered the bodies of Saul and his sons on this mountain (1 Samuel 31:8). A young man testified to having seen Saul wounded on the slope of Gilboa, pursued by the enemy's chariots (2 Samuel 1:6). These tragic events mark the end of Saul's reign and the establishment of Philistine dominance in Israel before David comes to power.
H1533H.origine: The name literally means "swollen heap" or "bulging mound," likely evoking the characteristic shape of this mountain ridge. The geographical site is located in Galilee, in the area corresponding to the current mountainous region of northwestern West Bank. The Hebrew name גִּלְבֹּעַ reflects the local relief features.
H1533H.emploi: Gilboa appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the accounts of the battle where Saul perished. It is mentioned in two parallel passages: 1 Samuel 31 and 1 Chronicles 10, both recounting Israel's defeat and the death of the king. A third testimony in 2 Samuel 1:6 reports the words of a survivor who saw Saul on the mountain, surrounded by enemy chariots. Thus, Gilboa becomes the symbol of the tragic end of the first reign and the fragility of human power in the face of trials.
H1533H.portee: The name Gilboa reminds the believer that even figures of power and prestige can experience a dramatic fall. It is a reminder that human victory is temporary without God's favor. For Bible readers, this place embodies a lesson in humility and the consequences of straying from divine obedience.

sens: Disk or cylinder that turns on an axis, used to move a vehicle or machine
Rapid and swirling rotational movement, particularly that of the wind which lifts dust or debris
Violent and chaotic natural phenomenon, an image of divine power or judgment
H1534.detail:
1. The wheel is the rotating disk that equips war chariots and carts: it rolls on the ground and allows the vehicle to advance. It is the major technical invention of the ancients, essential for military mobility. In Isaiah 5:28, the prophet describes the enemy army's chariots: "the wheels of its chariots" resemble a whirlwind, evoking both speed and destructive power.
2. The word also refers to the whirlwind or swirling of the wind that lifts dust and debris in a spiral. It is a violent, chaotic natural phenomenon, where everything wraps and is carried away. In Psalms 77:19, God acts "in the whirlwind" during the crossing of the Red Sea: the rotation of the waters symbolizes the irresistible force of divine judgment.
3. Figuratively, the wheel or whirlwind becomes an image of death, the passage of time, or judgment. In Ecclesiastes 12:8, the "wheel" that breaks symbolizes the collapse of the aging body and the approach of the end. It is a poetic image of inevitable decline.
H1534.origine: The word galgal comes from a root meaning "to roll" or "to turn." It is a pictorial word: it almost imitates the sound and movement of something rolling. The same root gives rise to related words denoting rolling, rotation, and cycle. In Hebrew, this word paints the image of circular movement, whether mechanical (the wheel of the chariot) or natural (the whirlwind of the wind).
H1534.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets and poems. It primarily designates the material wheels of war chariots (Isaiah 5:28, Jeremiah 47:3, Ezekiel 23:24 and 26:10), which embody military power and speed of destruction. It also describes the whirlwind of divine wind, particularly in contexts of judgment: Psalms 77:19 and 83:14 use this term to evoke God's anger or power. In Ezekiel (10:2, 10:6, 10:13), the wheels become mysterious and celestial, instruments of the theophany. The meaning thus nuances from the concrete (the wheel of the chariot) to the figurative (the whirlwind of judgment) to the symbolic and divine (the wheels of God's throne).
H1534.portee: This word reminds the reader that the earthly power of chariots and armies lasts only a moment in the face of divine power. The whirlwind symbolizes God's justice that lifts and carries away all that opposes Him. For the believer, it is an invitation not to fear the powers of the world, but to contemplate God's absolute sovereignty in judgment and the protection of His people.

sens: round object that turns on an axis
element of a chariot or mechanism
symbol of divine power and movement
H1535.detail:
1. A wheel is a circular object capable of turning on a central axis, used for transport or the functioning of machines. It is the concrete image of the word: something that rolls.
2. In ancient chariots and mechanisms, the wheel is an essential part that enables movement. It thus represents mobility and efficiency.
3. In Daniel's vision, the wheels of the Ancient of Days' throne are described as a burning fire (Daniel 7:9), which gives them a spiritual dimension: they symbolize divine power, inexhaustible energy, and God's present vigilance that oversees everything and acts at all times.
H1535.origine: This Aramaic word is closely related to its Hebrew equivalent (H1534). The wheel is a fundamental human invention, and the word takes up the image of something round and turning. In both Hebrew and Aramaic, the word evokes the action of rolling or turning. This same image appears in prophetic visions where the wheel becomes a symbol of divine movement and God's vigilance.
H1535.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament and the Old Testament in Aramaic: Daniel 7:9, in the grand vision of the Ancient of Days' throne. Here, the wheels are not ordinary chariot wheels, but elements of the heavenly throne itself. The prophetic context transforms the technical object into a theological symbol. The detail that these wheels are "like a burning fire" emphasizes their superhuman and divine nature, marking the distinction between a mundane earthly mechanism and a blazing celestial reality.
H1535.portee: This image of the burning wheels of the divine throne reminds the believer that God is not immobile or distant: He is present, in motion, active. The wheel also suggests that nothing escapes His attention and that His power is constant. For the Christian reading Daniel, this vision affirms God's eternal sovereignty over all earthly empires that pass away.

sens: flat disk that turns on an axis
that which rolls and carries a vehicle
H1536.detail:
1. A wheel is a flat disk, usually made of wood, that turns around a central axis. It is the invention that allows carts to move. In Isaiah 28:28, the prophet speaks of threshing wheat: the wheel of the cart is pushed, crushing the grains as it rolls on the ground.
2. By extension, the wheel also refers to the cart itself or the transport mechanism: it is what rolls to carry and move things or people. The image evokes movement, weight, and productive force.
H1536.origine: The Hebrew word galgal comes from a root expressing the idea of turning, rolling. This root is very ancient in Semitic languages and is rooted in the experience of circular rolling. The word literally designates that which turns and moves in a circle, the quintessential rolling object. Other words of the same family in Hebrew also evoke circular movement or the action of turning.
H1536.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Hebrew, in Isaiah 28:28. In this verse, Isaiah uses the image of threshing wheat to illustrate divine judgment: God does not break indefinitely, but acts with measure. The wheel of the cart, rolling over the grains, progressively crushes them—this is a common agricultural tool in Israel. The context shows the wheel as a daily element of plowing and threshing the harvests.
H1536.portee: This simple yet powerful image from Isaiah reminds us that God's judgment is intelligent and proportionate, like the farmer's work who uses the right tools at the right time. For the reader, it invites recognition that God acts with wisdom in what seems harsh: like the wheel that crushes the wheat to separate the grain, God works according to His knowledge and justice.

sens: City in the West Bank, first encampment of the Israelites after crossing the Jordan
Place of worship and gathering in ancient Israel
Sanctuary where sacrifices and religious rites were performed
H1537G.detail:
1. Gilgal is the name of a city located east of Jericho, in the West Bank. It is where the Israelites established their first encampment after crossing the Jordan under the leadership of Joshua (Joshua 4:19-20). The name evokes the idea of "circle" or "rolling," perhaps referring to the twelve stones set in a circle as a monument at this location.
2. Gilgal becomes the seat of power and justice in Israel. Samuel serves as a judge there, regularly traveling to this city to administer justice to the people (1 Samuel 7:16). It is also at Gilgal that Saul is proclaimed king by the assembly of Israel (1 Samuel 11:14-15).
3. The site is used for religious rites and sacrifices. Offerings are presented to the Lord there, including spoils after military victories (1 Samuel 15:21). However, during the time of the prophets, Gilgal becomes a place of idolatrous worship, and the prophets denounce illegitimate religious practices there (Hosea 4:15, Amos 4:4).
H1537G.origine: The Hebrew word גִּלְגָּל (gilgal) literally means "wheel" or "rolling"; it derives from the root galal which expresses the idea of rolling or turning. The name of the place alludes to the monument of the twelve stones rolled from the Jordan, set in a circle at Gilgal to commemorate the passage of God's people. This geographical name thus carries the memory of the miracle of the crossing.
H1537G.emploi: Gilgal appears more than thirty times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of Joshua and Samuel, which describe the time of conquest and judgment. It is first the gathering camp where Joshua establishes his headquarters during the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 9:6, 10:43). Later, it is the seat where Samuel administers justice (1 Samuel 7:16) and where Saul is anointed king (1 Samuel 11:14-15). Over time, Gilgal gains religious significance: sacrifices are offered there in honor of the Lord (1 Samuel 15:21). However, during the time of the 8th and 7th century prophets (Hosea, Amos, Micah), the city becomes a center of perverted worship, where Israel diverts true worship of God into idolatrous practices (Hosea 4:15, Amos 4:4).
H1537G.portee: Gilgal reminds the believer that the establishment of God's people in the promised land marked a decisive turning point in the history of salvation. It is a memorial place that celebrates God's faithful intervention. However, its evolution into a sanctuary of idolatrous worship warns the reader that proximity to a holy place does not guarantee spiritual fidelity: only a heart turned toward the true God truly matters.

sens: Residence of the prophets in Northern Israel
City near Bethel and Shiloh
H1537H.detail: Gilgal is a site inhabited in northern Israel, about seven kilometers from Shiloh and Bethel. It is where the prophets lived: Elijah and Elisha spent time there, as shown in the accounts where Elijah departs from Gilgal before being taken up to heaven (2 Kings 2:1), and where Elisha returns to teach the sons of the prophets gathered around him (2 Kings 4:38).
H1537H.origine: The name Gilgal literally means "wheel" or "roll" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a circular shape of the site or a movement of rotation. It is a proper place name, distinct from Gilgal in the West Bank mentioned in other biblical texts. The name reflects the geography of the biblical world where places often bore the name of a natural feature or visual impression.
H1537H.emploi: Gilgal appears twice in the Bible, both in the second book of Kings. It is the seat of a community of prophets living together under the leadership of a major prophet. In 2 Kings 2:1, Elijah departs from there to be taken up to heaven. In 2 Kings 4:38, Elisha returns there to share life with the prophetic disciples and provide for their food during a time of famine. This small prophetic center seems to have been an important spiritual home in northern Israel.

sens: Region of the territory conquered by Joshua
H1537I.detail: 1. Gilgal is a region that Joshua conquered upon entering the Promised Land. It appears in the list of defeated kingdoms (Joshua 12:23), where it is mentioned as an area that Israel subdued under Joshua's command.
H1537I.origine: The Hebrew word גִּלְגָּל (gilgal) literally means "a wheel" or "that which rolls," evoking the image of circular movement. It is another form of the word galit (גָּלִיל, Galilee), which designates the region of Galilee. The name likely reflects the characteristics of the terrain or landscape of this region.
H1537I.emploi: Gilgal appears only once in the Bible translated into French from the Segond 1910, in Joshua 12:23. It is included in the summary of Joshua's military conquests, listed as a region whose king was defeated. The context indicates that it was one of the lands administered by indigenous kingdoms before Israel took possession.

sens: The part of the human or animal body above the neck, containing the brain and face
The skull, bone of the head
A person, as a unit to count in a census
H1538.detail:
1. The head is the upper part of the body: it is the seat of life and personhood. In 2 Kings 9:35, only Jezebel's skull remains after her fall, an image of violent death and total destruction.
2. The skull specifically refers to the bones of the head. This is the literal and anatomical sense of the word.
3. In the sense of counting, "per head" means "per person": each individual is counted. In Exodus 16:16, the omer of manna is distributed "per head," that is, to each person according to their need. In Numbers 1:2 and 1:20, the counting of the Israelites is done "per head," meaning counting each man individually. This is the most common usage in the Bible.
H1538.origine: The Hebrew word גֻּלְגֹּ֫לֶת (gulgollet) is derived from a root that suggests something round or rolled. The head, due to its spherical shape, inspired this name. The same type of imagery exists in other languages: the round shape of the head gives it its name. The word evokes both the living head and the bony skull after death.
H1538.emploi: This word appears about 12 times in the Hebrew Bible. It has two main uses: first, it literally refers to the head and skull (2 Kings 9:35, 1 Chronicles 10:10). But most importantly, it is used in census texts: Exodus 16:16, Exodus 38:26, Numbers 1:2, 1:18, 1:20, 1:22, Numbers 3:47, 1 Chronicles 23:3, 23:24. In these administrative and religious contexts, "per head" means "per person" or "per individual," and the word designates the counting unit. It is a very practical term for the censuses of Israel and the distribution of offerings to the sanctuary.
H1538.portee: This word reminds us that each person counts in the eyes of God. When the Bible counts Israel "per head," it affirms that the Lord knows each of His children, not as a mass, but individually. This attention to the individual person runs throughout the entire biblical revelation.

sens: The outer covering that protects the human body
A visible sign of physical suffering or affliction
H1539.detail: 1. The skin is the natural covering that protects the human body. It is our first barrier with the outside world, what identifies and distinguishes us. 2. When speaking of "covering one's skin" or marking it, it expresses intense suffering and deep affliction. In Job 16:15, the suffering man says: "I have sewn sackcloth upon my skin," meaning he has put on the coarse garment of mourning over his entire body — a gesture that outwardly manifests the intimate pain he endures.
H1539.origine: The Hebrew word *gueled* simply refers to the skin that covers the body. It belongs to the basic vocabulary of the human body in the Bible. The skin is often mentioned as the seat or visible witness of illness, injury, or mourning — linking this word to the concrete experience of suffering.
H1539.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 16:15. It is Job who speaks, in the midst of his most intense sufferings, listing the signs of his affliction: he has donned a mourning sack upon his skin and has rolled in the dust. This passage shows how the skin becomes the visible place where inner distress is inscribed.
H1539.portee: This image reminds us that suffering does not remain hidden — it marks the entire body and manifests itself through our gestures, our clothing, our appearance. For the Christian reader, this reveals how the Bible takes seriously the physical reality of pain, without reducing it to something purely spiritual. Job truly suffers, in his whole body.

sens: A man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Ehud
H1540G.detail: Heglam is a descendant of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Ehud and the brother of Naaman, Ahijah, Uzza, and Ahihud (1 Chronicles 8:7). He is a figure from the time preceding the Israelite monarchy, of whom only the name and his place in the genealogy of Benjamin are known.
H1540G.origine: The name Heglam appears in Hebrew as a variant or another name for Gera (הֶגְרָא). The genealogies of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles preserve the names of ancient families, even when little information is given about these individuals.
H1540G.emploi: Heglam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:7, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. He is presented as the son of Ehud in the genealogy of this tribe. This genealogical context shows that the Bible carefully preserves the names of Israelite ancestors, even for figures whose particular history has not been reported.

sens: To uncover, expose, make visible what was hidden
To make known, manifest, speak openly
To show, appear, present oneself
To exile, take into captivity
H1540H.detail:
1. To reveal primarily means to uncover or expose what was covered or hidden. It is to remove the veil to make visible. Job speaks of one who "brings to light what is hidden in darkness" (Job 12:22): buried secrets suddenly become visible in the light.
2. The word also denotes the act of making known, communicating hidden or secret information. When Proverbs says that "a slanderer reveals secrets" (Proverbs 20:19), it speaks of someone who exposes what was entrusted to them in silence.
3. To reveal can mean to show oneself, appear, present oneself to someone. When Jonathan says to his armor-bearer, "let us show ourselves to them" (1 Samuel 14:8), he speaks of uncovering, allowing his presence to be seen.
4. In certain historical contexts, the word takes on the meaning of exiling or deporting: "to be revealed" can mean "to be taken into exile," a term that refers to the tearing away and forced removal from the land.
H1540H.origine: The Hebrew verb galah comes from a root that fundamentally means to uncover or discover what was covered. The image is that of lifting a veil, removing what hides. The word encompasses this idea of unveiling in all its aspects: physical (to expose), informational (to reveal a secret), or personal (to show oneself). This root has produced terms of the same family that reinforce the idea of uncovering what was previously concealed.
H1540H.emploi: The verb galah appears 41 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical books (Samuel, Chronicles), wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs), and prophetic texts (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). The meaning of "reveal" overwhelmingly dominates: God reveals Himself to Abraham (Genesis 35:7), to Samuel (1 Samuel 3:7, 3:21), He reveals His secrets to the prophets (Amos 3:7). The verb also characterizes one who divulges secrets or confidences (Proverbs 11:13, 20:19). In judgment or punishment texts, it expresses the uncovering of hidden crimes: "the earth will reveal the blood" (Isaiah 26:21), meaning that murders will finally be discovered and judged. The context always determines the precise meaning: spiritual and relational when it concerns God or His word, moral when it involves secrets and sins.
H1540H.portee: This word invites the believer to grasp that God is not silent or hidden forever: He reveals Himself, makes known His will and His works. It is a comfort for one who cries out to Him, knowing that God can manifest His power and mercy. Conversely, to reveal also reminds us that nothing remains hidden in God's eyes: crimes, secret thoughts, injustices will be brought to light. The believer is called to transparency, to reject lies and slander that reveal others' secrets inappropriately.

sens: Remove the veil or clothing that covers something or someone
Expose, reveal by uncovering intimacy or nudity
Reveal a secret, hidden information, make known
Show or make oneself clearly known, reveal one's nature or presence
Remove, take away completely
H1540I.detail:
1. Discover primarily means to remove what covers a thing or a person. When Noah gets drunk, he "uncovers himself" in his tent (Genesis 9:21): his garment falls off or he removes it, exposing his body. This is the most physical and concrete sense.

2. Discover can mean to lay someone bare or expose their intimacy, especially in the context of forbidden sexual relations. The laws of Leviticus repeat: "You shall not uncover the nakedness of" your mother, your sister, etc. (Leviticus 18:6-18). This is deliberate language for illegitimate unions.

3. Discover can also mean to reveal a secret or hidden information. When God "unveils" the hiding places of Esau (Jeremiah 49:10), He exposes them, makes them visible: He reveals what was concealed.

4. Discover also means to show clearly, to reveal the deep nature of something or someone. When the psalmist prays, "Open my eyes" (Psalms 119:18), he asks God to uncover for him, to reveal the wonders of His law: to make them perceptible and understandable.
H1540I.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that fundamentally means "to remove the cover" or "to unveil." The initial image is physical: to take away what covers. This root is used in many forms: the Qal (simple form) means "to uncover" or "to go into exile"; the Niphal (reflexive form) means "to uncover oneself" or "to be uncovered"; the Piel (intensive form) emphasizes the act of "completely revealing"; the Hiphil means "to cause an exile." The word combines the idea of physically exposing and spiritually revealing.
H1540I.emploi: This verb appears about 58 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is very frequent in the laws of Leviticus (18 and 20), where it describes forbidden sexual relations with various women: it is legal and moral language. It is also found in historical narratives (Genesis, Samuel) for concrete physical actions. In the Psalms and Isaiah, it takes on a more spiritual meaning: God "unveils" His counsel or judgments, He "reveals" what was hidden. The same word can thus refer to both physical nakedness and spiritual revelation, depending on the context.
H1540I.portee: This word shows the biblical thought on intimacy and revelation. In itself, "discover" is not wrong: God "uncovers" Himself when He reveals His mysteries to His prophets. But uncovering another's intimacy without respect or legitimacy is a serious act that violates dignity. The word reminds us that the Bible honors secrecy and intimacy, and that exposing what should remain hidden is a sin. It also speaks to us of God's action: He is the one who reveals the truth and uncovers what is hidden, for our judgment and salvation.

sens: make known officially
bring to the knowledge of all
disclose information
reveal what was hidden
H1540J.detail: 1. The primary and concrete meaning is that of "discovering" or "removing what covers" — the image of pulling aside a veil. In Esther 3:14 and 8:13, the word means "to publish" a royal edict: the king has his decree posted in all the provinces, making it public and official. It is an official communication intended to be known by all. 2. The word can also mean "to inform" or "bring to knowledge": the king's letters "informed" the peoples of the royal will and the appointed day. 3. In other books of the Bible, this verb also expresses the idea of "revealing" what was secret or hidden — whether it be news, a truth, or even an identity. 4. The word can finally evoke "exile" — the sense of "to go away" or "to depart" — because exile is a situation that "uncovers" or "reveals" God's judgment on a people.
H1540J.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּלָה (galah) comes from a root that primarily expresses the physical action of discovering or removing a cover. This concrete image naturally extends to that of making public, making known, revealing. The same family of words produces other verbs that retain these nuances: to remove the secret, to manifest, to bring to light. This is why the word can mean both "to publish an edict" (to publicly uncover a decree) and "to reveal" (to remove the veil of secrecy).
H1540J.emploi: This verb appears rarely in the Segond with the meaning of "to publish": the two main occurrences are in the book of Esther (3:14 and 8:13), where it describes the official publication of royal edicts. In these contexts, the edict "invited" or "informed" the peoples: the action was to circulate, to widely disseminate a decision of the king. Elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, this same verb takes on other meanings — notably that of revealing a secret, uncovering, or exiling — depending on whether the object complement evokes an act, a hidden truth, or a person. The common nuance remains the idea of making public or visible what was not.
H1540J.portee: This word reminds us that certain truths must be brought to light, communicated publicly to be heard by all. In the context of Esther, the royal edicts must be "published" so that everyone can prepare and understand the king's orders. For the believer, this evokes the importance of proclamation and revelation: God Himself "publishes" His plans, and His servants are called to make known His will, without keeping it hidden.

sens: To remove someone from their place, to lead them elsewhere, especially into exile or captivity
To transport something from one place to another, to take it away
To be taken, ripped from one's land and deported
To reveal, to uncover, to disclose
H1540K.detail:
1. Take captive: this means to tear someone away from their home to lead them into exile, often by force. This is what happens to the people of Israel deported to Babylon (Jeremiah 29:4: "Thus says the Lord... to all the captives whom I have taken from Jerusalem to Babylon"). The historical context involves kingdoms that deport conquered peoples.
2. To transport, to remove: the word describes the physical action of moving, of taking something or someone away from a place. Isaiah 38:12: "My dwelling is plucked up and removed far from me," where the prophet compares his life to a tent that is taken away. It is a violent or definitive movement.
3. To undergo captivity, to be exiled: this refers to being on the side of one who suffers abduction. The Danites do evil and remain in exile for a long time (Judges 18:30: "until the time of the captivity of the land"), or Judah is taken captive to Babylon (1 Chronicles 9:1).
4. To reveal, to uncover: beyond physical exile, the verb can mean to lay bare, to unveil what was hidden. This less common nuance in the provided usages shows that the word touches on the idea of removing a veil, making visible.
H1540K.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּלָה (galah) evokes the image of uncovering, removing a veil or an obstacle. It comes from a root that denotes the action of revealing by taking away what covers. In the Old Testament, the word carries a strong historical connotation: it refers to the mass deportation of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah by Mesopotamian powers (Assyria, Babylon). The same root produces words for exile and captivity, as stripping a people is to reveal their nakedness and humiliation.
H1540K.emploi: The verb galah appears approximately 66 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the historical books (2 Kings, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel) and the Chronicles, which recount the exile of Samaria (2 Kings 17) and Judah (2 Kings 24-25). The predominant meaning is "to take captive" (22 occurrences) and "to take away" (15 occurrences), showing that deportation is the central event. Jeremiah often repeats it: the Lord "takes away" His people because of unfaithfulness, but He will also bring them back (Jeremiah 29:14: "I will be found by you, and I will restore your captives"). Ezekiel uses the word to signify that God reveals His holiness to the nations by exiling Israel (Ezekiel 39:23-28). Thus, the word carries a theology: exile is not merely a political misfortune; it is the act by which God manifests Himself and purifies His people.
H1540K.portee: For the Christian reader, this word roots the reality of exile as God's judgment on unfaithfulness, but also as a step toward salvation: God does not reject His people; He disciplines them and brings them back. Exile reminds us that the absence of God in life is the true misfortune, and that returning to Him is the only liberation. It is a lesson on divine justice and mercy intertwined.

sens: To make known what was hidden, secret, or unknown
To bring to light, to discover what was concealed
To show openly, to manifest
To deport, to take into exile (secondary meaning)
H1541.detail:
1. To make known what was hidden, secret, or unknown: the word describes the action of unveiling a secret, a mystery. In Daniel 2:19, the secret of Nebuchadnezzar's dream is "revealed" to Daniel in a night vision — what was impossible to know suddenly becomes manifest. It is an action that transforms ignorance into knowledge.
2. To bring to light, to discover what was concealed: similar to the first meaning, but emphasizes more the aspect of what was buried. Daniel 2:22 describes it this way: God "reveals what is deep and hidden," suggesting that the secret already existed, but God brings it out of the shadow.
3. To show openly, to manifest: the word can refer to making visible or public what was private. God who "reveals secrets" (Daniel 2:28-29) acts as one who exposes hidden truth to the light of day.
4. To deport, to take into exile: a derived, less frequent meaning. In Ezra 5:12, the king "took the people captive" to Babylon — here the word means to remove and take away, to deport (a meaning that pertains to a particular nuance of the verb).
H1541.origine: The Aramaic word גְּלָא (gelah) is closely related to the image of making visible, of removing what covers. Its root suggests the action of denuding, of bringing to light — which explains the two main meanings: on one hand, to reveal a secret (removing what hides it), and on the other hand, to deport (removing someone from their homeland). In Hebrew, the verb גָּלָה (galah) has similar usages. The corresponding Hebrew word in the Greek Septuagint is often rendered by ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalyptô), "to reveal, to uncover."
H1541.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 8 times in the provided biblical texts, almost exclusively in the books of Daniel and Ezra, which are written in Aramaic. The meaning of "to reveal" overwhelmingly dominates: it is God who reveals mysteries, secrets hidden from men (Daniel 2:19, 2:22, 2:28, 2:29). This context of divine revelation is consistent with the theology of Daniel: God alone knows what is hidden and can make it known to whomever He wishes. The meaning of "to deport, to take captive" also appears (Ezra 4:10, Ezra 5:12), describing the actions of kings who transport peoples. Both meanings stem from the same root image: to bring to light, to remove from one's place.
H1541.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds a central truth: God is not limited by what is hidden from men. Secrets, mysteries, God's designs — all of this is transparent to Him, and He can choose to reveal it to His servants according to His wisdom. It is a source of assurance: we are not left in absolute ignorance. God can and wants to enlighten us about what truly matters for our lives and our future.

sens: mountain town in Judah
H1542.detail: 1. Guilo is a small town located in the mountains of Judah, listed among the cities of the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:51). It is a real geographical place, mentioned to mark the boundaries and possessions of God's people.
H1542.origine: The name Guilo literally means "exile" in Hebrew, which could evoke a particular past or situation of the place. Its inhabitants are called Guilonites (in Hebrew: Giléni).
H1542.emploi: Guilo appears twice in the Bible. First, it is simply listed as one of the cities in the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:51). Then, it becomes notable as the birthplace of Ahithophel, the very wise counselor of King David who revolts with Absalom and gives counsel against David himself (2 Samuel 15:12). It is through this connection with Ahithophel that Guilo gains spiritual significance in the biblical narrative.

sens: Basin or reservoir of water that springs naturally from the ground
Cup or bowl-shaped container designed to hold a liquid
Rounded or bulging part of a column capital
H1543.detail:
1. A source is a point where water naturally springs from the earth. It is a precious resource in arid or semi-arid regions: when Caleb gives his daughter in marriage, she asks him for land and also for water sources to irrigate it (Joshua 15:19). The word thus refers to both the springing forth and the natural reservoir itself.

2. In a more general sense, the word applies to any rounded, bulging container made to hold a liquid — a cup or a bowl. The lamp of the temple's menorah, for example, is made of small vases shaped like flowers (Zechariah 4:2).

3. In architecture, it also refers to the protruding and rounded part of a column capital — the ornament that crowns the top of a column. Solomon's temple had magnificent ones, decorated with pomegranates (1 Kings 7:41-42).
H1543.origine: The Hebrew word גֻּלָּה (gullah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of rolling, turning around, hence the bulging or rounded shape. This same family is found in other Hebrew words designating round or hollow objects. The basic image is that of something rounded — whether it is a source that forms a small natural basin, a container with curved walls, or the swollen part of a column.
H1543.emploi: The word gullah appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, distributed across two main usages. First as "source" in the accounts of Caleb and his daughter (Joshua 15:19 and Judges 1:15): it refers to perennial water sources, essential for irrigating the lands of the Negev. Secondly, as an element of religious architecture: in the descriptions of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7 and 2 Chronicles 4), it designates the rounded bulges of the capitals. It is also encountered in the prophetic visions of Zechariah to describe the shapes of the sacred menorah. The context reveals each time a useful or precious object — vital water, functional utensils, or ornaments of the sanctuary.
H1543.portee: This word reminds us of the vital importance of water in the life of God's people, especially in the promised land. A "source" is a gift that sustains life: it symbolizes abundance and blessing where dryness reigns. By asking Caleb for sources, his daughter is not asking for luxury, but for the ability to survive and thrive on her land. For the believer, it is an image of dependence on God as the source of life.

sens: Sculpted or shaped representation of a deity or supernatural being, object of worship and adoration
Painted or engraved image of a false deity
That which one turns their gaze and heart to worship instead of the true God
H1544.detail:
1. An idol is primarily a statue, a figure sculpted from stone or wood, used to represent and venerate a false deity. In Leviticus 26:30, the Lord promises to destroy the idols of the Israelites: these objects were visible, tangible, that could be overturned and burned. Ezekiel 8:10 describes "idols" painted on the walls of the Temple, showing that the word can also refer to images engraved or represented on surfaces.

2. The word more broadly designates any object, image, or statue that embodies a false deity and becomes the focal point of worship and adoration. In Ezekiel 23:37, the women (Samaria and Jerusalem) have "committed adultery with their idols" — the idol is the object of religious infidelity, showing that it represents an illegitimate and forbidden relationship.

3. Spiritually, an idol is what one looks at, that which one lifts their eyes to serve instead of the true God. In Ezekiel 18:6, the one who "does not lift their eyes to the idols" remains faithful to God alone. The word evokes a deviation of the heart: turning one's affection, hope, and obedience toward a creature or an illusion rather than toward the Creator.
H1544.origine: The Hebrew word גִּלּוּל (gillul) comes from a root meaning "to roll" or "to turn"; it carries the image of something round, formed, shaped. Some commentators also see a connection with the idea of "defilement" or "rolling away." This word is specific to biblical Hebrew and becomes particularly frequent in the writings of the prophet Ezekiel, who uses it to denounce Israel's religious infidelity. The term stands in stark opposition to any form of worship of the living God.
H1544.emploi: The word "idol" appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the books of Kings (notably during the religious reforms of Josiah in 2 Kings 23:24) and is heavily used by Ezekiel, who employs it nearly 30 times. In historical accounts, idols are what faithful kings destroy and what unfaithful kings tolerate or worship: they mark Israel's apostasy. In Deuteronomy 29:17, Moses warns the people not to turn to idols. In Ezekiel, the word becomes the central emblem of Jerusalem's spiritual corruption: the prophet repeatedly refers to "idols" to show that it is idolatry that provokes God's anger and justifies the Exile. The word always carries a strongly negative connotation: it is an abomination, a profanation, a betrayal.
H1544.portee: Understanding what an idol is in the biblical sense liberates the modern Christian reader. An idol is not just an ancient statue: it is anything we serve, look to, expect from, or worship instead of the living God — wealth, reputation, pleasure, personal ambition. The word invites every believer to examine their heart: what do they truly lift their eyes to? The eternal significance is that idolatry causes separation from God, while true faithfulness brings blessing and life.

sens: Mantle or sumptuous garment worn as adornment
Precious textile, richly dyed or embroidered
Luxury item or valuable merchandise
H1545.detail:
1. The word designates a garment of splendor, a mantle or a dress intended for adornment and ornamentation. It is a garment that elegantly envelops the body, one that is worn to be seen, not merely to cover. In Ezekiel 27:24, the prophet lists the luxury goods that peoples brought as tribute to Tyre, among which are these "blue-dyed mantles," adorned with embroidery: these were precious textiles, crafted with artistry.
2. The term emphasizes the richness and quality of the fabric: these mantles were not ordinary garments, but fine cloths, dyed in rare colors (such as blue), often enhanced with embroidery. Blue, in particular, was a costly hue in antiquity, reserved for the wealthy and powerful.
3. More broadly, the word can refer to any precious merchandise, any luxury item, because the sumptuous garment is, above all, an object of value and prestige: in the context of Tyre's commerce, these mantles are listed as riches, valuable goods.
H1545.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to wrap" or "to cover." This is why it primarily designates what envelops the body — a garment — and more specifically a garment of fine appearance, a mantle that frames and highlights the one who wears it. The family of this word includes terms related to wrapping, covering, and anything that adorns.
H1545.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 27:24. The prophet then lists the products that merchants brought to Tyre, the great trading city: among the goods — gold, silver, spices, precious stones — are these blue-dyed mantles, richly embroidered. The context clearly shows that these are luxury items, of prestige, goods of exceptional market value. These mantles are not utilitarian garments, but pieces of adornment, symbols of wealth and power.
H1545.portee: This passage about Tyre reminds the believer of the vanity of earthly riches. These magnificent mantles, these goods so precious in the eyes of the trading world, are listed in a prophetic oratorio about the fall of a splendid city — a fall that occurs despite all these riches. For the Christian reader, this invites them not to place their trust in luxury and adornment, but to seek first the riches of the Kingdom of God.

sens: State of one who is a prisoner, chained
Group of prisoners taken far from their country
Period or duration of imprisonment
Forced exile of a people far from their land
Condition of servitude or dependence
H1546.detail:
1. Captivity primarily refers to the state of being a prisoner: someone chained, confined, deprived of freedom. This is the situation of one who is forcibly held, like Jeremiah bound in chains among the captives of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 40:1).
2. It also refers to the group of captives themselves — the people taken prisoner. Jeremiah speaks of the captives of Judah who went to Babylon (Jeremiah 28:4), or Ezekiel of the captives of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 40:1).
3. Captivity can also measure the duration: how long one remains a prisoner. "The thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin" (2 Kings 25:27) or "the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin" (Ezekiel 1:2) count the years since the beginning of the exile.
4. For Israel, captivity becomes exile: the entire people taken far from their land by a foreign power. It is the collective uprooting, the time when God's people live in a land of slavery, far from their homeland.
5. Figuratively, it can denote any form of servitude or dependence, the idea that someone is held under the yoke of another power.
H1546.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be in exile" or "to be far away." The Aramaic galouta (גָּלוּתָא) is closely related. In the Old Testament, the term first applies to the Babylonian exile (587 B.C.), the major event in Israel's history when the northern and southern kingdoms fell into the hands of the Assyrians and then the Babylonians. The word denotes both the personal fate of prisoners and the collective fate of the people.
H1546.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and in the accounts of the Kings. It is associated with the Babylonian exile: Jehoiachin remains a prisoner there, and the text counts the years of captivity in relation to the beginning of his exile (2 Kings 25:27, Ezekiel 1:2, Ezekiel 40:1). In Isaiah 45:13, Cyrus is called to free the captives of Judah. The prophets also use the word for other peoples: Amos mentions the captives sold (Amos 1:6, 1:9), and Obadiah speaks of captives (Obadiah 1:20). The meaning remains concrete: it is political imprisonment, collective or individual, and the uprooting from a land.
H1546.portee: For the people of Israel, the Babylonian captivity is one of the greatest trials in its history: it raises the question of divine punishment, of exile far from the promised land, and of the hope of restoration. Understanding this word helps the Christian reader grasp how God tests His people, brings them back to Him, and ultimately restores them. It is also a reminder that spiritual slavery — being captive to sin — is the human condition without God, and that only He can free us from it.

sens: State of one who is a prisoner or exiled from their homeland
Group of people taken into exile
Period during which a people remains in captivity
H1547.detail:
1. Captivity first refers to the state of one who has been made a prisoner or deported far from their country. It is the fate of one who has lost their freedom and lives under the yoke of a conqueror. Daniel is called "one of the captives of Judah" (Daniel 5:13): he was forcibly taken from his homeland and lives in exile in Babylon.
2. The word also designates the entire group of prisoners or exiles — those who have collectively undergone this deportation. In Ezra 6:16, we speak of the "sons of the captivity," meaning the descendants of the Judeans who were taken captive and who have now returned or live in exile.
3. Finally, it can name the period itself during which this people remains in captivity — the time of exile, from deportation to liberation or return.
H1547.origine: This Aramaic word, used in the books of Ezra and Daniel, comes from the Hebrew root גָּלָה (gala), which means "to remove, deport, exile." The corresponding Hebrew word, galuth (גָּלוּת), carries the same meaning. The family of words evokes the idea of a forced separation, a rupture with the homeland — a profound experience for the people of Israel during the Babylonian deportation.
H1547.emploi: This Aramaic word appears four times in the Bible, all in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which recount the Babylonian exile and the return of the people. In Ezra 6:16, it refers to the descendants of the exiles who returned to Jerusalem for the dedication of the Temple. In the three passages of Daniel (2:25; 5:13; 6:13), the word characterizes Daniel himself and his companions as "captives of Judah" — men torn from their people and held far from home. The use of the Aramaic word rather than the Hebrew reflects that these books narrate a period when Aramaic was the language of the Babylonian empire's administration.
H1547.portee: For the Christian, this word recalls a major historical reality: the exile of God's people, a trial through which God allowed His people to be humiliated, judged for their unfaithfulness, but also purified and prepared for a return and restoration. It is an invitation to meditate on God's patience and on the times when He allows His children to go through trials for their spiritual good.

sens: To cut all the hair or beard completely with a razor or blade
To remove hair, especially as a sign of purification or mourning
To strip or humiliate someone by shaving their beard or head
To completely destroy, devastate (figurative sense)
H1548.detail:
1. To shave means to cut very short or completely remove hair or beard with a sharp instrument. Joseph "shaved" before presenting himself to Pharaoh (Genesis 41:14), ending his prison neglect. It is a practical and common gesture, particularly in Egypt where shaved men were the norm.
2. In Israel, shaving often had religious or ritual significance. The healed leper had to "shave" all his hair on the seventh day of his purification (Leviticus 14:9); the Nazarite who completed his vow "shaved" his consecrated head (Numbers 6:18). It was a mark of transition from one state to another.
3. Shaving someone could also be an act of humiliation. When King Hanun had half of David's servants' beards "shaved" (2 Samuel 10:4), it was a serious affront: removing the beard equated to stripping a man of honor and dignity.
4. Figuratively, the prophet Isaiah uses this word to describe devastation: the Lord "will shave" the land as a razor removes hair, leaving everything bare and devoid (Isaiah 7:20). It is the image of total destruction.
H1548.origine: The Hebrew verb galach primarily means "to pass a sharp instrument over." The root evokes the idea of removing, stripping bare. In Hebrew, derivatives of the same root refer to baldness or lack of hair. This word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of body care and hygiene, early amplified in the biblical text to express ritual transformations or acts of symbolic violence.
H1548.emploi: The verb "to shave" appears 18 times, mainly in the Law (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) where it frames purification rites — the healed leper, the Nazarite fulfilling his vow. It also appears in historical accounts (Genesis, Judges, Samuel) where it describes personal hygiene (Joseph) or acts of humiliation (Hanun against David's servants, Hanun again in the Chronicles). The prophets use it figuratively to evoke ruin and devastation (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). Samson would invoke his refusal to shave as proof of his consecration to God (Judges 16:17): as long as his hair remains intact, his strength endures. Thus, shaving appears as a powerful marker of change of state, rupture, or curse.
H1548.portee: For the Christian reader, this word illuminates the biblical importance of the body and visible signs. Shaving is not a trivial cosmetic act: it symbolizes dying to oneself, purification, entering a new phase of consecration. Samson's shaved beard reminds us that the abandonment of what distinguishes us, what makes us strong in our own eyes, can be the path to true strength — the kind that comes from God alone. The gestures of the body speak.

sens: Flat and smooth object intended to receive an inscription or an image
Polished mirror that reflects an image
H1549.detail: 1. A tablet is a flat and smooth surface on which one can write or engrave a message. The prophet Isaiah is commanded to write on a large tablet so that the message is clear and readable: "Take a large tablet and write on it in a clear script" (Isaiah 8:1). It is a practical object for conveying a public and lasting message. 2. A tablet can also refer to a mirror, that is, a polished and shiny surface that reflects the image of the one looking into it. Isaiah 3:23 lists among the ornaments of women "mirrors" — luxury items that shine like polished metals. The word evokes the general idea of a flat, smooth, and shiny surface.
H1549.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to roll" or "to unroll." It designates any flat and smooth object — whether used for writing or for looking at oneself. The same family of words expresses the idea of a bare and exposed surface, ready to receive a trace or an image.
H1549.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Isaiah. In Isaiah 8:1, it refers to a writing tablet: God asks the prophet to note a prophecy on a tablet to ensure public and clear reading. In Isaiah 3:23, it refers to a mirror among the luxurious adornments worn by the women of Jerusalem. These two uses show that the tablet is always a flat, smooth, and visible surface — intended either for reading or for reflection.
H1549.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of recording the divine word in writing, so that it is clear and lasting. A tablet is also an object of vanity — the mirror symbolizes self-concern. These two uses invite the reader to discern between what deserves to be written and transmitted, and what is merely fleeting vanity.

sens: bent or folded upon itself
(of a door) made of two hinged panels
H1550A.detail: 1. The word describes something that is bent, folded, or articulated — like a sheet that is folded. 2. In the Bible, it specifically qualifies the doors of the temple: each panel was made of two "folded" boards, that is, hinged to each other, which could close over one another (1 Kings 6:34). This system allowed each panel to fold upon itself to create a wider passage when the door was open.
H1550A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of bending, turning, or curving. The basic image is that of something changing direction or position — a movement of flexion or rotation. This is why the word fits well for the hinged doors of the temple: it is the part that "folds" or "turns" to open and close.
H1550A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 6:34, during the detailed description of Solomon's temple. It is a technical and concrete term used to accurately describe the construction of the temple doors: each door was composed of two panels, themselves made of two folded boards (hinged). It is a rare word, belonging to the specialized vocabulary of architecture and carpentry.

sens: circular or cylindrical object used to hold or adorn
Band or circular area delineating a space
Structural element in the shape of a circle or roll
H1550B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a ring or a circular object made of metal — particularly gold or silver — used to secure or suspend something. In the Song of Solomon, hands are compared to gold rings filled with precious stones, evoking both the circular shape and the ornamental beauty of the adornment (Song of Solomon 5:14).
2. It can also refer to a band or area in the shape of a circuit, a ring in the sense of a defined structure. In Esther 1:6, purple cords are attached to silver rings set in the columns of the royal palace: the ring here is the circular attachment point that allows the fabrics to be suspended.
3. More broadly, the word can designate any rolled or cylindrical shape, a scroll or a circuit — the fundamental image is that of something turning or coiling upon itself.
H1550B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking circular movement or coiling. The concrete sense of ring or band that returns upon itself makes it a term of structure and ornamentation. In biblical texts, it always refers to something circular or curved, that can be threaded, suspended, or serves as an attachment point.
H1550B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in contexts of luxury and decoration. In the account of Xerxes' banquet in Esther 1:6, the silver rings are the material elements that support and order the splendor of the palace. In the Song of Solomon 5:14, the gold rings adorn the beloved's hands, comparing human beauty to precious objects. These two uses highlight the richness and brilliance of the context: the ring is a sign of value and refinement.
H1550B.portee: This word reminds us that even small details — a fastening, an adornment — matter in the biblical vision of beauty and care for things. The gold and silver of the rings symbolize the value of what is held or adored. For the Christian, it is an invitation to notice how God adorns and structures His creation with grace and attention.

sens: mountainous region in northern Israel, territory of the tribe of Naphtali
circuit or group of cities clustered around a center
historically occupied area by non-Israelite populations
H1551.detail:
1. Galilee is a mountainous region in northern Israel, located in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It is a well-defined area, consisting of a cluster of cities and villages organized around Kedesh as an administrative center. Joshua 20:7 refers to it as one of the cities of refuge, and this location shows its importance in the northern part of the Israelite territory.

2. The name literally means "circuit" or "district," reflecting its administrative organization: it is a grouping of localities forming a coherent unit. This structure is clearly seen when Solomon gives twenty cities to Hiram, king of Tyre, as payment for the materials he provided for the Temple (1 Kings 9:11).

3. At the time of the establishment of Israel, Galilee was a region where Israelites and non-Israelite populations coexisted, which explains why the Bible describes it as largely occupied by peoples foreign to the beliefs of God. During the Assyrian invasion, the entire region was conquered and its population deported (2 Kings 15:29).
H1551.origine: The Hebrew word Galilee (גָּלִיל) comes from the root גָּלַל (gâlal), which means "to roll" or "to turn." From this idea of circular movement comes the sense of "circle" or "circuit," hence "district" or "grouped region." The name thus describes the geographical and administrative organization of a cluster of cities forming a unit around a center. It is a geographical term specific to this region in northern Israel.
H1551.emploi: Galilee appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always designating this specific region in northern Israel, in the territory of Naphtali. It is mentioned in administrative and legal contexts: as the seat of cities of refuge (Joshua 20:7 and 21:32), as a group of twenty cities given as tribute to Hiram for his assistance in the construction of the Temple (1 Kings 9:11), and as a region conquered by Assyria during the invasion of 733 B.C. (2 Kings 15:29). These references show that Galilee was a well-organized and strategically important region, but also exposed to foreign incursions and changes in political domination.

sens: Region or territory delineated within a country
Perimeter or circuit of a defined area
Inhabited land or zone of influence
H1552.detail:
1. A district is a well-defined region within a country, a geographical area with recognizable borders. In Joshua 13:2, the Israelites discover the districts of the Philistines — coastal areas that the Philistines control and that remain to be conquered.
2. The word evokes the idea of something that revolves around, encircles: this is why a region is called a district, like the outline of a city with its neighboring lands. In Ezekiel 47:8, the water flows toward the eastern district — the area that extends eastward.
3. A district can also refer to the territory of a people or a power: the districts of the Philistines in Joel 3:4 are the lands governed by this people, its area of habitation and influence.
H1552.origine: The Hebrew word גְלִילָה (gelilah) comes from a root meaning "to turn around" or "to encircle." The district is literally what revolves around a center, a circular or circumscribed region. This same word, with a slight nuance, gives in geography the name of Galilee — a region of Palestine characterized by its districts or circuits of cities. The family of this word includes other terms related to borders, limits, and outlines.
H1552.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. In Joshua 13:2 and the following verses, it designates the territorial districts of the peoples occupying Canaan — the Philistines and other nations — that the Israelites still need to conquer. In Ezekiel 47:8 and Joel 3:4, the word takes on a broader meaning: it refers to regions or zones of influence in relation to which God acts or pronounces judgment. In each case, the word emphasizes the concrete and geographical reality of a region with its boundaries and inhabitants.
H1552.portee: This word reminds us that God acts in concrete and geographical history. God's promises concern lands, districts, specific peoples. For the reader, this reinforces that the Christian faith is not abstract: it is lived in the real world, with its borders and peoples. God's promises to give land to Israel are not symbolic — they are districts, specific territories.

sens: Place-name on the border between Judah and Benjamin, in the Holy Land
H1553.detail: Guéliloth is a geographical landmark mentioned only once in the Bible, during the description of the borders of the territory of Benjamin. The name means "circuits" or "contours" in Hebrew, and refers to a location not far from Jerusalem, near En-Shemesh and the ascent of Adummim. It is another name for Gilgal, the famous sanctuary where Israel settled after crossing the Jordan. Guéliloth served as a concrete demarcation point between the territories allocated to Judah and Benjamin.
H1553.origine: The Hebrew name גְּלִילוֹת (Guéliloth) comes from a root meaning "circle" or "contour," hence "circuits." It is related to Gilgal (גִּלְגָּל), the name of the sanctuary where the Israelites camped after crossing the Jordan. Both names evoke the idea of rotation or circular arrangement, likely in relation to the geography of the place or its ritual function.
H1553.emploi: Guéliloth appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 18:17, during the detailed survey of the borders of the territory of Benjamin. The text precisely locates it between En-Shemesh and the ascent of Adummim, serving as a reference point for delineating the territory. Its identification with Gilgal suggests that it was an important and recognizable site, serving as a stable landmark for successive generations.

sens: Location situated north of Jerusalem
H1554.detail: 1. Gallim is a locality north of Jerusalem, mentioned on two occasions. The name literally means "springs" or "fountains," evoking a place where waters spring forth — suggesting a village with water resources. In 1 Samuel 25:44, it is the hometown of Paltiel, the husband to whom Saul gave Michal (David's wife) after David had to flee the royal court: thus, Gallim becomes the site of this act of marital injustice. In Isaiah 10:30, it appears during a prophecy of invasion from the north to the south, enumerating the threatened localities: "Raise your voice, daughter of Gallim!" — a dramatic address showing Gallim exposed to the ravages of war.
H1554.origine: The Hebrew name גַּלִּים (gallim) means "springs" or "fountains," from the verb גָּלַל (galal) which evokes what bursts forth or flows. The word belongs to the category of place names that characterize the relief or natural resources: it is a village identified by its hydrographic particularity. Although the word appears only twice in the Old Testament, its geographical meaning is clear.
H1554.emploi: Gallim appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 25:44, it is named as the hometown of Paltiel, son of Laish, to whom Saul entrusted Michal to remove her from David. In Isaiah 10:30, it is cited in the context of an invasion of northern Judah, listed among the cities invited to cry out in alarm: the locality symbolizes the vulnerability of the populations in the northern heights against threatening armies. Both instances anchor Gallim in the political and military geography of the northern kingdom of Judah.

sens: The Philistine giant from Gath defeated by David
A man of extraordinary height, six cubits and a span
The elder brother of other Philistine giants
A formidable adversary who challenged Israel
H1555.detail: 1. Goliath is a Philistine warrior from Gath, first mentioned in 1 Samuel 17:4 as coming out of the camp of the Philistines to advance between the two armies in formation. 2. He was of exceptional height — six cubits and a span (approximately 2.85 meters) — which made him remarkable even among strong men, as seen when Scripture emphasizes his dimensions in 1 Samuel 17:4 and 2 Samuel 21:19. 3. He was the elder brother of other Philistine giants, notably Ishbi-benob, Saph, and Lachmi, indicating that gigantism was a trait of his family. 4. Goliath was a terrifying fighter who challenged the army of Israel, and no warrior could confront him until David killed him with his sling (1 Samuel 17:4 and 17:23). 5. His sword became a prestigious object, kept in the temple and given to David who had defeated him, as shown in 1 Samuel 21:9 where the priest offers it to David.
H1555.origine: The name "Goliath" means "splendor" in Hebrew. He was a Philistine, a people who came from the Mediterranean region and settled in Canaan along the coastal area. The mention of Gath, one of the five major Philistine cities, precisely situates his origin in the southern Philistia.
