H1555.emploi: Goliath appears six times in the Bible, always in relation to his confrontation with David. The main account is found in 1 Samuel 17, where he comes out of the Philistine army to challenge the Israelites. David, the youngest son of Jesse, confronts him with his sling and defeats him. This significant event is recalled several times: Goliath's sword remains in the temple (1 Samuel 21:9 and 22:10) as a trophy of victory. A note in 2 Samuel 21:19 and 1 Chronicles 20:5 mentions another battle against the Philistines, where a brother of Goliath is killed, highlighting that his family consisted of formidable warriors.
H1555.portee: The story of Goliath teaches that physical strength and earthly power, even extraordinary, are not sufficient against faith in God. David, small and inexperienced in military matters, defeats the reputedly unstoppable giant because he acts in trust in the Lord. For the believer, Goliath becomes the symbol of every seemingly insurmountable obstacle that God allows to be overcome by faith, not by strength.

sens: To move something by turning it around itself
To remove or push aside by rolling
To entrust, abandon to someone else
To move by rolling, to stir
H1556.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning: to roll a stone, an object. Jacob and his shepherds "roll" the stone from the well to water the flocks (Genesis 29:3, 29:10) — it is a physical, concrete, everyday gesture.

2. To push aside or remove something by rolling. The Lord says to Joshua: "I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you" (Joshua 5:9) — the reproach is taken away, cast off like one pushes a stone away from oneself.

3. To entrust, abandon something to someone or to God by handing over all the weight. "Commit your works to the Lord" (Proverbs 16:3): one rolls their worries, their plans toward the Lord, like loading a heavy stone onto other shoulders — it is an act of trust.

4. To move by rolling, to stir or collapse. The armies come "with the crackling" (Job 30:14) — an image of destruction that rolls and ravages everything in its path.
H1556.origine: The Hebrew root גָּלַל evokes the action of rolling, of turning. The word has several forms: to roll simply (Qal), to roll together (Niphal), or to roll with force (Hiphil, "to roll away"). This image of what rolls, flows, or moves inspired the name of the sanctuary of Gilgal (Joshua 5:9), where the Lord "rolled away" the reproach of Egypt — the place bears the name of the act of removal.
H1556.emploi: The verb appears 18 times in the Bible, mostly in concrete narratives (Genesis, Joshua, Samuel) where it describes the rolling of stones from wells or graves. But its use expands to a deeper meaning: to entrust, to hand over to God. In the Psalms and Proverbs, this trust becomes the dominant meaning (Proverbs 16:3; Psalms 37:5; 22:9) — one "rolls" their worries onto the Lord, as one unloads a burden. The images of destruction (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos) also exploit rolling as an irresistible force.
H1556.portee: This word teaches a profound spiritual principle: what is too heavy for us, we can "roll" to God — to entrust it entirely. It is both a relief and an act of obedience. The image of rolling shows that once entrusted to the Lord, our burden no longer belongs to us; it rolls to the one who can bear it.

sens: Excrement, animal or human waste
H1557.detail: 1. The word designates fecal matter or waste that is rejected and swept away. In 1 Kings 14:10, the house of Jeroboam is swept "like one sweeps away refuse": it is an image of total destruction, as one gets rid of foul residues. In Zephaniah 1:17, the flesh of men is compared to refuse, to show the contempt and abjection to which sinners will be reduced.
H1557.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to roll" or "to make roll". Excrement is what is rejected, what is rolled away from oneself. In the Old Testament, the word describes what is most despicable, what one wants to get rid of as quickly as possible.
H1557.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. These two uses show how the prophets use it to express divine disgust and the humiliation of sinners: in 1 Kings 14:10, it is the judgment on Jeroboam's dynasty, and in Zephaniah 1:17, it is the image of the final desolation of the wicked. It is a crude, deliberately repulsive word that reinforces the gravity of the announced punishment.
H1557.portee: This brutally concrete word reminds the reader that God's judgment is not abstract: it reaches sinners in their bodies and their honor, reducing them to the most despicable state. It also invites to holiness and respect for God, whose name should not be defiled like this refuse.

sens: The reason something happens
The motive or foundation of an action
What explains a consequence or result
H1558.detail:
1. The cause is the direct reason for an event or action. It answers the question "why?". Genesis 39:5: the Lord blessed Potiphar's house "because of" Joseph — it is Joseph's presence that explains and provokes the blessing.
2. It can be a personal motive justifying a behavior or request. Genesis 12:13: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister "so that I may be treated well because of you" — her beauty is the reason he would be treated well.
3. It also expresses the logical or moral consequence: why God acts. Deuteronomy 1:37: "The Lord was also angry with me because of you" — the people's unfaithfulness is the cause of God's anger and Moses' exclusion from the Promised Land.
H1558.origine: The Hebrew word galal (גָּלַל) fundamentally means "to roll", "to make roll". From this comes the idea of "what sets in motion", "what advances things" — hence "cause" or "reason". The preposition "because of" (galal with the article or in construction) expresses what is at the origin of a movement, an action, or an event. It is the same root found in other Hebrew forms related to the action of moving or propelling.
H1558.emploi: This word appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and the Prophets. It serves to introduce the cause of a blessing (Genesis 30:27: Laban sees that God has blessed him "because of" Jacob; Genesis 39:5: the blessing on Potiphar because of Joseph), of anger (Deuteronomy 1:37: God's anger because of Israel), of a divine action (Deuteronomy 18:12: God drives out the nations "because of" their abominations), or of a sanction (Deuteronomy 15:10: God blesses the one who gives generously "because of this"). The word expresses both natural causes and the motives for divine interventions.
H1558.portee: Understanding biblical causes helps us grasp the logic of divine action: God does not bless or punish arbitrarily, but always "because of" something — an obedience, a prayer, an injustice. This reminds us that our actions have consequences and that God, in His wisdom, acts according to just reasons that we can understand and must respect.

sens: Levite, son of Asaph
H1559G.detail: Galal is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem. He appears in the list of singers and musicians of the temple who resumed their service after the Babylonian captivity (1 Chronicles 9:15). As a son of Asaph, he belongs to a famous family of sacred musicians serving the worship of the Lord.
H1559G.origine: The name Galal comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "to roll" or "to make roll" in a literal sense, but also in a figurative sense of "to carry", "to lift", or "to be important". In the context of a personal name, Galal means "influential" or "one who has weight", which suited well for a member of a respected family of musicians.
H1559G.emploi: Galal appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 9:15. There he is listed among the Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile, alongside other musicians and temple servants. His name appears in a genealogy of porters and singers responsible for liturgical service. Although little known, Galal represents those faithful Levites who contributed to the restoration of worship in the temple.

sens: Levite from the time of exile and return
Head of a Levitical family from the tribe of Asaph
H1559H.detail:
1. Galal is a Levite who appears during the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is the son of Jeduthun, a famous musician of the Temple, and the father of Schemaeja (in 1 Chronicles 9:16) and Galal (in Nehemiah 11:17). He belongs to the family of Levites responsible for worship and music in the Temple restored after the exile to Babylon.
2. His name means "influential" or "weighty," which suits his position as a high-ranking Levite: he descends from Jeduthun and begets sons who hold important roles in divine service, notably Schemaeja, who is mentioned among the Temple gatekeepers.
H1559H.origine: The name Galal comes from the Hebrew root galal (גלל), which means "to roll" or "to roll away," but also by extension "to clear away," "to remove," or "to transport." In the context of proper names, it carries the idea of something that rolls, that moves, hence the interpretation "influential" — one who has an action, an influence, like something that moves and carries along. It is a name borne by Levites of the lineage of Asaph, musicians and servants of the Temple.
H1559H.emploi: Galal is mentioned twice in the biblical texts of the return from exile. In 1 Chronicles 9:16, he is presented as the son of Jeduthun and the father of Schemaeja, being part of the genealogy of the Levites established in Jerusalem after the return from captivity. In Nehemiah 11:17, he reappears as the ancestor of Abda, son of Schammua, in a parallel genealogical list of the Temple servants. These two mentions show that Galal was an important link in the genealogical chain of the Levites assigned to the service of the Temple and sacred music.

sens: worked stone, carefully squared
dimension, size of a building stone
H1560.detail: 1. The word refers to a stone that has been worked, carefully squared and shaped to serve in construction. It is a rough stone transformed by the worker to fit perfectly in its place within a building. In Ezra 5:8, the temple under reconstruction in Jerusalem employs "cut stones": these are neatly cut blocks of stone, not randomly gathered pebbles. 2. The word also evokes the size and regular dimensions of the stone, its finished and majestic appearance. A dressed stone is imposing, visible, a testament to the care taken in construction. In Ezra 6:4, the materials of the temple are enumerated: rows of dressed stones, alternating with wood, give the building its character of solidity and harmony.
H1560.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root gālal (גָּלַל), which means "to roll." In the Aramaic language of the book of Ezra, gelāl is its adjectival form. The initial image is that of a large stone being rolled — a round, bulky, massive stone. The meaning has shifted towards "large" and "worked": a stone that builders roll, carve, and square becomes a "beautiful stone" worthy of a temple.
H1560.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Ezra, in chapters 5 and 6. These verses describe the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, around 515 BC. The context is that of a Persian royal administration that authorizes and finances these works. The "dressed stone" is therefore a material of quality, a sign of the importance and splendor of the restored building. The usage is technical and architectural: materials are enumerated, rows counted, and the solidity and beauty of the construction emphasized.
H1560.portee: This word reminds us that the Lord's temple deserved the best materials and the greatest care from the builders. The dressed stone, worked by hand with precision, evokes the solidity of faith and the holiness of the place where God dwelled. For today's Christian, it speaks of the importance of building one's spiritual life on solid ground, with perseverance and excellence.

sens: fecal matter, bodily waste expelled by the intestine
filth, vile and contemptible thing
symbol of humiliation or ignominy
H1561.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to excrement, the waste of the human or animal body. In Ezekiel 4:12-15, the prophet is commanded to bake his bread over a fire fueled by human excrement, and then this command is changed to use cow dung — an extreme violation of religious purity rules meant to signify the impurity of exile.
2. The word takes on a figurative sense of filth or something vile, deserving of contempt. In Job 20:7, it says of the wicked that he "will perish forever like his refuse," suggesting that the guilty will be as despised and forgotten as a repugnant substance.
3. By extension, excrement represents humiliation and spiritual defilement: that which has no value, that which degrades the one who touches it or is associated with it.
H1561.origine: The Hebrew word גֵּל (guèl) comes from a root that refers to the idea of rolling or forming a ball — an image that suits fecal matter. It is a simple and direct word, without circumlocution: biblical Hebrew does not shy away from the realities of the body. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), it is translated by equivalent words that retain this crudity.
H1561.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Old Testament, always in contexts of ritual purity or humiliation. In Ezekiel 4, it literally refers to the material used as fuel — a situation deeply contrary to the Mosaic law which prohibits becoming defiled by contact with the impure. In Job 20:7, it takes on a figurative sense to express the nothingness to which the wicked will be reduced. These three uses make the word a marker of impurity, degradation, or absolute contempt.
H1561.portee: This crude word reminds us that the Bible does not conceal the realities of the body and the human carnal condition. It also symbolizes divine judgment: being compared to refuse is to lose all dignity. For the believer, this underscores that only the grace of God lifts up one who has fallen into degradation — unlike the wicked of Job who will be cast aside.

sens: Levitical musician, son of Jonathan, brother of several other musicians
H1562.detail: Guilalaï is a Levitical musician mentioned only once in the Bible, during the ceremony of the consecration of the wall of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is the son of Jonathan and the brother of Schemaeja, Azareel, Milalaï, Maaï, Nethaneel, Judah, and Hanani — a whole family of musicians from the priests. He participates in this solemn procession by playing musical instruments of David (Nehemiah 12:36).
H1562.origine: The name Guilalaï literally means "weighty" or "serious" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a deep voice or an imposing presence. It is a typical name of Levitical families from Judah, giving this man a clear identity in his time and liturgical role.
H1562.emploi: Guilalaï appears only once in the entire Bible, in the context of Nehemiah 12:36. He is listed in a solemn list of Levitical musicians who lead the procession of the consecration of the wall of Jerusalem, rebuilt after the return from exile. His name and that of his brothers testify to the renewal of religious life and worship music in Jerusalem after the destruction of the Babylonian siege. He represents the restoration of Levitical practices and praise in the temple.
H1562.portee: Guilalaï illustrates how, even in the difficult return from exile, God restores worship and music of praise. His appearance shows that the Levites, musicians of the temple service, regain their place and role in collective worship. For the reader, this reminds us that God preserves His people and their means of celebration, even after destruction and exile.

sens: To roll something, folding it onto itself to compact it
To fold a garment into a ball or roll
H1563.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of rolling or wrapping an object around itself. It is a concrete, physical gesture: one takes something flexible or long and rolls it into a ball or a roll. This is exactly what Elijah does with his cloak in 2 Kings 2:8: he rolls it before using it to strike the waters of the Jordan.
2. By extension, it means to fold or wrap a garment by rolling it. The cloak becomes a compact object, ready to be used as a staff.
H1563.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּלַם (galam) comes from a root expressing folding and rolling. Its basic image is that of something folding in on itself, compacting. The root carries the idea of transforming a long or flexible object into something tight and closed.
H1563.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 2:8, where Elijah rolls his cloak to make it an instrument capable of striking the waters of the Jordan and dividing them. It is an act that accompanies a miracle: the cloak becomes the instrument through which God manifests His power.
H1563.portee: This passage shows that Elijah does not act by his own strength: it is God who divides the water in response to Elijah's prophetic act. The rolled cloak symbolizes the authority of the prophet, an instrument of God's word. For the reader, it serves as a reminder that God acts through simple means and empowers those He calls.

sens: Human body in its most primitive state, before taking shape
Embryonic stage of life, the child before birth
H1564.detail:
1. The word refers to the human body at its most rudimentary stage, before it has received its definitive form and characteristic features. It is the image of the fetus in the womb, a creature that exists but does not yet have the appearance of a formed being. In Psalms 139:16, the psalmist confesses that God saw this "formless mass" even before his days began.
2. By extension, the word speaks of human life at its absolute beginning, the moment when something exists that will one day be a complete human being. This emphasizes the continuity of life from its most obscure origins: God sees and knows the one who is still only an unfinished form.
H1564.origine: The Hebrew word golèm comes from a root meaning "to roll" or "to wrap" — the idea of a substance that has not yet taken its definitive form, like a formless mass waiting to be shaped. The same root appears in other contexts related to the form and structure of the body.
H1564.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 139:16. The psalmist celebrates absolute divine knowledge: even when he was just a formless mass in the womb, God saw him already. This passage situates divine value and knowledge well beyond human appearances and visible stages of development. It asserts that God knows and sees the human being in its entirety, even before birth.
H1564.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer who meditates on their existence: God did not create us by chance, and He did not wait for us to know us. Even before we were formed, before we breathed, we were present before God and recorded in His book. This comforts those who feel small or insignificant, and it disabuses those who might think that their life begins only when they become visible to the eyes of the world.

sens: Who cannot bear children, who is childless
Devoid of life, joy, or fertility
Who flees or withdraws
H1565.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a woman unable to conceive or have children. Isaiah 49:21 clearly shows this: the barren woman cries, "I was childless, I was barren," expressing the pain of being deprived of offspring.
2. By extension, the word designates anything that is empty, arid, devoid of life or blessing. Job 15:34 applies it to the house of the wicked: "The house of the wicked will become barren," which will be ravaged and desolate. A night can also be "barren" (Job 3:7), empty of joy and gladness.
3. In Job 30:3, the term takes on a nuance of fleeing or withdrawing: the miserable "flee to barren places," abandoned and desolate, evoking a movement of retreat to empty spaces.
H1565.origine: The Hebrew word expresses the idea of desolation and aridity. It comes from a root that paints the image of the dry, the empty, that which produces nothing. Barreness, whether physical (the absence of children) or moral (the absence of divine blessing), is a biblically significant theme: it signifies the absence of promise, of life given by God.
H1565.emploi: The word appears 4 times in Hebrew, primarily in the books of Job and Isaiah. It first qualifies the barrenness of women, a painful condition in the Bible. It then describes divine punishment: the house of the wicked becomes barren, emptied of its prosperity. Job 3:7 applies it to a cursed night, a symbol of darkness and death. In all these contexts, the word designates a state of deprivation: absence of children, absence of life, absence of blessing. The Segond translates it sometimes as "barren," sometimes as "to flee," depending on whether the emphasis is on barrenness or on fleeing from barren places.
H1565.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that barrenness, in the Bible, is never simply a biological condition: it is a call to cry out to God. The barren women of the Bible (Sarah, Rebekah, Elizabeth) discover that only God can open the closed womb. More broadly, this word invites us to recognize that without divine blessing, our spiritual life risks becoming barren: it must bear fruit, otherwise it does not glorify God.

sens: Conflict or dispute between people
Outburst of anger, passionate outburst
What opens or flows suddenly, like a breach
H1566.detail:
1. The word describes a quarrel or conflict that breaks out between people. It is a dispute that often arises from a small provocation: "Starting a quarrel is like opening a dam" (Proverbs 17:14). The image is that of a dam giving way, releasing the waters held back — once the first accusations are let out, everything overflows uncontrollably.
2. The word also designates an outburst, that sudden access of anger that drives us to dispute. Proverbs 20:3 contrasts the wisdom of one who "avoids quarrels" with the folly of one who "gives in to anger" — it is that moment when reason lets go and explosive passion takes control.
3. Concretely, the word evokes the idea of rupture or breach: something that breaks or spills out of its container. What is held back, hidden, suddenly pours out — whether it be water, anger, or hurtful words.
H1566.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to open" or "to expose." It refers to the image of what is revealed or escapes: a physical overflow that Hebrew applies to emotional and relational overflow. The form used here (hitpael) indicates an action that is done to oneself or expressed outwardly — one cannot contain the flow; it spills out despite oneself.
H1566.emploi: This word appears only 3 times in the Bible, all in the book of Proverbs, a context where moral judgment is sought and wisdom is cultivated. In Proverbs 17:14, it illustrates how a quarrel begins — from a small crack that enlarges. In Proverbs 18:1, it characterizes one who "gives in to desire" (another possible translation of the same context of contention). In Proverbs 20:3, it contrasts the wise who avoids quarrels with the fool who throws himself into them. The word remains linked to the dynamics of conflict and the necessity of restraint.
H1566.portee: These verses teach us that conflicts do not arise suddenly: they begin with a voluntary or involuntary rupture of peace, and whoever allows it to start lets everything overflow. Recognizing within oneself that moment of "outburst," that desire to "open the dam," is the chance to withdraw before the worst happens. For the Christian, it is a call to cultivate self-control and patience, knowing that "outburst" is the path to folly.

sens: Heap of stones erected as a witness
Mound between Jacob and Laban
Place of the covenant between two men
H1567.detail:
1. Galed refers to a heap or mound of stones that Jacob and Laban erected together to seal their agreement. It is a visible and lasting pile, meant to remain as evidence of the pact made between them. In Genesis 31:48, Laban says: "May this mound serve today as a witness between me and you," showing that this pile of stones is a tangible witness of the covenant.
2. This mound is located on Mount Gilead, at the border between Jacob's land and Laban's land. It marks the boundary between two territories and between two peoples who commit to honoring their mutual promises.
3. The heap of stones functions as a memorial monument: every time it is seen, one remembers the past alliance and the loyalty that each owes to the other. It is an ancient form of written contract, but in stone rather than on parchment.
H1567.origine: The word "Galed" literally means "heap of witnesses" or "witness heap" in Hebrew. Its name expresses its function: it is a structure of testimony. The Segond translates this proper name as is, retaining the Aramaic Jegar-Sahadutha (which Laban uses in his language) and the Hebrew Galed (which Jacob uses in his) — both names refer to the same reality, the same heap of stones, but in two different languages to mark the cultural separation of the two men.
H1567.emploi: Galed appears only twice in the Bible, both in Genesis 31, during the separation of Jacob and Laban at Mount Gilead. In 31:47, Jacob gives this Hebrew name to the mound that Laban calls in Aramaic Jegar-Sahadutha. In 31:48, Laban confirms the meaning of the monument: "May this mound serve today as a witness between me and you." This is the only place where this term appears, marking a unique and solemn moment in patriarchal history — the end of a tense relationship but the confirmation of a peace agreement.
H1567.portee: Galed shows how men of faith create visible signs of their commitments to God and to one another. This heap of stones reminds us that covenants are not just words: they require a concrete act, a memorial that cannot be ignored. It is a lesson in the seriousness of promises and the necessity of leaving a lasting mark of our commitments.

sens: Mountainous region east of the Jordan, between the Jordan to the west and the Arabian plateau to the east
Territory allocated to the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh
Region known for its balm, a symbol of healing and restoration
H1568G.detail:
1. Gilead is a mountainous and rocky region located east of the Jordan. It extends from the north (Bashan) to the south (at the borders of Moab and Ammon), forming a well-defined territory between the Jordan and the Arabian desert. When Jacob flees Laban, he "headed toward the mountain of Gilead" (Genesis 31:21), showing that the name primarily designates this mountain range.
2. After the conquest, Gilead becomes the possession of three tribes: Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh. Moses distributes these lands: "I gave the rest of Gilead to the half-tribe of Manasseh" (Deuteronomy 3:13). These tribes establish their cities and settlements there, making it a center of pastoral and agricultural life.
3. Gilead is famous in Scripture for its healing balm: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jeremiah 8:22). This renown makes it a symbol of healing and restoration, which the prophet uses to evoke the future restoration of Israel and the remedy for spiritual distress.
H1568G.origine: The name Gilead literally means "rocky region" or "heap of stones." It comes from Semitic roots evoking stone and rock: gal (stone) and ad (heap). The region bears this name because of its rugged and mountainous geography. The term is also related to a monument of stones, the cairn erected by Jacob and Laban in memory of their covenant (Genesis 31:47), a monument called Gilead in Hebrew.
H1568G.emploi: Gilead appears 82 times in the Old Testament, first in the patriarchal history (Genesis), then becoming central after the conquest. It is the scene of key events: Jephthah's exploits against the Ammonites (Judges 11), the movements of David and Saul (1 Samuel, 2 Samuel), and the military campaigns of the kings of Israel. Jeremiah and Ezekiel mention it during the captivity, as a promise of restoration. It also retains administrative importance: it is divided into north and south (Gilead and "rest of Gilead"), and cities of refuge are established there (Joshua 20:8; 21:38). Biblical geography uses it as a reference: "Gilead is mine, Manasseh is mine" (Psalms 60:9) invokes it as part of the promised kingdom.
H1568G.portee: Gilead symbolizes for the believer the possession of God's promises. It reminds us that the Lord allocates lands, concrete inheritances to His people. Its balm becomes an image of divine healing: when the prophet cries out, "Is there no balm in Gilead?" he teaches us that God has remedies for our spiritual wounds. This region anchors faith in real and geographical history, showing that God acts in space and time.

sens: Mountainous region east of the Jordan
Fortified city in this region
People living in this region
Son of Makir, grandson of Manasseh
Ancestor of Jephthah
Man of the tribe of Gad
H1568H.detail:
1. Gilead is primarily a mountainous, rocky, and hilly region located east of the Jordan. It extends from the north (where Bashan begins) to the south (where Moab and Ammon begin). It is a territory of war and pastoral wealth, inhabited by strong tribes.
2. Gilead also refers to a fortified city in this region, mentioned by the name "Jabesh" (Jabesh-Gilead).
3. By extension, Gilead can refer to the people who inhabit this mountainous region.
4. Gilead is also a man, son of Makir and grandson of Manasseh (Numbers 26:29). From him descend the families of the Gileadites, established in the region that bears his name.
5. Gilead is also the father of Jephthah, the judge of Israel.
6. A man of the tribe of Gad also bears this name, mentioned in the genealogies.
H1568H.origine: The name literally means "rocky region" (from the root gal: rock). It is a geographical name that likely comes from the structure of the terrain. Subsequently, the name of the man Gilead (son of Makir) gave his name to the region that his descendants occupied, showing how an ancestor can become the eponymous figure of an entire territory.
H1568H.emploi: Gilead appears nine times in the Old Testament, mainly in the genealogical lists of Numbers and 1 Chronicles. As a man, he is presented as the son of Makir (Numbers 26:29), the firstborn of Manasseh, a renowned warrior (Joshua 17:1). His descendants are significant: his six sons (Jezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Shemida, and Hepher) found as many families (Numbers 26:30). The mountainous region that bears his name becomes a major home of the territory of Israel east of the Jordan, occupied by the tribe of Manasseh and others.
H1568H.portee: Gilead reminds us how God establishes the tribes of Israel on a promised land, each receiving its inheritance. The story of the daughters of Zelophehad (granddaughters of Gilead) shows that God ensures that everyone, even the humblest, receives their share of the inheritance.

sens: Man father of Jephthah, judge of Israel
Mountainous region east of the Jordan
H1568I.detail:
1. Gilead is the father of Jephthah, the famous judge of Israel mentioned in the Book of Judges. He is a man from the region of Gilead who had a son with a prostitute; this son, Jephthah, was later rejected by the other sons of Gilead but became a powerful military leader called to lead Israel against the Ammonites (Judges 11:1-2).
2. The name Gilead also refers to a mountainous region located east of the Jordan, a rocky and hilly territory that served as a border area between Israel and neighboring peoples. This region, fertile and well-defined, played an important role in biblical geography and the history of Israel.
H1568I.origine: The name Gilead means "rocky region" or "heap of stones," evoking the mountainous and stony character of the territory. The word comes from Hebrew roots suggesting both the hardness of the rock and the accumulation of stones. In the Bible, Gilead refers to both a person and a region, this dual usage being common for proper names in the Old Testament.
H1568I.emploi: Gilead appears twice in the provided usages, both in chapter 11 of the Book of Judges, where he is presented as the biological father of Jephthah. Both passages highlight the difficult family context: Gilead had sons from a married woman who rejected Jephthah, the son of a prostitute. This context of family rejection prepares the reader to understand why Jephthah, despite his marginalized social status, would ultimately become the deliverer of Israel. The name Gilead is therefore primarily that of a specific person in the history of judgment in Israel.
H1568I.portee: The character of Gilead reminds us that God often chooses His instruments from among the marginalized and the rejected. His son Jephthah, although born of an illegitimate relationship and exiled by his half-brothers, was called by God to save Israel. This story teaches the reader that origin or social status does not determine God's ability to act; it is His faithfulness and calling that matter.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H1568J.detail: 1. Gilead is a man of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in Scripture (1 Chronicles 5:14). He belongs to a genealogy known as the list of Gadites, that is, the descendants of Gad, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. It is a name that appears in a long ancestral chain without anecdotes or particular stories.
H1568J.origine: The name Gilead (in Hebrew Gilead) literally means "rocky region." This same name designates a famous geographical region in the Bible east of the Jordan, known for its forests and heights. The character Gilead bears the same name as this region, as was common in Israel; several other biblical characters also bear this name (a son of Machir, a father of Jephthah), but this one is distinct from them.
H1568J.emploi: Gilead appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:14, in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad. This passage lists the ancestors of Abichail, and Gilead is mentioned as the son of Michael and father of Jaroach. He is a simple link in a long family chain, with no active role in the history of Israel. His inclusion in this genealogy shows that the Gadites preserved the memory of their ancestral lines at the time when the kingdom was divided.

sens: mountainous region of Palestine east of the Jordan
territory rich in pastures and forests
H1568K.detail: 1. Gilead is a mountainous region located east of the Jordan, between the Jordan to the west, Bashan to the north, the Arabian plateau to the east, and Moab and Ammon to the south. It is an area with marked geographical features, rocky and rugged, from which it gets its name. 2. This region was fertile, covered with vegetation and forests, renowned for its excellent pastures, making it a land suitable for livestock and agriculture.
H1568K.origine: The name "Gilead" (gil'ad in Hebrew) literally means "rocky region." This region was significant and well-defined enough for the Israelites to give it its own name, which designated a recognizable and strategic territory in their geography.
H1568K.emploi: Gilead appears in the Old Testament as an important territory of Transjordan. It is mentioned here during the story of Gideon, who gathers an army on the mountain of Gilead to fight the Midianites (Judges 7:3). The region was well-known and distinct enough for God to command Gideon to call warriors from this specific area, showing that Gilead was a significant center of population and military resources.
H1568K.portee: This biblical geography reminds us that God knows the regions and peoples intimately, and that He places His people in concrete locations. The account of Gideon in Gilead illustrates how God acts through real territories and the men who inhabit them, inviting the reader to see the physical world as the stage for God's action.

sens: rocky region of Transjordan, east of the Jordan
fortified city in this region
H1568L.detail:
1. Gilead is primarily a mountainous and stony region located east of the Jordan, in Transjordan. It extends over a vast territory between the Jordan and the Aramean desert.
2. Jabesh in Gilead is a particular city in this region, famous in the Old Testament for its civic courage. During a serious crisis (Judges 21), only Jabesh in Gilead refused to participate in a general assembly of Israel at Mizpah, which provoked a punitive expedition against it (Judges 21:8-10). Later, the inhabitants of Jabesh in Gilead rose up to defend King Saul when he was attacked by the Ammonites (1 Samuel 11:9), and after his death, they undertook the perilous journey to retrieve his bones left in the hands of the Philistines, in order to honor him with a burial (2 Samuel 21:12).
H1568L.origine: The Hebrew name Gilead literally means "rocky region" or "heap of stones of witness." According to Genesis 31:47-48, the name comes from a heap of stones erected as a monument between Jacob and Laban. Jabesh means "dry" or "withered," which evokes the dry climate of this region. Together, Jabesh in Gilead designates this particular city in the region of Gilead.
H1568L.emploi: Jabesh in Gilead appears mainly in the accounts of the Book of Judges and the first Book of Samuel. It is known for two major events: its isolation during the Benjamite affair (Judges 21), where it refused to participate in the assembly of Israel and was punished; and especially its heroic role during the siege of Saul by the Ammonites (1 Samuel 11), where its inhabitants showed loyalty to their king. After Saul's death at Gilboa, the men of Jabesh in Gilead risked their lives to recover his remains and those of Jonathan from the Philistines to bury them with dignity (2 Samuel 21:12). It was a city in Transjordan, difficult to access, but inhabited by people of conscience and loyalty.
H1568L.portee: Jabesh in Gilead embodies in the Bible the fidelity to those who have perished and the courage to honor the dead according to the law. The inhabitants of this city show that a small community can perform remarkable acts of devotion, at the risk of their own safety. Their gesture towards Saul's bones—transporting his remains despite the danger—illustrates a form of piety towards deceased rulers and the respect for the right to burial, deep values in Israel.

sens: Mountainous region east of the Jordan, between it and the Arabian plateau
Land promised to the tribe of Manasseh and the tribes of Reuben and Gad
Site of wars and conflicts between Israel and its Syrian neighbors
H1568M.detail:
1. Gilead is a mountainous region located east of the Jordan, bordered to the west by the river, to the north by Bashan, to the east by the desert plateau of Arabia, and to the south by the territories of Moab and Ammon. It is a land of rocky and wooded hills, rich in resources. The name means "rocky region."

2. This land was given to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh after the conquest of Canaan. It included important cities, notably Ramoth in Gilead, mentioned as a stronghold (1 Kings 4:13).

3. Gilead becomes famous in Israel's history as the stake of repeated wars between the king of Israel and the king of Syria. The two kingdoms dispute control of this strategic region, particularly Ramoth in Gilead (1 Kings 22:3-12; 2 Kings 8:28; 2 Kings 9:14).
H1568M.origine: The Hebrew name גִּלְעָד (Gilead) literally means "rocky region" or "land of stones," formed from a root denoting stones. The Bible often associates it with Ramoth (רָמֹת), which means "heights," giving "Ramoth in Gilead" to designate the fortified strategic city. This region was known in antiquity as an important territory of the Levant, located on the trade routes.
H1568M.emploi: Gilead is mentioned 18 times in the Old Testament, especially in the books of Kings and Chronicles. It first appears as a region of Israel (1 Kings 4:13), then becomes the theater of conflicts between Israel and Syria during three military campaigns reported in parallel in 1 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 18: the first where King Ahab seeks to conquer Ramoth in Gilead with the support of the prophets (1 Kings 22:12), and others where the kings of Israel engage against Hazael, king of Syria (2 Kings 8:28; 2 Kings 9:14). The name regularly appears in these military and political narratives.
H1568M.portee: Gilead reminds us that the territory of Israel extended beyond the Jordan and that possession of certain lands required constant vigilance against external threats. These repeated wars for Ramoth in Gilead illustrate the fragility of peace and the consequences of unfaithfulness to God: leaders seek military victory without truly turning to the Lord (1 Kings 22:6-12).

sens: inhabitant of the region of Gilead
member of the Gilead branch of the tribe of Manasseh
H1569.detail:
1. A Gileadite is someone from Gilead, a mountainous and rocky region east of the Jordan. It is an inhabitant or native of this land. Jair the Gileadite (Judges 10:3) and Jephthah the Gileadite (Judges 11:1) are two famous examples who served as judges in Israel.
2. More specifically, the Gileadites form a branch of the tribe of Manasseh, descended from Gilead, the son of Machir (Numbers 26:29). They are the descendants of a single family settled in this region, which made them a recognized group within Israel.
H1569.origine: The word comes from Gilead (גִּלְעָד), whose name means "the heap of witnesses" or "rocky region." The suffix -י (-i) adds the idea of belonging or origin, as one would say in French "un Parisien" or "un Alsacien." Gilead was a fertile but mountainous region located east of the Jordan, and its inhabitants carried this territorial identity that distinguished them in the tribal life of Israel.
H1569.emploi: The term appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to identify people from or descended from Gilead. It is encountered mostly in the book of Judges, where several judges of Israel are referred to as Gileadites: Jair (Judges 10:3), Jephthah (Judges 11:1, 11:40, 12:7). It also appears in the accounts of David in exile (2 Samuel 17:27 with Barzillai the Gileadite, who brings supplies to the king), and in later genealogical lists (Ezra 2:61, Nehemiah 7:63). The word always serves to geographically or genealogically situate a character, marking their belonging to this region and to their tribe.
H1569.portee: Knowing that a character is a Gileadite helps to understand their roots, social context, and sometimes their tribal responsibilities. It shows how the Bible anchors narratives in the real geography of Israel and emphasizes the importance of family and territorial heritage in the life of God's people. For the reader, it is a reminder that each character has an identity rooted in the land that God gave to Israel.

sens: slope of a mountain or hill
side part of an animal's body
set of things arranged on one side
H1570.detail:
1. The flank is the slope or side of a mountain — what you see when looking at the mountain from the side. In the Song of Songs, the beloved's hair is compared to goats hanging on the flanks of the mountain of Gilead (Song of Songs 4:1): like goats clinging to the rocky slope, the hair falls in waves over the shoulders.
2. The flank also refers to the side of an animal's body — where one touches the animal laterally, between the front and back legs. It is the same image: goats pressing on a slope, huddled together, represent the undulating and lively mass of hair.
H1570.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּלַשׁ (galash) fundamentally evokes the idea of sitting or resting somewhere — hence the image of a goat sitting or clinging on a rocky slope. The word paints the action of goats descending or standing on the steep flanks of mountains, creating an image of graceful movement and compact presence. It is a rare verb in biblical Hebrew, used mainly in the poetic context of the Song of Songs.
H1570.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Song of Songs (4:1 and 6:5), at the heart of two poems describing the beloved. Each time, it describes goats "hanging on the flanks" of the mountain of Gilead — a comparison intended to express the grace, delicacy, and undulating beauty of the woman's hair. The image is one of agility and graceful nimbleness: like mountain goats moving nimbly on steep slopes, the hair falls fluidly and elegantly. The word thus remains attached to this kind of poetic and lyrical description, with no common usage or abstract meaning.
H1570.portee: This image reveals how the biblical poetry of the Song of Songs celebrates the beauty of the female body with delicacy and respect. By comparing the beloved's hair to agile goats on the mountain, the sacred text affirms that physical beauty is a creation of God worthy of admiration and praise. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that the Bible does not shy away from expressing marital love and appreciation of the body with poetry.

sens: addition of a person or thing to another
inclusion of a case in a general category
emphasis or insistence on a fact
correspondence or reciprocity between two situations
negation concerning two elements
light opposition or concession
H1571.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to add someone or something to a set. Eve eats the forbidden fruit and gives "also" to her husband (Genesis 3:6): she associates him with her act. Leviticus 25:45 allows for the purchase of "also" foreign slaves, in addition to other possibilities.
2. To include a case in a general rule, often to emphasize that it is not exempt. Jeremiah 8:7 states that "even" the stork knows its season: it is an animal, yet it knows; this reinforces the reproach directed at Israel.
3. To strengthen an assertion or emphasize it. 1 Samuel 19:24 states that Saul prophesied "also" and asks "is he also among the prophets?"; the word creates a sort of surprise or insistence.
4. To mark correspondence or reciprocity between two actions. Genesis 4:4 speaks of Abel who offered "also" a sacrifice, as Cain had done: two parallel acts.
5. To deny two things together (with a negation). "Neither one nor the other" is expressed in Hebrew with this word and a negation.
6. To create a slight opposition or concession. The word can mean "and yet" or "certainly," introducing a gentle contrast.
H1571.origine: This word comes from a simple Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "with" or "together." In Hebrew, gam is very frequent and fundamental: it is a small connecting word that links, adds, and emphasizes. It does not derive from a complex verbal root but stems from a notion of accumulation or association. Its use in ancient texts shows it as a universal connector of Hebrew thought.
H1571.emploi: This word appears 661 times in biblical Hebrew, making it one of the most frequent. It appears everywhere, especially in Genesis, the narrative books, and Proverbs. In Genesis 3:6 and following, it links the actions of several characters or adds details. In Leviticus, it expands prescriptions. In 1 Samuel 19:24, it creates an emphasis: "is he also" highlights the surprise. In Jeremiah 8:7, the word "even" marks that the animal in question enters a category that nothing should prohibit it from. Its meaning varies according to the context: rarely does it oppose (a "but"), most often it adds or insists.
H1571.portee: This small word teaches that God sees and counts every detail, every person, every act. When Scripture says "also," it shows us that we are never alone or forgotten in God's plan. It is a lesson in humility and trust: God cares about who we are and what we do, just as He cares about the stork and the swallow.

sens: To absorb a liquid through the mouth
To devour, consume with fervor
H1572.detail:
1. To drink means to absorb a liquid, usually water, by passing it through the mouth. It is the simple and concrete act of quenching thirst: Abraham's servant asks Rebekah, "Let me drink, I pray, a little water from your pitcher" (Genesis 24:17).
2. To devour or consume is used figuratively to describe someone who moves with impetuosity, who covers space with eagerness, like a war horse "boiling with fervor" that "devours the earth" (Job 39:27). The word then evokes impatient violence, an irrepressible ardor that engulfs space.
H1572.origine: The Hebrew verb gama essentially means "to swallow" or "to engulf." It describes the action of absorbing something into one's throat or mouth, whether it be a liquid or, figuratively, a distance or difficulty. The image is of something disappearing inside, consumed in one go.
H1572.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 24:17, it designates the ordinary action of drinking water to quench thirst. In Job 39:27, it depicts the war horse traversing the battlefield with fervor, not as a mechanical act but as a manifestation of warrior ardor. It is therefore a rare verb, used in concrete and vivid contexts.
H1572.portee: These two uses show that drinking is not always a simple physical need: it can reveal a fervent desire or trust in the one offering the drink (like the water offered to a weary traveler), and the image of devouring the earth speaks to each of us of that inner ardor that drives us to move forward without stopping.

sens: Aquatic plant with flexible stems that grows in marshes and shallow waters
Material used to make objects, including boats
Object or construction made of reed
H1573.detail:
1. The reed is a plant with a flexible stem that thrives in wet areas. When Job asks, "Does the reed grow without marsh?" he emphasizes that this plant needs water to live (Job 8:11). It is typical vegetation along the Nile and in the marshy areas of the ancient Near East.
2. The Bible also mentions reed as a building material. In Exodus 2:3, Moses' mother makes a basket of reeds, coated with bitumen and pitch, to protect her baby from the waters of the Nile. This material was practical, accessible, and sufficiently waterproof when treated.
3. The Egyptians built reed boats to travel on the Nile and the seas. Isaiah 18:2 speaks of "reed boats sailing on the surface of the waters" sent by a powerful nation, illustrating the ingenuity of ancient river peoples.
H1573.origine: The Hebrew word גֹּמֶא (gomé) specifically refers to reed or papyrus. Its etymology relates to the idea of flexibility and aquatic growth. This word appears mainly in contexts related to Egypt and rivers, as reeds were abundant along the Nile and constituted a major resource for that civilization.
H1573.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. It has concrete and complementary meanings: first, the plant itself in its natural habitat (Job 8:11, Isaiah 35:7, where the reed reappears in lands regaining water), then the worked material from which objects are made (Exodus 2:3, Moses' basket) and boats (Isaiah 18:2). The Egyptian context predominates, reminding us that the reeds of the Nile were essential to daily life and river commerce in ancient Egypt.
H1573.portee: The reed in Moses' basket symbolizes both human fragility in the face of danger and divine providence: a simple natural material becomes the instrument of salvation for a future liberator of the people. The reed also reminds us that God preserves life in the most precarious circumstances, transforming a humble resource into a means of protection.

sens: an ancient unit of length, measured from the elbow joint to the tip of the fingers
by extension, a short and defined distance
H1574.detail:
1. The cubit is a practical and natural unit of length: it corresponds to the distance from the elbow to the tip of the outstretched fingers. It is a unit that can be measured on oneself, hence its usefulness in antiquity before modern systems. In Judges 3:16, Ehud's sword is a cubit long, making it a short weapon, easy to conceal under clothing.
2. By extension, the word simply designates a measured and defined distance, which can be applied to any object or space. The cubit becomes the standard for assessing the dimensions of buildings, furniture, or objects of worship in the Bible.
H1574.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "the arm" or "the elbow," hence the original image: it is literally the length of an arm. This system of measurement is very ancient and shared by Near Eastern civilizations, each retaining its own variations in length. The cubit was approximately 45 to 50 centimeters depending on the regions and periods.
H1574.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond with this spelling. However, the measurement of the cubit is very frequent in the Bible, particularly for the dimensions of the Tabernacle, the Ark of the Covenant, and the Temple. In Judges 3:16, it designates the length of a combat weapon: Ehud's short sword, which allows him to carry it easily in ambush. It is a concrete example of the word used for a practical and tactical measure.
H1574.portee: For the Christian, this short cubit-long weapon reminds us that God can accomplish great feats with seemingly weak or limited means. Ehud, the deliverer of Israel, triumphs not by the power of a great sword, but by cunning and obedience. It is a lesson on dependence on God rather than on our visible resources.

sens: A brave and fearless man in battle
A warrior of worth, capable and experienced
By extension: a man of strength and bravery
H1575.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a brave and fearless man, capable of standing firm in the face of danger and the trials of battle. He is a fighter who does not flee.
2. More broadly, it is a warrior of worth, someone capable and experienced in the art of war, who inspires confidence in his comrades-in-arms. In Ezekiel 27:11, the valiant men of Tyre occupied its towers and lined its walls with shields to defend it: they were the city's bulwark.
3. The adjective can also evoke any form of moral bravery and personal strength, not just military.
H1575.origine: The Hebrew word גַּמָּדִים comes from a Semitic root expressing the idea of strength, solidity, and capability. It is close to roots evoking robustness and imposing stature. In Hebrew, words from this family express physical vigor and power in battle. It is a valorizing term, referring to the image of a strong man, capable of protecting and conquering.
H1575.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 27:11, in the poetic description of the city of Tyre at the height of its splendor. In this passage, the "valiant" men form the city's garrison, tasked with defending the walls and towers. They are listed among the military forces that constituted the power and beauty of Tyre before its prophesied decline. The context shows that they are an elite warrior class, men of experience and recognized worth.
H1575.portee: This word reminds us that valor, courage, and strength are valued qualities in human life. For the believer, it invites reflection on true courage: not confidence in walls and warriors, but trust in God. Tyre relied on its valiant men, but it is God who sees cities fall. Human valor has its place, but it is never sufficient without God's help.

sens: What one receives in return for their deeds or actions
Salary, remuneration, price of work
Fair treatment, reciprocity
Retaliation, vengeance, deserved punishment
Benefit, grace, blessing received
H1576.detail:
1. The word "retribution" expresses the idea of a consequence or payment that returns to someone based on what they have done. It is the reward or punishment that corresponds exactly to the act: "Render to them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their actions" (Psalms 28:4). 
2. It also designates the salary or remuneration given in exchange for work or service rendered. Jerubbaal helped his people, and the question arises whether he is repaid "according to the services he has rendered" (Judges 9:16). 
3. The word expresses reciprocity or fair treatment: doing good merits a good reaction in return, doing evil calls for a corresponding reaction. "Each receives according to the work of their hands" (Proverbs 12:14). 
4. Often used for retaliation or vengeance: God "will repay His enemies" (Isaiah 59:18), meaning He will apply the same treatment that one has earned through their evil deeds. 
5. The word can also signify the benefits and graces received: "Bless the Lord, and forget not any of His benefits" (Psalms 103:2) — all that God fills us with through His goodness.
H1576.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to render," "to give back." It is related to verbs expressing the action of paying, restoring, or remunerating. The underlying image is that of a hand giving or returning something: each "gathers the product of their hands" (Isaiah 3:11), what they have sown by their deeds is returned to them. It is the fundamental biblical principle of the correspondence between action and consequence.
H1576.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and prophetic books. It is used to express divine justice: God "renders to each according to their works" (Psalms 28:4, Isaiah 59:18). It also applies to men: one can repay good or evil to someone according to what they have deserved. The Psalms use it to ask God to punish enemies who have done wrong (Psalms 94:2, Lamentations 3:64). The wisdom books use it to emphasize that each "receives according to the work of their hands" (Proverbs 12:14, Proverbs 19:17). It is the key word to express the principle of divine retribution: God's justice is never arbitrary; it always responds exactly to what has been done.
H1576.portee: This word reminds us that our actions have consequences: there is nothing hidden or unpunished before God. It invites us to reflect on the good and evil we do, knowing that God renders to each according to their works. This should encourage us to do good and to keep away from evil. At the same time, it shows us that God is just: He never leaves evil unpunished, but He also generously rewards good and faith.

sens: A priest during the time of the divided monarchy, responsible for a group of service in the temple
H1577.detail: Gamul is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the distribution of priestly duties by King David. He was the head of the twenty-second group of priests who served in rotation in the temple, according to a strict organizational system where each division assumed its responsibilities for a set period (1 Chronicles 24:17).
H1577.origine: The name Gamul literally means "weaned" or "one who has been weaned," evoking the image of a child detached from its mother. This type of name was common in Israel and often reflects a memorable context or action at the time of birth. Here, it is simply the proper name of a priest from the line of Levi.
H1577.emploi: Gamul appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 24:17, in the list of the heads of the priestly divisions established by David. This list enumerates twenty-four groups of priests (descendants of Aaron) who succeeded one another in the service of the sanctuary. Gamul holds the rank of twenty-second chief, which means he led a specific group of priests. His unique mention shows that he was a man of status, recognized for his role as a religious leader in temple worship, even though no other details of his life are reported.

sens: What one receives in return for an action, good or bad
A benefit, a mark of recognition
A salary, a payment for work
God's judgment that gives to each according to their deeds
H1578.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to what one receives in exchange or in return for an action: it is an action or treatment that corresponds to another. In 2 Samuel 19:36, the servant asks the king for a small favor in recognition of his devotion.
2. It can refer to a benefit or act of kindness offered as a reward or in gratitude. It is the positive gesture by which one acknowledges the service rendered.
3. It also applies to the notion of salary or payment: everyone receives according to their work and deeds (Jeremiah 51:56). It is what comes back to someone for what they have done.
4. Isaiah 59:18 and Jeremiah 51:56 show that the word takes on a divine and moral dimension: God gives to each according to their works. It is the principle of judgment where everyone receives the fruit of their deeds, good or bad.
H1578.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to give back" or "to return." The basic idea is that of an action that returns, that comes back: what goes out returns transformed into reward or punishment. Words of the same family express the idea of "weaning" or "finishing," as an action completes what it has begun by producing a result.
H1578.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always with the nuance of "what comes back in return." In 2 Samuel 19:36, it refers to a concrete benefit requested from the king. In the other two passages (Isaiah 59:18 and Jeremiah 51:56), the word takes on a theological significance: it designates how God treats people according to their deeds. It is an act of just retribution, where everyone receives what corresponds to what they have done.
H1578.portee: This word reveals that the Bible does not conceive of human actions as without consequence: there is a justice that gives to each according to their works. For the believer, this teaches that God does not remain indifferent to what we do, and that our conduct has real effects. It is a call to live with awareness, knowing that our actions will bear fruit.

sens: City of Judah in ancient Israel
H1579.detail: Gimzo is a small city of Judah located south of the road that connected Jerusalem to Joppa. Its Hebrew name evokes a fertile place with sycamores, trees that produced fruit resembling figs. The only mention we have of it in the Bible shows it captured by the Philistines, along with its dependencies, during the reign of King Ahaz.
H1579.origine: The name Gimzo literally means "fertile in sycamores" in Hebrew. The sycamore was a common fruit tree in Palestine, and the name of the city reflects the characteristic vegetation or resources of the place. Like many city names in Israel, it described what distinguished the territory.
H1579.emploi: Gimzo appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 28:18, where it is listed among the cities that the Philistines conquered in the south and west of Judah during the reign of King Ahaz. This mention shows that it was a city significant enough to be fortified and to have dependent villages under its authority, but small enough to have completely disappeared from history after this period.

sens: To stop breastfeeding a child and feed them other food
To treat someone in a certain way, based on their actions
To give someone what they deserve, for good or for bad
To mature, to come to maturity (for a fruit or a plant)
H1580.detail:
1. Weaning means to stop breastfeeding a child to feed them solid food. It is an important moment in the life of the child and the mother. In Genesis 21:8, Abraham holds a great feast on the day Isaac is weaned, marking the transition to a new stage in his life.

2. To treat someone in a certain way means to act towards them according to what they have deserved. This can be a good or a bad action. In Psalm 18:21, the psalmist says, "The Lord dealt with me according to my righteousness," meaning that God acted towards him based on his justice and upright conduct.

3. To give someone their reward or punishment means to give them exactly what they deserve. In Psalm 137:8, it refers to giving Babylon "the evil it has done" to Israel—a just vengeance for that oppressed people.

4. To mature or come to maturity describes the natural process of a plant or fruit developing to its fullness. In Isaiah 18:5, grapes ripen before the harvest, an image of the complete development of things according to God's timing.
H1580.origine: The Hebrew verb gamal carries the idea of bringing to completion, of leading to fulfillment. The root evokes an action that goes all the way through. In Hebrew, the word gamal also refers to the camel, an animal known for its strength and endurance. The verb is used in contexts where something is finalized: a weaned child is a child who has become more independent, a rewarded or punished action is an action brought to its logical conclusion.
H1580.emploi: This verb appears 32 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms (where it occurs 10 times) and in the prophets. Its primary meaning, to wean, is found mainly in the early Torah (Genesis 21:8; 1 Samuel 1:22-24), describing a concrete rite of passage. Its second meaning, to treat or give according to merits, dominates in the Psalms and in calls for divine justice: David asks God to deal with him according to his righteousness (Psalm 18:21; 2 Samuel 22:21), and the psalmists plead with God not to treat them according to their sins (Psalm 103:10). The meaning of giving evil for evil appears in cries for vengeance (Psalm 137:8; Joel 3:4). Finally, to mature applies to fruits and plants (Isaiah 18:5; Numbers 17:8). The word thus encompasses the general idea of completion or fulfillment.
H1580.portee: Understanding this verb helps the Christian reader grasp how the Bible speaks of divine justice. God leaves nothing unfinished: He treats each according to their works, with fairness. This gives weight to the call for moral uprightness and reminds us that God sees and rewards every act, mercy as well as wickedness. For the believer, it is an invitation to trust: God brings all things to their conclusion, according to His wisdom.

sens: Domesticated animal of the Middle Eastern Asia, capable of carrying loads and traveling long distances in the desert
Precious asset that is part of the livestock and wealth of a family
Mount for transport and travel for people and goods
Animal considered unclean in the law of Moses, forbidden for consumption
H1581.detail: 1. The camel is an animal that the Hebrews of antiquity regularly encountered in the Middle East. Its utility is primarily practical: it is a sturdy pack animal that can carry heavy loads over long distances (the Queen of Sheba arrives in Jerusalem with camels carrying gold and spices: 1 Kings 10:2). 2. As a material asset, the camel represents an important form of wealth in society at the time, alongside sheep, cattle, or donkeys. Abraham, Job, and other patriarchs owned many: Job had three thousand camels before his trials, and God restored six thousand to him (Job 1:3 and 42:12). 3. Practically, the camel serves as a mount for long journeys. This is why Elisha receives a camel as a royal gift: it is a considerable gift, a sign of honor (2 Kings 8:9). 4. According to Mosaic law, the camel is among the unclean animals that are forbidden to eat, despite the fact that it chews the cud (Deuteronomy 14:7). This shows that one can associate with and utilize it for work, but not consume it.
H1581.origine: The Hebrew word gamal (גָּמָל) has an ancient root that simply reflects the name of the animal as known by the peoples of the Levant. There is not really a "verbal root" in the sense of a primitive action: it is a fundamental name. In other closely related Semitic languages (Aramaic, Arabic), very similar forms designating the same animal can be found, which shows its importance throughout the ancient Middle East. The Greek of the Old Testament translates this word as kamelos.
H1581.emploi: The word camel appears 51 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the narratives of Genesis and the historical books. In the account of Abraham (Genesis 12 to 24), camels are signs of wealth and social status: Abraham receives them from Egypt (12:16), and Abraham's servant uses camels for his long journey to Aram (24:10 and following). They also appear in tribulations: the Midianites take the camels of the Israelites during raids (Judges 6:5 and 7:12). Mosaic law classifies them among the unclean animals (Leviticus 11:4; Deuteronomy 14:7). In the time of the return from exile, camels are counted as community property (Ezra 2:67; Nehemiah 7:69). The prophets mention camels as symbols of distant trade or enemy wealth (Isaiah 21:7; Ezekiel 25:5).
H1581.portee: The camel reminds the biblical reader of the concrete reality of the ancient Middle Eastern world: the Bible speaks of people in their real context, with the animals, landscapes, and economy that are theirs. It is also a lesson on material wealth: it is recognized (Abraham, Job), but it is never presented as the supreme good. Finally, the mention of the camel as an unclean animal in the law shows us that God establishes a clear distinction between what can be used and what cannot, including for reasons of ritual purity.

sens: father of Ammiel, one of the twelve spies sent by Moses
H1582.detail: Gamaliel is the father of Ammiel, who was chosen as a representative of the tribe of Dan among the twelve men that Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:12). He appears only once in the Bible, named only because his son was one of the spies.
H1582.origine: The name Gamaliel literally means "camel driver" in Hebrew (from gamal, camel). It is a name that likely reflects the activity or profession of the father — perhaps he was a herder or camel driver — according to the Semitic custom of giving names derived from daily life.
H1582.emploi: Gamaliel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:12. The context is that of the exploration of Canaan: after the exodus from Egypt, Moses chooses twelve men, one from each tribe, to scout the land that God had promised to Israel. Ammiel, son of Gamaliel, was designated for the tribe of Dan. We know nothing more about Gamaliel himself or about the further history of Ammiel.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Manasseh during the exodus from Egypt
H1583.detail: Gamliel is a figure from the Old Testament, son of Pedahtsur, who played a prominent role in organizing the people of Israel in the desert. His name means "God's reward." He is designated as the prince (leader) of the tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 1:10), one of the large tribes descended from Joseph. In this capacity, he organizes the camp of his tribe alongside the others (Numbers 2:20), offers sacrifices during the consecration of the Tabernacle (Numbers 7:54-59), and leads his army during the march through the desert (Numbers 10:23). His name, which means "God's reward," reflects divine grace upon the chosen people.
H1583.origine: The name Gamliel comes from Hebrew and literally means "God's reward" or "God is my reward," composed of "gamal" (reward, retribution) and "El" (God). This type of theophoric name, containing the divine name, was common in Israel to express God's blessing and covenant with His people.
H1583.emploi: Gamliel appears five times in the Pentateuch, always in the book of Numbers, always alongside his father Pedahtsur and always in relation to his role as chief of Manasseh. He is first named during the census of the twelve tribes (Numbers 1:10), which organizes the people for conquest. He then appears in the arrangement of the camp (Numbers 2:20), where each tribe receives its place around the Tent of Meeting. His name reappears during the dedication of the Tabernacle (Numbers 7), where each prince offers sacrifices and gifts for the consecration. Finally, he is mentioned at the head of his army during the departure from the desert of Sinai (Numbers 10:23). Gamliel embodies order, continuity, and the commitment of God's people to His sanctuary.
H1583.portee: Gamliel illustrates the importance that God places on organization and responsibility within His people. As a tribal leader, he represents the authority that organizes, offers, and leads. His name, which means "God's reward," reminds the reader that all dignity and leadership are gifts from God, not personal conquests. His constant commitment to lead his people and participate in sacred rites shows how faith translates into community practice and devotion to God.

sens: To finish, to cease, to bring to completion
To exhaust, to completely make disappear
To fulfill, to successfully carry out an action on behalf of someone
H1584.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of finishing something, bringing it to completion. It conveys the idea of "putting an end to": in Psalm 7:10, the psalmist asks God to put an end to the wickedness of the evildoers, as one stops something that is flowing or progressing.
2. It can also mean "to exhaust," "to completely make disappear." In Psalm 77:9, it is asked whether God's goodness is exhausted, meaning if it has come to an end, like a spring that runs dry.
3. However, the word takes on a more active and benevolent nuance when it means "to accomplish" or "to fulfill on behalf of someone." In Psalm 138:8, God will accomplish His work for the one who prays: it is to complete an action that has been started, to bring it to a good conclusion for the benefit of someone.
H1584.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּמַר comes from a root that evokes the idea of completing, perfecting. It is close to the idea of fulfillment: transforming something unfinished into something finished. The Aramaic גְּמַר (gmar) carries the same meaning. The Hebrew verb retains this richness: to finish can mean both to destroy (to put an end to evil) and to perfect (to complete the work).
H1584.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Psalms. It denotes both the action that the psalmist asks God to take against his enemies — to finish their wickedness, to put an end to their opposition — and the anxious questioning about divine resources — could God's goodness be exhausted? — as well as the confidence that God will accomplish His work for the faithful. The contexts show that the word oscillates between two poles: the idea of cessation (something disappears, comes to an end) and the idea of accomplishment (something is brought to its beneficial conclusion).
H1584.portee: This word invites the Christian to believe that God never leaves His works unfinished. When one pleads with Him to put an end to evil, one acknowledges that God alone directs history. When one wonders if His goodness is exhausted, one learns to combat doubt: God's faithfulness has no end. And when one asserts that He will accomplish what He has begun for us, one touches the very heart of Christian hope — not by our strength, but by His certain completion.

sens: to complete a work, an action until its fulfillment
H1585.detail: 1. To complete means to bring a work to its perfection, to carry it through to its full term. The idea is one of finishing, of completeness achieved through action. In Ezra 7:12, the word denotes the fulfillment of a mission or project.
H1585.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root that fundamentally means "to finish" or "to complete." It is related to the idea of perfection and totality. In biblical Aramaic, this verb expresses the action of bringing something to a successful conclusion, leaving no part unfinished.
H1585.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 7:12, a text written in Aramaic. It describes the complete fulfillment of a task or decision. Its unique context shows its use in an official and solemn register, speaking of the faithful execution of a charge or mission.
H1585.portee: This word reminds the believer that God desires to see works accomplished with integrity and perfection. Completion is not just an end, but an accomplishment that honors the one who entrusted it.

sens: Eldest son of Japheth and grandson of Noah
Ancestor of the Cimmerian peoples and ancient Celtic branches
Unfaithful wife of the prophet Hosea
H1586G.detail:
1. Gomer is primarily a character from the Old Testament: the eldest son of Japheth, himself a son of Noah (Genesis 10:2). He has three known sons: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah (Genesis 10:3). This genealogy places him at the dawn of humanity, after the Flood.
2. According to ancient historical traditions, Gomer is considered the ancestor of the Cimmerian peoples and certain Celtic branches that settled in Northern and Western Europe. His descendants formed powerful nations, mentioned even in prophecies such as in Ezekiel 38:6, where Gomer and his troops are listed among the peoples who will rise up.
3. Gomer is also the name of the wife of the prophet Hosea (not mentioned in these specific uses, but this union was symbolic: God commanded Hosea to marry her to illustrate Israel's unfaithfulness to the Lord). This prophetic act showed how Israel, despite God's love, turned towards idolatry.
H1586G.origine: The name Gomer means "complete" or "the one who completes." This meaning reflects his role as the eldest son completing Japheth's lineage. The name appears in Noah's genealogy in Genesis 10, a foundational text in the biblical history of nations. Several members of his direct descendants bear names that themselves become historical peoples (Ashkenaz, Togarmah).
H1586G.emploi: Gomer appears five times in the Segond: twice in Genesis 10 (vv. 2-3) and twice in 1 Chronicles 1 (vv. 5-6), where he is listed among the sons of Japheth with his own sons. These genealogical passages place Gomer in the table of nations, establishing the kinship links of ancient peoples after the Flood. Ezekiel 38:6 mentions him prophetically, including him among the peoples who will rise against Israel in the last days. Although these uses only mention the genealogical Gomer, the Bible also identifies a Gomer as the wife of Hosea, whose story symbolizes God's judgment and grace towards unfaithful Israel.

sens: Unfaithful wife of the prophet Hosea
Woman whose story symbolizes Israel's unfaithfulness to God
H1586H.detail:
1. Gomer is the woman that God commands the prophet Hosea to marry (Hosea 1:3). She is presented as unfaithful: she conceives children of whom Hosea is not the father, causing a marital drama at the heart of the prophetic ministry.
2. Her story is not trivial: God asks Hosea to live this marital suffering to make it a living sign of the relationship between God and Israel. Just as Israel turned to other gods and betrayed the covenant, Gomer betrays her husband. The broken and restored relationship (Hosea will take Gomer back) foreshadows God's restoration towards His unfaithful people.
H1586H.origine: The name Gomer means "complete" or "perfect" in Hebrew. Gomer is also the name of the eldest son of Japheth (grandson of Noah), who gave his name to the ancient Cimmerian peoples. But here, in the book of Hosea, it refers to a historical woman whose life becomes the stage for a prophetic lesson on faithfulness and forgiveness.
H1586H.emploi: Gomer appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 1:3, where she is presented as the daughter of Diblaim and the wife that God commands Hosea to take. She is a singular character: not a heroine, not a virtuous one, but a woman called to live and embody the prophetic message. Hosea 1:3 simply states: "He went and took Gomer, the daughter of Diblaim. She conceived and bore him a son." This seemingly ordinary phrase introduces the marital drama that will be at the heart of Hosea's ministry and the key to the message of the book: God loves Israel despite its unfaithfulness.
H1586H.portee: The story of Gomer reveals a profound truth: God does not choose His instruments from the pure or the blameless, but from those who live and embody His compassion. The marriage of Hosea and Gomer becomes a living parable of God's heart for His unfaithful people. It reminds us that even in brokenness and unfaithfulness, God continues to love and desires restoration. It is a message of formidable grace.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi during the time of the divided monarchy
Son of Hilkiah, tasked with royal missions
