H1587G.detail: Guemaria is a little-mentioned biblical figure, known only from an appearance in Jeremiah 29:3. He was a man of the tribe of Levi who lived during the time when the kingdom was divided between Israel and Judah. He was the son of Hilkiah. His main role was to serve as an emissary: King Zedekiah sent him to Babylon, alongside Elasa (son of Shaphan), to deliver a letter from Jeremiah to the captive Jews. This mission shows that he enjoyed royal trust and held a fairly important position at the court of Judah.
H1587G.origine: The name Guemaria means "Jehovah has accomplished": it combines the idea of divine accomplishment (root "gamar") with the name of God ("Yah"). It is a typical theophoric name of the time, expressing confidence in God's completed action.
H1587G.emploi: Guemaria appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 29:3. He is presented as the son of the priest Hilkiah and as one of the two messengers sent by King Zedekiah of Judah to Babylon to deliver a letter from Jeremiah to the Jewish exiles. This mention in a diplomatic and religious context indicates that he belonged to the administrative and religious elite of Judah during this critical period of captivity.

sens: Noble Judean during the time of the divided kingdom
Son of the scribe Shaphan
Father of Micah
Man who defended the word of the Lord
H1587H.detail: Guémaria is a figure from the final days of the kingdom of Judah, before the exile to Babylon. He is the son of Shaphan, an important figure at the royal court (scribe or secretary to the king). Guémaria has a chamber in the temple of Jerusalem, which shows his high rank among the nobles of Judah (Jeremiah 36:10). It is in this chamber that the prophet Baruch publicly reads the scroll containing the words of the prophet Jeremiah before all the people. Guémaria is also the father of Micah, who hears these words and bravely reports them to the leaders of the kingdom (Jeremiah 36:11). Finally, Guémaria himself is among the nobles who attempt to prevent the king from burning the sacred scroll, showing his respect for the word of the Lord (Jeremiah 36:25).
H1587H.origine: His name means "The Lord has accomplished" in ancient Hebrew. Guémaria belonged to an influential family: his father Shaphan was a key figure in the royal administration, and his brother Ahikam also played an important political role.
H1587H.emploi: Guémaria appears in four passages in the book of Jeremiah, all in chapter 36, which recounts how the prophet Jeremiah has his words inscribed on a scroll and read publicly. The four mentions show Guémaria in three roles: first as the owner of a chamber in the temple from which his scroll is read (verse 10), then as the father of the young Micah who reports the words to the leaders (verse 11), then sitting among the nobles listening to these words (verse 12), and finally as one of the three men who plead with the king not to burn the scroll (verse 25).
H1587H.portee: The story of Guémaria reminds Christians that they are never alone in defending the word of God. In times of trial and opposition, men and women of sense and courage rise up to protect and transmit what God has said. Faith is often carried and preserved by chains of faithful witnesses.

sens: enclosed space planted with trees or plants
enclosure, defined and arranged land
H1588G.detail:
1. A garden is a cultivated space, surrounded and arranged, where plants are grown or where the dead are buried. The word primarily evokes the image of an organized and closed area. In 2 Kings 21:18, kings were buried in the garden of their house: it was an honor to rest in a private, sheltered, and recognizable place.
2. The word more broadly designates any defined and maintained space, an enclosure that is not just a simple field. In the time of the kings of Judah, owning a garden — especially a burial garden — marked the rank and wealth of a royal family.
H1588G.origine: The Hebrew word gan comes from a root meaning "to close, to surround." It refers to the idea of a protected and defined space, separated from the wild world. It is the same root that gives the word "gan-Eden," the "garden of Eden": the enclosed and ordered space that God created for man at the beginning of Genesis.
H1588G.emploi: The word appears only twice in these verses from Kings, both to designate the garden of Uzza, a private royal cemetery in Jerusalem. It is there that King Manasseh was buried (2 Kings 21:18) and his son Amon (2 Kings 21:26). The usage shows that the kings of Judah made a dignified burial in the lands adjacent to their palace, which was a mark of power and dynastic stability.
H1588G.portee: The garden reminds us that the dead, even kings, return to the earth. These royal burials in gardens show that death was accepted and ritualized: a decent and orderly place was prepared to welcome the deceased. For the Christian, this evokes the reality of death and the importance of respecting the bodies, while awaiting the promised resurrection.

sens: Cultivated land with trees, flowers, or vegetables
Enclosure or wooded area attached to a house
Figuratively, a place of delight or fertility
H1588H.detail:
1. The garden is primarily a piece of land where useful or ornamental plants are intentionally cultivated. It is a managed and maintained space, distinct from wild lands. In 2 Kings 9:27, "the house of the garden" (Beth-haggan) refers to a locality or place characterized by a domain with trees and plantations, a site where Ahaziah hoped to find refuge.
2. More broadly, the word evokes a fertile and protected enclosure, often associated with a dwelling or property: it is the ordered and productive space that the owner cultivates and enjoys.
3. In biblical thought, the garden symbolizes abundance, life, and rest — the garden of Eden being the supreme image.
H1588H.origine: The Hebrew word gan comes from a root meaning "to enclose" or "to protect," which reflects the idea of the garden as a defined and defended space. The garden is by nature a closed place, distinguished from the wild world — an ordered refuge. In the Old Testament, this term applies to both royal gardens and the paradise of Eden.
H1588H.emploi: The word gan appears rarely in the Bible. In 2 Kings 9:27, it appears in a place name "Beth-haggan" ("house of the garden"), a stop on King Ahaziah's flight. This context shows that the garden was a remarkable feature of the landscape: notable enough to give its name to a place. The usage underscores both the agrarian reality of the biblical world and the importance of tree crops in Judah.
H1588H.portee: The garden reminds the believer that God creates order, beauty, and abundance. It is a symbol of blessing and happy life. Meditating on the garden — this place that man must cultivate and keep — invites one to see their own role as a responsible steward of what God entrusts to them.

sens: Enclosed cultivated space with plants, fruit trees, or flowers
Fertile and well-watered land, an image of prosperity and blessing
The Garden of Eden, the original dwelling place of humanity created by God
Place of burial, particularly a garden adjacent to a house
(Fig.) The beloved or the spouse, compared to a closed and blooming garden
H1588M.detail:
1. The garden is primarily a defined and cultivated space where plants and trees are grown. It is a place of work and productivity: watering and harvesting take place there. In Egypt, gardens had to be artificially irrigated (Deuteronomy 11:10), unlike the promised land watered by rain.

2. Through its abundance and greenery, the garden becomes an image of a prosperous and blessed life. Isaiah 58:11 promises that one who fasts in faith will be "like a watered garden," an image of a heart continually revitalized by God.

3. The Garden of Eden is the garden planted by God Himself in Genesis 2:8, the wonderful place where He placed the created man. It symbolizes the lost paradise and the original bond between God and humanity.

4. In biblical times, gardens also served as family burial places, dug into rock or arranged on the property of the house, like that of Uzzah where King Manasseh was buried (2 Kings 21:18).

5. In the Song of Songs, the bride is a "closed garden" (4:12) and a "garden" where the beloved comes to gather its fruits (4:16), an image of the hidden and precious beauty of marital love.
H1588M.origine: The word הַן (gan) comes from an ancient Semitic root expressing the idea of enclosure or enclosure. The biblical garden was a *closed* space, defended, separated from the surrounding desert or steppe. This root is found in other Semitic languages with the meaning of shelter or protection. The Hebrew word emphasizes less the mere cultivation than the enclosed and defined character of the place — a haven of order and life amidst a wild world.
H1588M.emploi: The word appears 35 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis (the Garden of Eden is the foundational narrative), but also in Kings and the prophets. In historical accounts, royal gardens or burial gardens are mentioned. In the poetry of the Song of Songs, the garden becomes the dominant metaphor for the beloved woman: closed, secret, blooming, filled with exquisite perfumes. In the prophets, the garden reappears as a sign of hope (Isaiah 51:3, Jeremiah 31:12): when God restores His people, the desert becomes a garden again. This alternation between garden and desert organizes all the biblical symbolism of blessing and judgment.
H1588M.portee: The garden reminds us that God loves beauty, order, and abundant life. This is His original will for us. But the account of the fall also shows that we lost access to this paradise through sin. The prophets promise us that one day, God will restore what we have lost: the desert will become a garden again. Finally, the Song of Songs speaks to us of love and beauty in marriage as a reflection of what God wants to give to His creatures.

sens: To take someone else's property secretly
To remove or carry someone away secretly
To divert, to take out of sight
To act with cunning or deceit
H1589.detail:
1. To take someone else's property secretly: to steal, to appropriate what does not belong to you in secret. This is theft in the literal sense, condemned by the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:15). A man who steals an ox or a sheep must return it (Exodus 22:1), and one who steals a person to enslave them commits a serious crime (Exodus 21:16).
2. To remove or carry someone away secretly: to snatch someone from a perilous place by discreetly taking them away. Jehosheba took her little nephew Joash from among the other sons of the murdered king and thus removed him from the murderous queen (2 Chronicles 22:11).
3. To divert, to take out of sight: to camouflage, to hide something or someone to remove them from view. Rachel had stolen her father's idols without Jacob knowing (Genesis 31:32).
4. To act with cunning or deceit: to deceive or mislead through clever words. Jacob said to Laban: "You have deceived me" (stolen the truth) by giving me Leah instead of Rachel (Genesis 31:26).
H1589.origine: The Hebrew root ganav expresses the idea of taking secretly, of acting furtively. The word evokes the stealthy movement of the thief who slips away into the shadows. The Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament, translates it as kleptein (κλέπτειν), which has given rise to the French term "kleptomania."
H1589.emploi: This verb appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the accounts of Genesis (the matter of the idols and the goats with Laban), in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) where theft is prohibited and punished, and in biblical wisdom (Proverbs). It also appears in the prophets (Jeremiah, Hosea) to denounce Israel's transgressions. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: it can refer to material theft, the abduction of a person, or deception through words. In Proverbs 9:17, stealing water and bread means stealing one's pleasure (seducing through secrecy).
H1589.portee: This word reminds us that God protects the property of others and the dignity of each person. Theft in the Bible is never a trivial act: it transgresses the covenant and the order that God establishes. But the word also reveals the vigilance of the Lord: He knows how to detect hidden theft and can rescue someone from death — as He saved Joash. For the Christian, it is an invitation to honesty and trust that God provides without the need for subterfuge.

sens: one who takes someone else's property secretly or by force
one who commits theft, a robbery
figuratively, one who acts in secret or shamefully
image of shame and confusion
H1590.detail:
1. The thief is someone who seizes another's property: in Exodus 22:2, it is one who is caught "stealing" by breaking in, and the law provides for what happens if he dies during his theft. The word designates the concrete act of theft, the robbery.
2. It is also the person themselves, one who lives by plunder: in Proverbs 29:24, one who shares with a thief becomes his own enemy, for he makes himself an accomplice to the crime.
3. Figuratively, the thief becomes the image of one who acts dishonestly or disgracefully: in Jeremiah 2:26, the leaders of Israel are "ashamed like a thief when he is caught," meaning caught in their guilt.
4. The shame of the discovered thief represents the humiliation and confusion of one exposed in their sin.
H1590.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the action of appropriating furtively what does not belong to you. It literally designates one who steals, and is also used as a verb to mean "to steal" or "to take away." It is a simple and direct word, which does not hide anything of the guilt of the act.
H1590.emploi: The word appears about 17 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the laws (Exodus, Deuteronomy) and in biblical wisdom (Proverbs, Job). In Exodus 22, the law deals with the rights of the caught thief and his possible punishment. In Proverbs, the thief illustrates folly and dishonesty: associating with him is to lose oneself. In Jeremiah and the prophets, the confused thief becomes an image of the shame of the princes and prophets of Israel exposed in their unfaithfulness to God. The word shifts from the concrete meaning (one who steals goods) to the figurative meaning (one who acts with duplicity or moral dishonesty).
H1590.portee: The figure of the thief reminds the reader that God sees everything, even what is done in secret. It also shows that dishonesty is always discovered and brings confusion. For the believer, it is a call to righteousness and integrity, to refuse both material theft and spiritual theft — duplicity, deception, and bad faith in our relationships with God and our brothers.

sens: act of stealing, taking what belongs to someone else
stolen item, loot
H1591.detail:
1. Theft is the act of secretly or furtively taking what belongs to someone else. In Exodus 22:3, the Law speaks of "theft" as a transgression that engages the responsibility of the thief: if he is caught in the act at night and killed, the one who killed him is not guilty; if he survives, he must pay back the equivalent of what he took.
2. The word also designates the stolen object itself, what has been taken. In Exodus 22:4, if the "stolen" — an ox, a donkey, or a lamb — is still alive in the possession of the thief, he must return it double: the item itself plus its value as compensation for the harm done.
H1591.origine: The Hebrew word גְּנֵבָה (gneivah) comes from the root גנב (ganav), which means "to steal" or "to take away." This root expresses the action of taking secretly, in hiding. It is related to other Semitic words that denote theft or shoplifting. In the Law of Moses, it is a technical term used to describe this infraction against another's property.
H1591.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Exodus 22, at the heart of the restitution code. In Exodus 22:3, it designates the guilt of the thief who has committed theft; in Exodus 22:4, it designates the stolen object itself. These two usages show that biblical Law takes theft seriously: it demands not only restitution of the property but also additional compensation (double or more), depending on the circumstances and the nature of the object. The context is always legal and legislative.
H1591.portee: Theft is one of the fundamental moral transgressions recognized in the Law. The Law does not hesitate to prescribe restitution and even overcompensation: this teaches God's people that another's property is sacred, and that causing harm requires reparations far beyond mere balance. For the believer, this word reminds us that integrity regarding the property of others is not an option, but an obligation of justice based on respect for one's neighbor.

sens: son of King Hadad and an Egyptian princess
child raised in Pharaoh's court
H1592.detail:
1. Guenubath is the son of Hadad, an Edomite prince from the royal family, and an Egyptian princess, sister of Tahpenes, queen of Egypt at the end of David's reign. He embodies the political and dynastic alliances of the Old Testament — the mingling of Eastern and Egyptian powers.
2. From his birth, he is raised in Pharaoh's house, among the royal Egyptian children (1 Kings 11:20). His adoption by the Egyptian court makes him a foreign prince to his Edomite heritage, living a court life far from his homeland.
H1592.origine: The name Guenubath literally means "theft" or "that which is stolen" in Hebrew. This particular name likely reflects the circumstances of his birth — a hidden or secret son in a foreign court — or the nature of his existence in exile from his native land. It symbolizes the estrangement and family separation that marks his life.
H1592.emploi: Guenubath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 11:20. He is mentioned as the son that Hadad the Edomite had with the sister of Tahpenes, queen of Egypt. His story fits into the complex political context of Solomon's reign, where neighboring kingdoms, particularly Edom, seek to strengthen themselves through marital alliances with Egypt. Guenubath represents a future generation that could become a threat to the stability of the united kingdom of Israel.
H1592.portee: The story of Guenubath reminds us how political stakes and human alliances shape individual destinies, and how a child can be caught between two worlds. It also illustrates how God oversees the unfolding of global events despite the intrigues of nations.

sens: cultivated land with plants, fruit trees, or ornamental trees
green space and fertility, often near a water source
image of abundance, prosperity, and divine blessing
place of idolatrous practices and worship of false gods
H1593.detail:
1. The garden is primarily a cultivated area where one plants: houses, orchards, fruit trees (Ecclesiastes 2:5; Jeremiah 29:5). It is a space for food production, a material good to which one invests labor.
2. It is especially a place of greenery and life, often nourished by running water: the prophet compares Israel's prosperity to gardens near a river (Numbers 24:6), while a garden without water evokes infertility and desiccation (Isaiah 1:30). The image is that of an oasis.
3. The garden symbolizes blessing and abundance: God's justice and goodness cause flourishing gardens to grow (Isaiah 61:11). It is a sign of a prosperous and blessed life.
4. Ironically, the word also designates cursed places where the Israelites practice idolatry: sacrificing and burning incense in gardens means worshiping false gods (Isaiah 65:3; 66:17). The garden then becomes a symbol of seduction away from the true God.
H1593.origine: The Hebrew word גַּנָּה comes from a root that evokes the idea of enclosure and protection: a garden is a space that is surrounded, delimited, and cared for. This same root is found in other Hebrew words related to protection and enclosure. Thus, etymologically, the garden is a closed and controlled space, distinct from the desert or wild land.
H1593.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the wisdom books and among the prophets. It always designates a cultivated space, but its usage is tinted according to the context: in Ecclesiastes, it is a material and earthly good; in Jeremiah and Amos, it is a sign of a stable life (one plants gardens when one builds houses); in Isaiah, the garden becomes an image of messianic blessing or, conversely, a sign of religious degeneration when it becomes a place of idolatrous worship (Isaiah 65:3; 66:17). The spiritual context changes the tone of the word.
H1593.portee: The garden reminds us that God blesses the work of our hands and the cultivation of the earth. It is a call to stability, productivity, and stewardship: planting a garden means rooting oneself and contributing to community life. But the word also warns: when we cultivate gardens for false gods instead of honoring the living God, we lose true blessings. The garden can be a sign of spiritual prosperity or seduction away from God.

sens: enclosed space planted with trees and flowers, adjacent to a royal or noble residence
place of greenery and walking in a palace
H1594.detail:
1. The word designates a garden in the proper sense: a landscaped and planted area, generally close to a palace or an important house. In the book of Esther, the king of Persia has a garden adjacent to his royal palace where he can retreat; it is a place for walking and relaxation (Esther 7:7-8). In the Song of Solomon, the beloved descends to the walnut garden to admire the greenery and see if the vines and pomegranates are in bloom (Song of Solomon 6:11).
2. By extension, the garden is a place of relaxation and freshness, where the king can escape the tension of the feast and palace affairs. When the king rises in anger during the feast, he retreats to the palace garden to calm down (Esther 7:7).
H1594.origine: The Hebrew word גִּנָּה (ginnah) is a variant or doublet of גַּנָּה (gannah), both derived from the same root that evokes the idea of enclosing or protecting. The garden is thus a delimited, closed, and protected space, intended for cultivation and enjoyment. This root is found in other Hebrew words related to enclosure and separation.
H1594.emploi: The word appears only 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the book of Esther (3 times) and in the Song of Solomon (1 time). In Esther, it refers to the garden of the royal palace of Susa, a prestigious and calm place where the king can retreat. In the Song of Solomon, it is a natural garden planted with walnuts, vines, and pomegranates, symbolizing a place of beauty and fertility. The context is always that of a privileged and aesthetically appreciated space.
H1594.portee: The garden reminds us that the beauty created by God inspires contemplation and rest. In contrast to the chaos of palace affairs, the garden offers a refuge of calm and greenery. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize the beauty of the natural world and to seek moments of peace in the presence of God's work.

sens: Chest or container intended to hold valuable objects
Place where the goods and riches of a king or a city are stored
Accumulated wealth or treasure in the sense of precious goods
H1595.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a chest, a closed container where precious things are kept — like richly embroidered cloaks tied with cords and stored in cedar chests as seen in Ezekiel 27:24. It is the image of a box that is filled and closed.
2. It then extends to the place, the building where wealth is accumulated: the royal treasury. In Esther 3:9 and 4:7, it refers to the king's treasury, the place where revenues, taxes, tributes converge — in our case, the enormous sum that Haman proposes to pay to finance the massacre of the Jews.
3. By extension, the word can mean the wealth itself, the money and goods that are kept there — the talents of silver mentioned in Esther 3:9.
H1595.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of keeping, preserving, hiding. This is why it means a chest or a closed place where one puts away what one wants to protect. Contemporary Aramaic uses the related word "gnaz" (גְּנַז) with the same meaning of treasure or hidden thing. This root reflects the idea that what is precious must be kept safe, hidden from the sight of thieves.
H1595.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the context of royal goods. In Esther, it refers twice to the treasure of the Persian king, the place where the promised fortune by Haman should end up: it is a political and administrative treasure, linked to power and state money. In the same verse in Esther, one can also refer to chests as physical containers. In Ezekiel 27, the word appears speaking of merchant chests filled with fine fabrics: here, it is a commercial treasure, carried by ships, a symbol of wealth and prosperous trade. The meaning varies slightly: sometimes the container, sometimes the place, sometimes the very idea of guarded wealth.
H1595.portee: This word reminds the reader that human riches, no matter how precious they are when locked away in chests or palaces, can be at the heart of the most malevolent intentions — Haman uses access to the royal treasury to corrupt the king and perpetrate genocide. This invites reflection on the true treasure: not money and material goods, but what lasts eternally.

sens: Building or place where the riches of a king or a state are stored
Collection of goods, reserves accumulated and kept in this place
H1596.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a building, a house intended to store royal wealth: in Ezra 5:17 and 6:1, it speaks of "the house of the treasures of the king" in Babylon, as one would for a depot or a fortress filled with provisions and precious metals. It is a controlled, official place where power centralizes its resources.

2. By extension, the word also refers to the wealth itself, the contents of this place: in Ezra 7:20, "to draw from the house of the treasures of the king" means to take the money or goods that are stored there to meet the needs of God's temple. The treasure, therefore, is what has value and is accumulated with care.
H1596.origine: This Aramaic word is related to the Hebrew ge.nez (גְּנָז) which has the same root and meaning. The word belongs to the administrative and official language of the Persian empire: it describes a well-known concept in ancient kingdoms, that of the king's house where the resources of the state are centralized. The root evokes the idea of putting aside, keeping precious things.
H1596.emploi: The word appears three times in the book of Ezra, all verses dating from the Persian period when the temple of Jerusalem was being rebuilt. In Ezra 5:17 and 6:1, it specifically refers to the royal archive or depot in Babylon, where official documents were consulted and where the king's goods were kept. In Ezra 7:20, it is King Artaxerxes who authorizes the scribe Ezra to draw from the royal treasury to finance offerings and expenses for the temple. In all cases, the word is used in a technical and administrative manner: it refers to official wealth, controlled by power, stored in a safe place.
H1596.portee: This word reminds us that even during exile and oppression, God provided for the reconstruction of His temple by moving the hearts of kings to contribute. The riches of the powers of the world, no matter how well guarded they are, remain at the disposal of those who fear God. It is a lesson in trust: God directs the decisions of kings and can lead them to support His work.

sens: Building or place where the riches of a king or a temple are kept
Reserve of precious goods accumulated and protected
Collection of material resources of a state or an institution
H1597.detail:
1. The treasure is primarily a physical building, a chamber or a set of rooms intended to store and protect the riches of the king or the sanctuary. When David hands over to Solomon the plans for the future temple, he shows him notably the model of the treasure (1 Chronicles 28:11): it is a construction as important as the porch or the chambers of the mercy seat, as it houses the gifts, gold, and silver that the people bring to God.
2. By extension, the word refers to the wealth itself that is accumulated there: the precious resources, gold, silver, and valuable objects that a sovereign or a temple gathers and uses to govern, make sacrifices, or honor God.
H1597.origine: The Hebrew word גַּנְזַךְ (ginzakh) is borrowed from Persian and ancient Babylonian (ganzu, meaning "treasure"). This borrowing is explained by the historical context: after the exile of Judah to Babylon (586 B.C.), the administrative and court vocabulary of the Middle East penetrated the Hebrew language. Words from the same family all refer to the accumulation and management of goods.
H1597.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 28:11, where David enumerates to Solomon the different parts of the temple he has planned. It appears alongside terms describing the architecture of the sanctuary (porches, inner chambers), which shows that the temple's treasure was a major architectural structure, central to the religious and economic organization of Israel. Its unique and late occurrence (Chronicles dates from the Persian or near-Persian period) marks the influence of Eastern administration on the religious and civil vocabulary of post-exilic Judaism.
H1597.portee: The treasure reminds us that God approves of the wise and orderly administration of goods, both at the royal and religious levels. Seeing the temple's treasure among the divine plans for the sanctuary invites the reader to recognize that material resources, far from being secular, are part of the just order that God establishes. This aligns with Christ's teaching on the faithful management of the talents and riches entrusted by God.

sens: Defend someone or something against danger or attack
Surround with protection, like a covering or a rampart
Spare, preserve from destruction
Watch over someone with vigilance and tenderness
H1598.detail:
1. To protect primarily means to actively defend: it is to intervene to stop or repel a threat. God says to Hezekiah: "I will protect this city to save it" (2 Kings 19:34), meaning He will personally defend it against the king of Assyria.

2. The word also evokes the image of a covering that envelops and shelters. In Isaiah 31:5, God "spreads His protection over Jerusalem like birds spreading their wings over their brood": a tender and vigilant action that completely surrounds.

3. To protect also means to spare someone from ruin: "I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria; I will protect this city" (2 Kings 20:6). God not only defends but prevents destruction.

4. The word also carries the meaning of attentive guarding, of constant vigilance: the Lord of hosts "will protect" Israel (Zechariah 9:15), meaning He will watch over it with a guardian's vigilance.
H1598.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּנַן (ganan) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering and surrounding. Its primary image is that of enveloping protection, like a wing or a shield that wraps around the one being protected. The word is related to the idea of a garden (gan) — a fenced and protected space. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this verb is often rendered by Greek words meaning "to keep" or "to cover," which carry the same nuance of benevolent vigilance.
H1598.emploi: The verb גָּנַן is primarily used in prophetic passages where God promises to protect Jerusalem or Israel. It appears 7 times in the Segond, mainly in 2 Kings (three times: 19:34, 20:6) and in Isaiah (three times: 31:5, 37:35, 38:6), as well as once in Zechariah (9:15). The contexts are marked by threat: Assyrian invasions, diseases, wars. Each time, God personally commits: He will not protect Jerusalem merely as a city, but because of His covenant with David and for His own honor. The verb emphasizes active and determined protection, not just a simple benevolent presence.
H1598.portee: This word teaches the believer that God is not distant but vigilant and protective. When we read that God "will protect" a city, it is an invitation to trust in His faithfulness: He spreads out like a mother covering her young, and He will not allow His purposes to be thwarted. For us today, this reminds us that our security is not primarily in our strength or our walls, but in the vigilance of a personal and committed God.

sens: Priest returned from exile with Zerubbabel
Signatory of the covenant made under Nehemiah
H1599.detail:
1. Guinnethon is a priest who was part of the group of exiles returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple. His name appears in the official lists of those who participated in this restoration (Nehemiah 12:4).
2. He is among the priests and elders of Israel who signed the solemn covenant made under Nehemiah, a collective commitment to observe the Law of God (Nehemiah 10:6). This act demonstrated the commitment of the restored people to live according to divine will.
H1599.origine: The name Guinnethon means "gardener" or "one who cultivates the garden" (from the root gannen). It is a meaningful name that evokes the idea of cultivating, nurturing, making grow — an appropriate image for a priest called to cultivate the spiritual life of the people.
H1599.emploi: Guinnethon is mentioned three times in the book of Nehemiah, in chapters 10 and 12. In Nehemiah 10:6, he is listed among the priests and leaders of the people who seal the solemn covenant of restoration after the return from exile. The same person reappears in Nehemiah 12:4 in a list of priests returning with Zerubbabel, and in Nehemiah 12:16, where he is mentioned in the context of subsequent generations of priests. These three occurrences present him as an important figure in the community of the restored.
